#5494. Talkdesk’s life sciences play shows why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.

Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.

Talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the company introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.

That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.

The new offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.

The platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.

One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.

“A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” said Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because quickly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”

Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.

Talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller company cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.

What it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.

The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.

In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.

The industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.

“We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he said. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”

The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving issues across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.

That is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.

Each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.

This is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.

The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.

For life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.

For buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.

For Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5493. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5492. Alex Vidal to oversee REMAX Canada as company clarifies remit

REMAX said its president role has always included oversight of Canada, confirming Alex Vidal also leads REMAX Canada. Don Kottick, president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15.  AI Summary

Not only is Alex Vidal the new president of REMAX, but the company has clarified that his appointment to this position also encompasses REMAX Canada, making him the leader of REMAX’s Canadian operation.

Vidal was named president of REMAX in September, after The Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of REMAX, forming the Real REMAX Group.

In an emailed statement, a REMAX spokesperson told HousingWire that the president of REMAX has always overseen the company’s Canadian operation.

As Vidal moves into the Canadian leadership position, Don Kottick, who has served as the president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, has announced plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15. This information was conveyed to REMAX brokers and franchisees via an internal memo reviewed and confirmed by HousingWire.

“This move helps ensure every REMAX region around the world receives as much of the same focus, momentum and opportunities as possible,” the internal memo stated. “The next few months will be pivotal as we roll out new technology and invest in further strengthening the REMAX brand in Canada and around the world.”

Prior to joining REMAX, Kottick was the president and CEO of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada.

Before joining REMAX, Vidal served as the president of ERA Real Estate, helping lead the brand through Compass International Holdings’s acquisition of its parent company Anywhere Real Estate. Compass and ERA are currently suing Vidal, claiming that he violated non-compete agreements through his move to REMAX. In the legal complaint filed in mid-October, Compass claims that the non-compete agreement prevents Vidal from serving as president or providing service to any competing business for a period of one year from his departure from ERA.

#5491. Nasdaq Drops 2.5% for a Third Straight Loss as AI Hardware Stocks Slide

NEW YORK, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- USA News Group News Commentary - Stocks tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure led Wall Street lower on Monday. The S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.49% to 24,509.76 on Monday, according to CNBC's closing report. It was the third consecutive losing day for both indexes, and Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX, rose 19%, according to CNN. The long-term demand picture remains large: Grand View Research, in a report released on PR Newswire, puts the AI data center market at USD 147.3 billion in 2025 and forecasts USD 810.6 billion by 2033, a 23.9% compound annual growth rate. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO), CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV), GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE: GEV), Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC).

Policy added to the day's news. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on Monday addressing remote access to advanced computing chips and servers, designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries. Under the rule, licenses are required to export, reexport or transfer advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

Rates offered some relief. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.13% from 5.15% on Friday as lower oil prices reduced inflation pressure, according to the Associated Press. Investors are also heading into a week that includes a closely watched chipmaker earnings report on Tuesday.

In other industry developments and happenings in the market this week include:

Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO) fell 3.9%, its second straight loss, according to the Associated Press. In its most recent quarterly report, released September 2, 2026, Broadcom reported third quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $29.6 billion, up 86% from the prior year period, and guided fourth quarter revenue to approximately $34.8 billion, an increase of 93% from the prior year period.

The company has said it will report its fourth quarter and fiscal year 2026 results after the close of the U.S. trading session on Wednesday, December 9, 2026.

CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV), which rents access to AI computing power over the cloud, fell 6.1%, according to the Associated Press. On November 10, CoreWeave reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% from a year earlier, and a revenue backlog of approximately $132.5 billion at September 30, up from approximately $104 billion at the end of June.

The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion. It also reported a third quarter net loss of $709 million, compared with a net loss of $110 million a year earlier.

GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE: GEV), which helps power AI data centers, fell 4.9%, according to the Associated Press. In its third quarter 2026 results, GE Vernova reported orders of $29 billion, up 96% organically, and backlog growth of $20 billion sequentially to $197 billion in total.

Third quarter revenue was $12.6 billion, up 27%, and the company raised its 2026 guidance, increased its share repurchase authorization and announced an agreement to acquire Trench Group, a high-voltage grid equipment company.

Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC) fell roughly 7% as selling spread across semiconductor stocks, according to CNN. In its third quarter 2026 results, Intel reported revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year over year, with Data Center and AI revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78%.

The company forecast fourth quarter 2026 revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion. Intel's CFO said the company sees the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year.

#5490. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5489. Villa hires former Century Communities CFO Messenger as CEO

Villa has named homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO to lead the offsite homebuilder’s next growth phase. Villa says its integrated offsite model, which has delivered more than 425 homes since 2019, positions it to support larger communities. The move signals a push toward disciplined, community-scale growth and deeper partnerships with institutional housing players.  AI Summary

Villa, a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company announced on Monday.

Founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods. The company manages feasibility, design, permitting, site preparation and installation, and partners with a network of factories for production, according to the announcement.

Messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities. During his tenure, Century expanded from about 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states, grew to $4.5 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,000 annual closings, completed seven acquisitions and raised more than $3 billion in debt and equity capital, the company said.

He also led Century’s initial public offering and helped launch its mortgage, title and insurance subsidiaries, giving him direct experience with the vertically integrated models many large homebuilders use to manage costs and capture more of the housing value chain. Earlier in his career, Messenger spent roughly a decade at UDR, a publicly traded multifamily real estate investment trust, where he advanced through senior finance roles to become CFO.

Messenger’s appointment comes as Villa looks to expand beyond individual ADUs and small projects into larger communities in partnership with land developers and homebuilders. The company is already working on new neighborhoods including the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado, and homes in Altadena, California, for families rebuilding after the Eaton Fire, according to the release.

Investors say his background in scaling a public homebuilder and in capital markets was a key factor in the decision.

“Villa has demonstrated its capabilities across ADUs, multifamily properties and new neighborhoods, and Dave is the right leader to build on Villa’s success and advance its growth strategy,” said Aaron Marsh, partner and CFO at Unless, an investor in Villa and member of Villa’s board of directors. “He brings deep housing experience, a track record of scaling businesses nationally and a clear understanding of what land and development partners need to move projects forward.”

Messenger said he sees an opportunity to apply processes from large-scale homebuilding to Villa’s offsite platform.

“This team has done what much of our industry has only talked about: delivering quality homes through offsite construction across individual properties, multifamily communities and new neighborhoods,” Messenger said in the announcement. “I see great potential to build on that foundation by bringing a large-scale homebuilder’s operating discipline to Villa, with an emphasis on predictable execution and profitable growth.”

Villa’s model aims to give homeowners, multifamily operators and developers a single partner from concept through completion. The company handles site feasibility, site and home design, permitting and on-site work and uses factory partners to build homes offsite, aiming for more predictable timelines and costs than traditional stick-built construction, according to the release.

“Dave has an exceptional track record spanning homebuilding, multifamily real estate, capital markets and land development,” said Heather Miksch, chief operating officer at Villa. “As we build on Villa’s momentum and pursue development opportunities, his experience will be invaluable in helping us grow our business while continuing to serve both homeowners and development partners.”

#5487. Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales

Land & Buildings sent an open letter to Invitation Homes shareholders arguing the single-family rental REIT trades about 40% below the value of its homes and has underperformed major benchmarks for years. The activist investor is urging the company to sell homes individually at retail prices and commit to returning at least $2 billion a year to shareholders via buybacks or special dividends, while sharply reducing acquisitions and development. The clash could reshape capital allocation strategies in the institutional single-family rental sector and, if the plan gains traction, would push more homes from rental portfolios into the for-sale market.  AI Summary

Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses.

In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap.

Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets.

Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire.

The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home.

“REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter.

“Invitation Homes’ Board of Directors and management team are committed to acting in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders to deliver long-term, sustainable value,” says a prepared statement from the company. “Our focus is on strengthening our foundation and enhancing the resident experience that sets us apart. This focus has resulted in solid operational and financial performance in recent quarters, supported by consistent demand, strong retention, and continued execution across our core markets.”

“We are always open to hearing and considering the perspectives of our shareholders. Members of our Board and management team have had numerous discussions with Land & Buildings over the past several months to better understand its views, as we would with any shareholder. While we are disappointed that Land & Buildings has chosen to make its issues public at this time, we remain open to further engagement.”

Land & Buildings has highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter said.

Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb.

The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter.

Land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm said.

The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm.

“This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said.

The activist laid out a three-part plan it says could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value:

Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value.

The letter criticized what Land & Buildings characterized as incremental steps by Invitation Homes, including recent home sales and share repurchases, arguing those moves have not been sized or communicated in a way that would change how investors value the company.

“Half measures appear to be this Board’s modus operandi: do just enough to relieve pressure while preserving the status quo,” the firm wrote.

Land & Buildings also objected to the board’s Nov. 11 appointment of Colin Connolly, CEO of office REIT Cousins Properties, as a new director. The firm said the board had previously told it that refreshment was not needed and argued that adding another sitting REIT chief executive provided “duplicative skill sets” rather than shareholder alignment and capital allocation expertise.

The activist said independent research firm Green Street wrote less than a year ago that Invitation Homes should “shrink its portfolio, return capital to shareholders, and redirect the bulk of its energy internally on operations until its valuation improves.” Land & Buildings said it had urged management to outline a clear, multi-year capital return plan at REIT conferences in September but came away with “little more than lip service.”

Invitation Homes did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter or the firm’s proposals. The company has previously defended its strategy of balancing internal growth, acquisitions and select dispositions as it manages a large, geographically diverse portfolio in a tight housing market.

The campaign underscores how corporate decisions at large institutional single-family landlords can influence for-sale and rental supply in already constrained markets. Land & Buildings’ proposal would require Invitation Homes to sell thousands of homes a year to owner-occupiers or directly to existing tenants at retail pricing.

For homebuilders and real estate agents, a large program of individual home sales by Invitation Homes could add incremental existing-home inventory in high-demand metros where resale listings remain scarce. The suggested 6% down-payment rebate for tenants could create a new pipeline of first-time buyers but might also draw scrutiny from policymakers and tenant advocates who have criticized investor ownership of single-family homes.

For other single-family rental REITs and institutional owners, the dispute highlights growing pressure from investors to prioritize buybacks and capital returns over portfolio growth when shares trade at discounts to estimated property values. If Invitation Homes embraced or was forced into a multi-year shrink-to-grow strategy, it could reset expectations for capital allocation across the sector.

Land & Buildings said it prefers to work “constructively” with Invitation Homes but “will not hesitate to take whatever steps we believe are necessary to maximize value,” a signal that a proxy fight or board challenge is on the table heading into the 2027 proxy season.

#5486. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5485. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit 2026

AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in. Knowledge graphs could consolidate the enterprise context currently fed to different AI agents into a single knowledge layer.

Developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts. But without a central source of truth, they must repeat that work every time they build a new agent, rather than drawing on a shared knowledge layer, according to Jesús Barrasa (pictured), field chief technology officer of gen AI at Neo4j Inc.

“This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he said during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”

During interviews at GraphSummit, theCUBE Research’s John Furrier spoke with industry experts from Collibra BV, Blitzy Inc., Raymond James Financial Inc., and Qiagen N.V., among others. They discussed how knowledge graphs can ground AI agents in shared, traceable enterprise knowledge to improve explainability, enable safer coding at scale, support drug discovery and transform business operations. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jesús Barrasa:

Governance is a key question for enterprise AI deployments. How do you ensure AI agents behave appropriately as they become more autonomous? Judgment calls that used to be made by people now need to be made by agents in seconds, requiring a shift toward runtime governance, according to Felix Van de Maele, chief executive officer and co-founder of Collibra BV.

Collibra has introduced several capabilities – Live Map, Maestro, Guardian Agents and Agent Contracts – built on Neo4j’s graph database. Together, they form a control system that helps businesses make sure their AI agents use the right information and follow the rules.

“The challenge is: how do you govern at the speed of AI, which is different than the way we had to govern five years ago?” Van de Maele told theCUBE. “Maestro gives our customers the ability to build these governance steward agents that automate up to 80% of the governance work. You’re able to govern quickly and efficiently enough to keep up with the demands of new AI workloads.”

Other solutions, such as Agent Contracts, focus on enforcing boundaries around AI agents’ behavior. They monitor agents’ actions and block those that violate predefined rules, helping prevent unauthorized actions, according to Van de Maele.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Felix Van de Maele:

Changing one small piece of software can unexpectedly break something somewhere else. For Blitzy Inc., which runs thousands of AI coding agents at once to help businesses make large-scale system changes, a knowledge graph can map dependencies and the risks of change within a system.

A knowledge graph gives agents the context they need to make changes safely without being overwhelmed by millions of lines of code, according to Neeraj Deshmukh, director of engineering at Blitzy. The company also uses human-approved action plans and automated testing to keep the coding process on track.

“On top of that, we have agents who are watching other agents to make sure that they abide by the spec, the plan that we had created and approved by the human in the loop,” Deshmukh told theCUBE. “That ensures that there is no drift or hallucination.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Neeraj Deshmukh:

A knowledge graph helps Raymond James Financial Inc. put AI agents to work on data from established sources, according to Naveen Mahankali, vice president of technology at Raymond James.

We have golden sources; we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” he told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j, and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”

Raymond James is also exploring how AI agents can help financial advisors serve clients more efficiently. The company has already launched Raimond, its proprietary AI assistant, explained Jeff Griffith, vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James, who joined Mahankali during the interview.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people — how everyone — works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jeff Griffith and Naveen Mahankali:

#5484. Olight's ArkTac Series Sets a New Reservation Record Ahead of Its November 19 Launch

The tactical flashlight series goes on sale after a record 80,000-plus reservations, the most in Olight's history.

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Olight, a global portable lighting brand, today announced that its ArkTac tactical flashlight series will go on sale November 19 at 12:00 a.m. Pacific Standard Time (PST). Since its September debut, the series has drawn more than 80,000 reservations worldwide, a new record for Olight. Joining ArkTac this holiday season are the V8 smart charging system, Perun work lights, and new ArkPro and Oclip 2 Pro colorways, bringing dependable performance and practical gift options to Black Friday and beyond.

ArkTac Series: Flagship Performance, Ready for the Moment

Built for fast response and dependable performance, the ArkTac Series brings intuitive controls and versatile lighting into one slim, flat flashlight.

Its dual control zones offer immediate response at the tail and more lighting options at the front. A light press of the dual-stage Main Tail Switch activates Pure Flood; a firm press delivers Turbo Spotlight. The dedicated CommandPoint button offers instant access to Strobe or a customizable light source, keeping essential functions at users' fingertips.

At the front, a rotary selector makes switching between lighting modes easy. The ArkTac combines Spotlight, Pure Flood, Red Light and UV, while the ArkTac Ultra adds a side-mounted Green Laser, bringing five light sources into one compact tool. Both models feature a ToF sensor to help prevent accidental pocket activation.

Durability is equally central. The ArkTac Ultra features Olight's second-generation OALÂ² aluminum alloy, with 1.86 times the hardness of standard 6061 aluminum, and the series adds silicon nitride ceramic beads to its strike bezel for emergency window-breaking.

For a complete setup, the ArkTac Ultra Premium Kit includes the ArkSnap magnetic holster, a vehicle charging mount and other accessories for secure carry and quick charging. From demanding shifts to outdoor adventures, ArkTac delivers the versatility and reliability users can count on, day after day.

V8 Smart Charging System: Smarter Power for the Holidays and Beyond

The V8 and V8 Pro offer smart, eight-slot charging for OLi-ion rechargeable AA and AAA batteries in a compact, pocket-ready design. Each battery's built-in Smart BMS shares real-time data with the charger, enabling adaptive charging and improved thermal management. The V8 Pro adds a full-color display showing charge levels, battery health and cycle counts, plus support for standard NiMH batteries. With stable 1.5V output and over 1,000 recharge cycles, OLi-ion batteries help reduce replacements and disposable-battery waste beyond the holidays.

Perun Series: Reliable Lighting for Those Who Get the Job Done

From equipment inspections to overnight maintenance, the new Perun X and Perun Ultra right-angle headlamps keep light where the work happens. Both use a glass optical lens with up to 90% light-output efficiency, combining Spotlight, Pure Flood and Red Light in one system, with a Spot + Flood mode for near and far at once. Head-worn, handheld and magnetic mounting let the lights adapt as the job changes, while a wider, breathable 35 mm headband adds comfort over long shifts. The Perun Ultra's DialFit system allows quick, precise fitting.

ArkPro and Oclip 2 Pro: Fresh Looks for Everyday Carry

The best-selling ArkPro flat flashlight introduces Mech Green, pairing fluorescent green with matte black for a bold, industrial look that is also easier to spot in dim garages or cluttered workspaces. The Oclip 2 Pro adds matching Mech Green and Nebula Violet, the latter's deep purple finish given extra dimension by intricate textures and shifting reflections.

ArkPro Mech Green and the new Oclip 2 Pro colorways are available November 16, priced at $99.99 and $54.99 respectively. The ArkTac Series, V8 charging kits, and Perun Series go on sale November 19 at 12:00 a.m. PST, with U.S. starting prices of $119.99, $46.99 and $89.99 respectively.

Olight's Black Friday event runs from November 19 at 12:00 a.m. through November 30 at 11:59 p.m. PST, with up to 50% off select products, complimentary laser engraving, and special gift offers. Discounts do not apply to the new ArkTac, V8 and Perun series or the featured ArkPro and Oclip 2 Pro colorways. Pricing, availability and promotions may vary by region. Explore Olight's Black Friday offers.

Since 2007, Olight has innovated the way portable lighting can be used across everyday carry (EDC), outdoor, home, security and professional applications. Olight holds over 1,200 patents, and its products have earned international recognition, including the Red Dot Design Award and iF Design Award. Today, Olight's products are available in over 100 countries and regions, and the brand operates the world's first flashlight experience store in Las Vegas.

#5483. Ackman says Trump can still end GSE conservatorships, relist this term

Bill Ackman and Pershing Square CIO Ryan Israel argue in a shareholder letter that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can exit their 18-year conservatorship and relist on the NYSE during the remainder of President Trump’s second term using executive authority, without Congress.  AI Summary

Bill Ackman still believes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can be relisted on the New York Stock Exchange and exit their conservatorships before the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, even after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections.

In a letter to Pershing Square Holdings shareholders signed in early November, Ackman, the company’s founder and CEO, and chief investment officer Ryan Israel wrote that “a relisting and release from conservatorship can be accomplished by the President using his executive authority without any involvement of Congress.”

They argue that the administration has a political incentive to act before 2029 to avoid “handing control” of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) to a future administration, given the influence they have over housing policy.

Ackman and Israel said the GSEs can be released “in a manner that maintains and enhances mortgage affordability while maximizing the long-term value of American taxpayers’ 79.9% ownership of the two companies.” The Department of the Treasury holds warrants to acquire 79.9% of each enterprise’s common stock.

Pershing first detailed a road map in November 2025. The plan begins with a new agreement between the Treasury and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) that addresses repayment or restructuring of Treasury’s senior preferred stock. The next step would be for the Treasury to exercise its warrants to purchase 79.9% of the GSEs’ common shares. The final step would be FHFA approval for the GSEs to relist on the NYSE as privately owned operating companies.

“The relisting and release of F2 will be one of the few major pieces of economic policy the President can still achieve after the midterms,” Ackman and Israel wrote. “We believe that there is no credible alternative to F2 exiting conservatorship and relisting on the NYSE as private-sector-owned operating companies.”

The memo also says Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has indicated the administration will focus on the GSEs and their future ownership status in 2027 and 2028.

Fannie and Freddie have been in conservatorship for 18 years. According to the Pershing memo, they now have more than $200 billion of shareholder equity. Over the past decade, average annual credit losses have been “only 0.05%,” and current capital levels are described as roughly 50 times that loss rate.Ackman and Israel estimate that combined capital could grow to more than $375 billion over the next five years, or more than 4% of the mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by the enterprises.

On valuation, the memo says the GSEs currently trade at about 1.5 times their earnings. From Trump’s election through the end of last year, when talk of a relisting was more active, their share prices rose by about eight times. This year, by contrast, their share prices have fallen more than 60% as the administration has remained “silent” on the issue, the investors said.

Pershing Square is heavily exposed to the outcome. The fund holds about 99 million shares of Fannie Mae, with a market value of roughly $422.5 million, along with roughly 95 million shares of Freddie Mac valued at about $386.9 million, according to the memo.

#5481. Infill outlier Thomas James Homes ‘landmaxxes’ lots with ADUs

TJH leverages attached ADU options across Seattle area floor plans to increase usable square footage on small lots. The company points to state legislation allowing 2 ADUs per lot and local treatment of ADUs as 2 units that can increase allowable floor area.  AI Summary

Where new construction is scarce and lots are tight, luxury homebuilder Thomas James Homes (TJH) has pivoted to offering accessory dwelling units (ADUs) to entice its homebuyers by adding more square footage on parcels with little room to spare.

For the firm’s Pacific Northwest division, which operates in Seattle and nearby suburbs where lots are small and space is at a premium, the approach is a natural fit. While detached ADUs are the more common use case nationwide, TJH’s PNW division uses attached ADUs because they offer cost efficiencies and add functional living space to small infill lots without sacrificing as much yard.

Most TJH floorplans in the region, which typically sell for $2 million to $5 million, include an attached ADU option, according to PNW division president Adam Rohde. More than half of buyers choose to include one.

Founded in 2006, TJH is a high-end, scattered-lot homebuilder that operates in California, Washington and Arizona. The company specializes in building replacement homes on individual lots in established neighborhoods where new construction is limited, either on homeowner-owned lots or through spec home sales. The goal is to bring the efficiency and predictability of production building to the infill market.

ADUs, which TJH began incorporating into more floor plans around 2022 or 2023, nest within that strategy by helping owners get more out of limited space, a trend the builder calls “landmaxxing.” Luxury buyers increasingly want flex space, and as Washington has passed stronger ADU laws allowing more density, TJH has used the new rules to fit more square footage on its buyers’ lots.

For builders operating in dense urban and suburban markets, TJH’s playbook offers a case study in making every square foot of a lot count.

“It’s our job to work with buyers to figure out how to best maximize the building value on their land,” Rohde said in an interview. “Our view of ADUs is that it’s a great way to expand the amount of home you can build, which, in and of itself, is a good proposition.”

TJH’s ADU strategy varies by division and market. While other divisions build detached ADUs, the PNW division favors attached units, which function as independent living spaces connected to the main house or built within it.

Buyers use the extra space in varying ways, from a home office or gym to bonus square footage, a rental unit or a place for multigenerational living.

According to Rohde, attached or integrated ADUs make more sense than detached ADUs for two main reasons.

First, the company builds on smaller infill lots with limited outdoor space. A detached ADU cuts into that space more than an attached alternative.

“We’re typically acquiring lots that…already have limited yard space. So, to put a detached unit in, you’re then eating further into that ability to create a very livable yard,” Rohde explained.

Second, attached ADUs share walls with the primary residence, which reduces the amount of additional construction required. Unlike detached units, they don’t require a completely separate structure, additional siding or separate utility connections. That creates efficiencies and makes them more cost-effective, with a better return on investment.

“With the integrated system, you’re already having some shared wall space, so you’re already getting some economies of scale and efficiency that make it a lot more cost-effective than the detached-style units,” he explained.

Still, that efficiency doesn’t make ADUs a simple project, and Rohde argued against the notion that they are an easy add-on, particularly detached units.

“There’s this perception in the market, especially when the new regulations were hitting to allow the expansion of detached ADUs in particular, that, ‘Hey, it’s really easy. You just pick up a module, plop it in your backyard, and presto, you have additional living space,’” he said. “The reality is, it’s just frankly not that simple.”

He pointed to several reasons why ADUs can be challenging to build, including fire separation and building codes, utility connections, site access and logistics, zoning and permitting timelines and the burden of ongoing maintenance costs.

“What people found is that it’s not that simple. And then it became, ‘How do we integrate ADUs into a more thoughtful development process?’ I think we’re really seeing a lot of traction around that [strategy],” Rohde explained.

Washington House Bill 1337, passed in 2023, helped make TJH’s approach possible. Under the legislation, cities statewide must allow two ADUs per lot. The legislation requires municipalities to allow ADUs with a gross floor area of at least 1,000 square feet. That legislation made it far easier for TJH to offer an attached ADU in most of its Seattle floor plans.

The real density gain, according to Rohde, comes from how Seattle treats a home with an ADU as two units, which increases floor area ratio and lets TJH build more total square footage, including the integrated ADU, on the same lot within zoning limits.

To comply with the law, Seattle updated its ADU rules in 2025 to treat a home with an ADU as two units, which may allow additional floor area ratio (FAR) on the lot. That allows TJH to build more total square footage when including an integrated ADU.

“It allows us to build more home on a given lot,” Rohde said. “But it’s not just building square footage for the sake of building square footage. It’s building thoughtful, value-add square footage.”

Rohde also pointed to Washington House Bill 1096, passed in 2025, which requires qualifying cities to create an administrative process for splitting a residential lot in two. Cities are phasing it in ahead of the 2027 state deadline.

“That will allow existing landowners who want to extract some value from a large parcel that they own to split and sell. It will allow owners of larger lots to put two complete, independent single-family residences that will then have their own opportunities to enact the ADU laws and things of that nature. Those types of things are really going to help us drive value,” Rohde added.

#5479. Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max with training, attention optimizations

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. today introduced Qwen4-Max, its newest and most capable large language model.

The algorithm not only generates higher-quality output than its predecessor but also costs less. Those improvements are the result of a new architecture, Qwen4, that made the LLM’s training run more efficient. Additionally, Alibaba has equipped the model with an upgraded attention mechanism.

Qwen4-Max’s backbone, the part of an LLM that functions as its main processing engine, comprises 2.4 trillion parameters. The model activates only 71 billion at any given time. The backbone is supported by 328 billion so-called N-gram parameters, which function as a kind of cache. They save the results of oft-repeated calculations and thereby remove the need to compute them from scratch every time.

An LLM’s artificial neurons are organized into sets known as layers. When the model learns something new during training, a piece of data called a gradient travels through the layers and refines their output. The gradient moves through them one by one starting from the last layer, which finalizes and displays prompt responses.

Qwen4-Max includes a feature that enables the gradient to skip some layers. That feature, or residual, is effectively a shortcut inside the LLM. Its purpose is to reduce errors during the training workflow, which in turn lowers costs and improves output quality.

Residuals can also be found in many other LLMs. Historically, the mechanism was implemented as a single gradient transportation channel. Qwen4-Max’s implementation of the technology features four channels. Moreover, those channels have a “gate” that can adjust the movement of gradients to further improve the training process.

Qwen4-Max’s attention mechanism, a module that helps it understand user prompts, features two key customizations. The first is a technology called Gated DeltaNet that lowers the amount of hardware needed to process large prompts. The second optimization, QSA, skips pieces of data that the LLM doesn’t need to answer a prompt. That arrangement further lowers infrastructure costs.

Alibaba compared Qwen4-Max with its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, using an internal benchmark that includes knowledge work tasks. The former model achieved a higher score and used up to 35% fewer tokens to complete tasks. Those savings grew to 49% when the models were tested using the Terminal-Bench 4.0 suite of coding challenges.

Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s cloud platform. The company plans to open-source a collection of smaller models based on the same technologies further down the line. It’s also open-sourcing Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, an extension that makes Qwen4-Max better at performing time-consuming tasks.

When an LLM is assigned a long-horizon project, users often have to wait until the model completes its work before they can review the results. Alibaba’s plugin shortens the wait. It enables Qwen4-Max to quickly deliver an initial draft and then iteratively add improvements. Users can give the model feedback along the way to refine its work.

#5477. NAMB opposes VA loan fee increases in Senate bill

NAMB launched an advocacy campaign urging mortgage professionals to oppose Section 104 of S. 4744, which would raise VA IRRRL and assumption fees and make them permanent. The group estimates $4 billion in added borrower costs and backs the Major Richard Star Act as an alternative.  AI Summary

The National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB) is urging mortgage professionals to contact their senators and oppose proposed increases to fees for veterans using Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) home loans, arguing the changes would shift the cost of new benefits onto other veterans.

The advocacy campaign, posted on NAMB’s website, comes as the Senate considers S. 4744, its version of the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (H.R. 9237), which passed the House by voice vote on Veterans Day. The Senate bill is on the calendar and is eligible for debate and a vote.

NAMB supports the legislation’s goal of providing additional benefits to combat-injured veterans but opposes Section 104, which would increase fees associated with VA loans.

“Our biggest issue is the fact that our veterans serving our country took an oath to serve and defend. They didn’t take or raise their hand to receive a bill to pay for benefits for their fallen or disabled brothers and sisters. That is not the obligation of the soldier. That’s the obligation of the taxpayer and the disbursement of those tax dollars on the appropriations,” NAMB President Michael Farrell said in a conversation with HousingWire.

Under the Senate proposal, the funding fee for Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loans (IRRRLs) would increase from 0.5% to 1.42%, while the VA loan assumption fee would double from 0.5% to 1%. The increases would also become permanent, eliminating a 10-year sunset provision.

“For the veteran doing the IRRRL and raising that 1.42% from 0.5% on a $400,000 average loan is taking [the fee] from $2,000 to $5,680. And the the concept of, ‘Well, it doesn’t affect their recoupment’ in regards to justifying doing the loan … it does affect and impact the cost of doing the loan,” Farrell added.

NAMB estimates the changes would add $4 billion in costs for veteran borrowers, or an average of $3,780 per veteran. The association also argues the higher IRRRL fee could conflict with the VA’s 36-month recoupment requirement, potentially making some veterans ineligible for the refinancing program.

“It seems like there’s other solutions that can be looked into to raise the funding to support the benefit. … But to alienate it just to one aspect of the IRRRL, when home affordability is a huge concern and veterans are looking to step down their rate or step down their payment to better their family living expenses, now we’ve tripled the cost of getting that done,” Farrell said.

Instead, NAMB is advocating for passage of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102/S. 1032), a bipartisan, standalone measure that would allow approximately 54,000 combat-injured military retirees to receive both full retirement pay and VA disability compensation.

The legislation was introduced by Rep. Gus Bilirakis (R-Fla.) in the House and by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) in the Senate. On Veterans Day, the House voted 245-175 to discharge a resolution to consider the legislation separately and, on Nov. 12, passed the act.

“We are supportive of every veteran receiving their benefit,” Farrell said. “And if this is going to help 54,000 combat injured military retirees receive both their retirement pay and their disability pay, we stand to support the standalone Major Star Act. We do agree with that, but [regarding] Section 104, we have huge concerns on the feasibility of putting this bill on the backs of fellow veterans.”

#5476. d-Matrix Named a Top 5 Vendor to Watch in 2026 HPCwire Editors' Choice Awards

d-Matrix earns a spot on the 23rd Annual HPCwire Awards list for its breakthrough memory-centric compute platform for AI inference

CHICAGO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- d-Matrix has been named one of the Top 5 Vendors to Watch in the 23rd edition of the HPCwire Readers' and Editors' Choice Awards, presented at the 2026 International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis (SC26). d-Matrix was named to this list because of its innovation in purpose-built inference silicon, which tightly integrates compute and memory to efficiently accelerate AI inference.

"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates, we're honored to be recognized as a vendor to watch by HPCwire," said Sid Sheth, founder and CEO of d-Matrix. "Inference is fast becoming the defining AI workload, and we built d-Matrix on the principle that tightly integrating compute and memory delivers the ultra-low-latency and energy efficient inference needed for AI to thrive. This recognition comes as the industry sees the need for specialized compute that can deliver efficient and fast inference at scale."

The coveted annual HPCwire Readers' Choice Awards are determined through a nomination and voting process with the global HPCwire community, as well as selections from the HPCwire editors. The awards are an annual feature of the publication and constitute prestigious recognition from the HPC community. They are revealed each year to kick off the annual supercomputing conference, which showcases innovation in high-performance computing, networking, storage, and data analysis.

"As HPCwire celebrates 38 years of covering high-performance computing, the combined power of HPC and AI is accelerating discovery and reshaping what science and industry can achieve. Our 2026 Readers' and Editors' Choice Awards celebrate the people, organizations, and innovations driving that progress," said Tom Tabor, CEO of TCI Media, publishers of HPCwire. "Throughout the world, our community is tackling grand challenges whose solutions will improve lives for generations to come. Yet too often, these accomplishments remain out of the spotlight, and the people behind them receive even less recognition for their contributions to society. These awards help bring their achievements to light. Drawing on the expertise of our worldwide readership and the perspective of our editorial team, they recognize the depth, ingenuity, and impact of HPC innovation across the globe. To all of this year's winners, our sincere gratitude and heartfelt congratulations."

More information about the awards and a full list of winners is available here: https://www.hpcwire.com/2026-hpcwire-awards-readers-editors-choice
