#5474. Sabre Accelerates Agentic Travel Leadership with First-Mover Travel Experience within Grok Bot and Next-Gen Proactive Travel APIs

SOUTHLAKE, Texas, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sabre (NASDAQ: SABR) will tomorrow preview an agentic travel integration that will bring conversational booking and proactive disruption servicing into frontier AI, beginning with a travel plug-in within Grok Bot.

The breakthrough pairs two industry firsts: the first global travel experience in the Grok Bot ecosystem to enable end-to-end booking and servicing, alongside travel's first proactive, event-driven, agentic-friendly APIs â built to spot flight disruptions and price drops in real time and act automatically without waiting for a prompt.

At Sabre's 2026 Investor Day in New York on Tuesday, November 17, Sabre leadership will highlight both advances and show how agentic infrastructure underpins its multi-year growth plan as the transactional operating system for autonomous travel.

"This is travel's next Internet moment â and our collaboration with SpaceXSI shows where the industry is heading: people asking an AI agent to take care of their end-to-end trip," said Garry Wiseman, President of Product & Engineering, Sabre. "It expands distribution channels for Sabre and our customers by helping them meet travelers wherever they're shopping. And with event-driven APIs behind the scenes, systems won't just wait for questions; they'll spot problems and opportunities early, so an advisor, a bot, or an automated workflow can act fast."

End-to-end agentic solution for all large language models (LLMs): Sabre Mosaic Travel ConnectorWhile basic AI trip search has become widely commoditized, intelligent retailing and post-booking servicing remain travel's complex, high-value next frontier. Sabre Mosaic Travel Connector, which is rolling out in Beta imminently, will enable individual travelers or travel managers to engage directly with an AI assistant to search, book, and service end-to-end itineraries through natural dialogue. Sabre Mosaic Travel Connector will let consumers shop flights and hotels side by side, see what's included and restricted, then book and manage the full trip in one place.

Crucially, the bot will be powered by Sabre's channel-agnostic agentic architecture â connecting conversational interfaces directly with Sabre's Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server and new proactive, event-driven APIs. While debuting in a dedicated environment inside Grok Bot, this underlying modular foundation is designed to scale across all major LLM ecosystems, allowing travel sellers to connect with travelers wherever discovery happens.

Sabre Mosaic Travel Connector joins more than 80 partners in pilot or production with Sabre's MCP services. Having staked out a first-mover position with the launch of its initial agentic APIs and MCP Server in 2025, Sabre maintains nearly a year's head start in live, in-production agentic travel.

Sabre Mosaic's event-driven intelligence is delivered across the full trip lifecycle. Live booking-window insights identify the optimal moment to purchase â down to the ideal number of days in advance, day of the week, or time of day â while Beta air and hotel price-monitoring capabilities track fare and rate thresholds and push alerts the moment prices drop, helping suppliers and agencies re-engage shoppers with timely offers or capture net savings automatically.

Sabre's new proactive, event-driven APIs deliver speed, control, and direct booking integration, working in the background 24/7. This first-to-market technology continuously monitors disruption signals, immediately pinpoints impacted travelers when a flight is delayed or canceled, and pushes real-time alerts into agency systems and connected AI tools without waiting for a prompt.

That intelligence gives travel sellers of all sizes enterprise-grade flexibility in how they respond: a human advisor can step in immediately without manual searches; a conversational interface like Sabre Mosaic Travel Connector can automatically surface policy-compliant options in chat for one-tap traveler approval; or an autonomous agent can execute the fix directly.

Agentic as a Total Addressable Market multiplier

Scaling agentic commerce across new conversational channels represents a significant commercial catalyst for Sabre and its customers. Sabre plans to extend Sabre Mosaic Travel Connector and its channel-agnostic agentic infrastructure across major conversational models and agency workflows throughout 2027 â laying the foundation for proactive, end-to-end agentic travel at scale.

With its technology transformation substantially complete â more than 99% of compute now in the cloud, processing over one billion travel shopping requests daily across roughly 50 petabytes of travel data â Sabre is positioned to convert agentic adoption into profitable growth.

Powering the agentic revolution in travel. Sabre is an AI-native technology leader, backed by one of the world's largest travel data clouds. With AI at its core and operating at unparalleled scale, Sabre transforms insights into innovation, empowering airlines, hoteliers, agencies and other partners to retail, distribute and fulfill travel worldwide. Sabre is built on an open, modular, cloud-native architecture and serves as the backbone for both established leaders and bold, new disruptors, guiding them to the next age of travel retailing through intelligent, connected, and personalized experiences.

#5473. Noeri raises $110M to help companies build living AI systems that self-improve over time

Noeri Inc., a startup developing artificial intelligence systems that continuously improve their outputs as they learn from an organization’s data and work, is launching with $110 million in funding.

Today’s round was led by Menlo Ventures and saw participation from Seattle-based Madrona Ventures, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Snowflake and Cisco Ventures also took part in the round.

Noeri is the brainchild of Yejin Choi (pictured, left) and Carlos Guestrin (right), two prominent AI researchers from Stanford University, who spent years developing self-improving systems at the University of Washington prior to moving. The startup’s software is designed to study a company’s data, workflows and business processes.

Then as it learns about them, it will begin to propose changes regarding specific tasks, in order to make them more efficient. The co-founders refer to it as a “living” AI system that gets better at what it does over time.

For instance, it might offer different instructions, suggest different tools or switch out the model that handles each step of a workflow for another. Each of these suggestions comes with an explanation and is sent to a human for review before it’s accepted, similar to how AI-generated code changes are implemented.

Noeri is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary AI models and ensures that customers retain full ownership of their workflows and the AI systems they develop. Choi told Bloomberg in an interview that Noeri is trying to appeal to organizations that find themselves having to choose between either paying fees they can’t afford for the most capable AI models, or else accepting results from a less effective one.

The idea for the company stemmed from an effort to help a microbiology and immunology team at Stanford use OpenAI Group PBC’s models in a more cost effective way. According to Choi, she and Guestrin developed a small AI model that learned how to use OpenAI’s older models, and to their surprise, managed to fine-tune it to perform better than the more advanced GPT-5 on that research team’s projects.

The startup’s name was carefully chosen. Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” and it’s meant to reflect Choi’s and Guestrin’s belief that the future of AI won’t be dominated by just one or a handful of extremely powerful AI models.

Guestrin especially is a big proponent of choice in the AI industry. In a speech at Madrona Ventures’ IA40 Summit in September, he notably argued that the future of intelligence cannot be controlled by just one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in a blog post outlining the startup’s mission. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t the only proponent of such a multimodel future. Similar arguments have been made by Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Labs Inc., which last year debuted Tinker, a cloud-based service that anyone can use to fine-tune AI models and enhance their performance. Similarly, Applied Compute Inc. embeds engineers with its customers to help them fine-tune AI systems.

Guestrin previously helped develop a popular machine learning tool called XGBoost, which is used by researchers to boost the performance of AI models. He also co-founded an early machine learning startup GraphLab Inc., later known as Turi Inc., which was acquired by Apple Inc. in 2016.  After that, he joined Apple too and went on to lead that company’s machine learning and AI research organization.

Choi previously led the Allen Institute for AI’s common-sense reasoning research team before joining Nvidia Corp. in 2024 as a distinguished scientist. She quit about a year later to join Stanford in early 2025, from where she helped Guestrin start Noeri in May.

Noeri represents the culmination of two separate research projects. Guestrin pioneered a new self-distillation technique that allows AI models to become their own teachers, turning mistakes into lessons that allow them to improve their responses over time. Meanwhile, Choi’s work on agentic orchestration has shown that smaller models that conduct teams of AI agents and tools can outperform much larger frontier models at lower costs.

Those two projects are the foundation of Noeri’s systems. The startup says it’s now working with partners across multiple industries, including some of its investors, which were deliberately chosen to ensure its systems could be exposed to a wide variety of work.

“Most new AI labs ask the market to wait years for a breakthrough,” said Menlo Ventures Partner Venky Ganesan. “Carlos and Yejin are doing world-class research and putting it to work inside companies at the same time. That combination is rare, and it’s why we moved quickly to lead this round.”

#5472. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

#5470. Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

No Flock cameras in Seattle, ever. New protections against potential abuses drawn from an outside audit. A handful of cameras in new neighborhoods. Here's what the RTCC looks like from the inside. pic.twitter.com/QeYUg8ZkW3

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025, pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon said. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

“Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.

#5469. Grupo Supervielle Reports 3Q26 Results

Return to loan growth, with net loans up 1.3% QoQ in real terms and accelerating to 3.7% MoM in September

NPL ratio improved to 5.4%, approximately 200 bps below industry, with net cost of risk down 100 bps to 4.6%

â Lower cost to serve, with personnel expenses excluding severance down 14% QoQ and administrative expenses down approximately 10%

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Grupo Supervielle S.A. (NYSE: SUPV; BYMA: SUPV), ("Supervielle" or the "Company") a universal financial services group headquartered in Argentina with a nationwide presence, today reported results for the three- and nine-month period ended September 30, 2026.

Starting 1Q20, the Company began reporting results applying Hyperinflation Accounting, in accordance with IFRS rule IAS 29 ("IAS 29") as established by the Central Bank.

Commenting on third quarter 2026 results, Patricio Supervielle, Grupo Supervielle's Chairman & CEO, noted: "The third quarter marked a return to loan growth as we began to deliver on the priority we outlined last quarter: selectively expanding lending in strategic products and sectors with stronger credit profiles while maintaining disciplined risk management and a clear focus on profitability. Our net loan portfolio grew 1.3% sequentially in real terms, with momentum strengthening in September, when loans increased 3.7%, and 2% in October.

Asset quality continued to improve. Our NPL ratio edged down to 5.4%, remaining 200 basis points below the industry, while net cost of risk declined by 100 basis points sequentially to 4.6% and loan loss provisions fell 14.5%. Although conditions remain challenging, particularly for some SMEs, these results reinforce our confidence in our approach to managing credit risk and rebuilding lending momentum.

On the funding side, we actively managed our deposit base as interest rates increased, reducing high-cost institutional peso deposits (as interest rates increase) to better align funding with our lending needs and contain interest expense, while dollar deposits continued to grow.

Net interest margin decreased to 16.0%, while the year-to-date margin stood at 18.0%, within our full-year guidance range. As anticipated, the temporary benefits we highlighted last quarter unwound as asset yields repriced, following the prior quarter decline in funding costs. Lower inflation reduced income from inflation-linked loans, and lower investment securities gains also contributed to margin compression. Renewed loan growth is an important step toward strengthening our earnings capacity, with its contribution is expected to build as origination volumes recover. We reported net income of AR$6.8 billion, equivalent to 2.2% ROAE. Excluding extraordinary severance charges associated with the completion of our rightsizing plan, adjusted net income was AR$10.7 billion, equivalent to 3.4% adjusted ROAE.

The transformation of our operating model is translating into a lower cost to serve. Personnel expenses excluding severance charges declined 14% sequentially, while administrative expenses fell approximately 10%, reflecting savings from branch consolidation and a leaner operating structure. Although lower revenues weighed on efficiency during the quarter, the year-to-date efficiency ratio excluding extraordinary severance charges stood at 55.5%. Building revenues on this lower cost base remains central to improving operating leverage and sustainable profitability.

On November 5, we marked an important milestone in Supervielle's transformation, unveiling a new brand identity that brings to life the integrated financial ecosystem we have been building over the past two years. Our renewed SuperApp connects everyday banking, family finances and investing through "SuperFamilia", closer integration with IOL Inversiones and AI-assisted customer service needs within a simpler, more personalized experience. We also launched "Pollen X", our Banking as a Service platform, enabling companies, fintechs and digital platforms to embed our financial services into their own offerings. Together, these capabilities strengthen our role in customers' everyday financial lives and open new opportunities for growth through a broader range of channels.

At IOL, assets under custody increased 20% sequentially in U.S. dollar terms to US$3.5 billion, while total accounts reached 2.5 million. Assets under management in mutual funds managed by IOL also continued to grow, reaching US$ 492 million at quarter-end. This growth underscores the opportunity to connect our banking and investment capabilities more closely and support a broader range of our customers' financial needs.

Looking ahead, our priorities remain clear: sustain the improvement in asset quality, build on the return to lending growth and continue our permanent agenda of lowering the cost to serve into stronger, sustainable returns. Argentina's low level of financial penetration presents a significant long-term opportunity. With a solid CET1 ratio of 13.5%, we are well positioned to pursue it through disciplined risk management, close customer relationships and a more efficient operating model. As we mark ten years as a publicly listed company, we look forward to sharing our Five-Year vision and strategic priorities at our Supervielle Day on November 23," concluded Mr. Supervielle.

The Company reported an Attributable Net Income of AR$.6.8 billion in 3Q26, compared to Ps.13.6 billion in 2Q26 and an Attributable Net Loss of AR$.67.0 billion in 3Q25. In 9M26, the Company posted an Attributable Net Income of Ps.1.1 billion, compared to an Attributable Net Loss of Ps.35.9 billion in 9M25. Group headcount was 16% below year-end 2025 levels at quarter-end, following the headcount rightsizing plan implemented in 1H26 across its Banking ecosystem to align its workforce with a more efficient distribution model, as a growing share of customer activity migrates to digital and virtual hub service channels. Excluding severance charges, which in 3Q26 were limited to residual charges related to the headcount rightsizing plan implemented in 1H26, the Company posted an Adjusted Net Income of AR$.10.7 billion in 3Q26 and AR$.56.5 billion in 9M26.

During 3Q26, the structural improvements implemented in recent quarters became increasingly visible in the Company's efficiency metrics, with a lower cost base driving the cost-to-assets ratio to 7.9%, its lowest level in the last five quarters. Credit costs also continued to decline, reflecting the sustained impact of portfolio management, collection and refinancing initiatives undertaken since 2025, together with a disciplined and cautious origination strategy. These trends translated into improved asset quality indicators, with the NPL ratio improving to 5.4% and net cost of risk easing to 4.6%.

However, these improvements were more than offset by lower Net Financial Income, reflecting the anticipated unwinding of the temporary spread benefits observed in the previous quarter, together with lower returns on UVA loans and CER-adjusted securities as inflation slowed. As a result, Net Income declined sequentially. In 9M26, results continued to reflect a transitional period, with underlying cost and credit trends improving.

3Q26 ROAE was 2.2% while adjusted ROAE was 3.4%, and Structural ROAE, which reflects the full run-rate of the salary savings associated with the headcount reductions under the voluntary retirement program, as if those reductions had been fully in effect throughout the period, was 3.5%. ROAA was 0.3%. 9M26 ROAE was 0.1%, while adjusted ROAE was 6.1% and structural ROAE was 7.2%.

In 3Q26, the Company reported Profit Before Income Tax of AR$.12.2 billion, compared to a Profit Before Income Tax of AR$.20.4 billion in 2Q26 and a Loss Before Income Tax of AR$.108.3 billion in 3Q25. This result included approximately AR$.5.9 billion in residual severance charges, compared with AR$.38.1 billion in 2Q26. Excluding these charges, Adjusted Profit Before Income Tax, was AR$.18.1 billion in 3Q26.

The sequential decline primarily reflects a 22.4% QoQ decrease in Net Financial Income, to AR$.241.8 billion, as the lagged repricing of interest-earning assets to lower market rates and to lower inflation, compressed spreads following the exceptional margin expansion recorded in 2Q26. This was partially offset by a 26.5% QoQ reduction in personnel and administrative expenses, to AR$.141.5 billion (down 12.2% excluding severance charges in both quarters), and a 14.5% QoQ reduction in Loan Loss Provisions, which declined to AR$.61.5 billion, extending the downward trend from the AR$.133.9 billion peak reached in 4Q25. Additionally, the loss from the net monetary position (RECPAM) declined 1.8% QoQ as inflation moderated. Net Service Fee Income decreased 6.7% QoQ to AR$.53.2 billion, primarily reflecting lagged fee repricing, as account package repricing was only implemented in September, and lower credit card commissions amid lower  loan volumes, together with a weaker performance in asset management fees, partially offset by a 4.1% increase in net fee income from the IOL brokerage business.

On a cumulative basis, the Company posted a Profit Before Income Tax of AR$.7.4 billion in 9M26, compared to a Loss Before Income Tax of AR$.73.7 billion in 9M25. Excluding extraordinary severance charges, Adjusted Profit Before Income Tax amounted to AR$.92.6 billion in 9M26.

3Q26 Net Financial Income totaled AR$.241.8 billion in 3Q26, decreasing 22.4% QoQ and increasing 45.0% YoY. The sequential decline reflects the unwinding of the temporary spread benefits observed in the previous quarter, as anticipated. In 2Q26, the sharp decline in market rates, with average TAMAR falling to 22.8% from 32.0% in 1Q26, was passed through quickly to funding costs, while asset yields adjusted with a lag, temporarily widening spreads. In 3Q26, average TAMAR edged up slightly to 23.5%, keeping funding costs broadly stable, while interest-earning assets continued to reprice to the lower rate levels reached in the prior quarter, compressing spreads, together with lower inflation, which reduced the accrual on inflation-linked (UVA) loans and CER-adjusted securities. YoY, the increase reflects the recovery from the exceptionally compressed margins of 3Q25, when the monetary tightening ahead of the mid-term elections drove the average TAMAR to 46.4%, alongside historically high reserve requirements. Net Financial Income plus the Result from exposure to changes in the purchasing power of the currency totaled AR$. 208.5 billion, decreasing 24.9% QoQ, but increasing 63.1% YoY.

In 9M26, Net Financial Margin amounted to AR$841.1 billion, increasing 16.4% from 9M25.

Net Interest Margin (NIM) was 16.0% in 3Q26, declining 430 bps QoQ from the exceptionally high level recorded in 2Q26, but 520 bps above YoY. As anticipated in the previous quarter, the sequential compression reflects the lagged repricing of interest-earning assets to the lower rate environment, after funding costs had adjusted faster in 2Q26, as well as lower inflation, which reduced the accrual on inflation-linked (UVA) loans and CER-adjusted securities. The impact was reflected across the balance sheet: Loan Portfolio NIM was 17.2%, down 360 bps QoQ, and Investment Portfolio NIM was 13.7%, down 410 bps QoQ. AR$ NIM was 19.4% in 3Q26, 480 bps lower QoQ but 770 bps higher YoY. In pesos, loan portfolio NIM fell 450 bps to 21.8%, as loan yields caught up with lower market rates, while the AR$ cost of funds remained broadly stable. The peso investment portfolio NIM contracted 560 bps to 14.4% reflecting lower yields on AR$ government securities although 1,250 bps above 3Q25 level.

YoY, the expansion in NIM reflects the normalization of funding costs from the exceptionally elevated levels of 3Q25, when the monetary tightening ahead of the mid-term elections drove average TAMAR to 46.4%, compared to 23.5% in 3Q26.

The Total NPL Ratio was 5.4% as of September 30, 2026, down from 5.5% as of June 30, 2026 and approximately 200 bps below the industry average. While the ratio continues to reflect the carry-over effects of credit stress from prior quarters in a challenging macroeconomic environment, portfolio dynamics continued to improve, with delinquency indicators declining consistently since March. The 90-day delinquency ratio was 4.4% at the end of 3Q26, 100 bps below the reported NPL ratio. This gap reflects exposures classified as non-performing under Central Bank criteria that were performing or less than 90 days past due according to the Bank's records. The Retail NPL ratio declined to 8.6% from 9.6% in June, while the retail 90-day delinquency ratio improved to 7.1% from 7.9%.

Quarterly NPL formation declined for the third consecutive quarter and stood approximately 25% below the 4Q25 peak, with retail NPL formation down 44% from that peak.

Measured in constant pesos, the stock of retail loans more than 90 days past due declined every month since February 2026, ending the quarter 27% below its peak and 16% below June. This reflects improved collection and refinancing dynamics resulting from active portfolio management and a disciplined origination strategy in place since early 2025, with origination cohorts since 4Q25 continuing to perform meaningfully better. In contrast, the commercial portfolio showed some deterioration during the quarter, with higher delinquency and NPL formation, reflecting the lagged impact of the high interest rate environment in prior months on SME customers. While conditions remain challenging, the sustained improvement in retail and the stronger performance of recent origination cohorts reinforce our confidence in our credit risk management approach.

Loan Loss Provisions (LLPs) declined 14.5% QoQ to AR$61.5 billion in 3Q26. This reduction was consistent with easing delinquency trends throughout the quarter and reflects the early benefits of the collection and refinancing initiatives implemented since December 2025, together with disciplined risk-adjusted loan origination. The Coverage Ratio was 92.8% as of September 30, 2026, compared to 98.9% as of June 30, 2026, and 112.2% as of September 30, 2025. The decline reflects the contraction of the retail portfolio over recent quarters, where loans require higher provisioning. At the same time, NPL formation increased in the commercial portfolio, where loans require lower allowances relative to their outstanding balance under the IFRS 9 expected credit loss model. On an adjusted basis, considering loans to individuals more than 90 days past due at the Bank, the coverage ratio was 105%.

Efficiency Ratio was 61.3% in 3Q26, compared with 63.4% in 2Q26. The sequential improvement mainly reflects lower severance charges, which declined to approximately AR$5.9 billion in 3Q26 from AR$38.1 billion in 2Q26, with 3Q26 charges mainly reflecting residual costs related to the voluntary retirement program. Excluding these items, the adjusted efficiency ratio would have been 59.2% compared with 52.3% in 2Q26. The increase in the adjusted efficiency ratio reflects the 19.7% sequential decline in revenues, driven by lower net financial income as asset yields continued to reprice downward while funding costs remained broadly stable, compressing spreads. This more than offset the 9.2% decline in operating expenses excluding severance charges, reflecting continued cost discipline and the benefits of the structural efficiency initiatives implemented across the organization. In 9M26, the efficiency ratio was 64.6%. Excluding AR$ 85.2 billion of extraordinary severance costs, the 9M26 efficiency ratio would have been 55.5%.

The Loans to Deposits Ratio was 82.8% as of September 30, 2026, compared to 72.6% as of June 30, 2026, and 67.3% as of September 30, 2025. The QoQ increase mainly reflects the 11.6% decline in deposits during the quarter reflecting asset and liability management, combined with the 0.9% growth in the net loan portfolio.

Total Deposits were AR$ 5,587.6 billion at quarter-end, decreasing 11.6% QoQ and 17.2% YoY. The sequential decrease was driven by asset and liability management initiatives reducing high-cost institutional peso deposits and a seasonal decrease in savings accounts.

Total private sector deposits were AR$ 5,367.6 billion, decreasing 11.5% QoQ and 17.8% YoY. AR$ deposits totaled AR$ 3,676.0 billion, decreasing 15.9% QoQ and 17.8% YoY.

The QoQ performance of AR$ Deposits, down 15.9%, or AR$ 695.2 billion, primarily reflects lower institutional funding, together with the reversal of the seasonal increase in retail deposits recorded in the previous quarter. During the quarter, the Company continued to actively manage its funding mix, reducing higher-cost institutional time deposits as well as corporate and public sector deposits, and partially replaced them with alternative funding sources, mainly repo transactions. As a result, the blended AR$ and US$ cost of funds declined approximately 50 bps QoQ, while the AR$ cost of funds increased only 10 bps sequentially, significantly less thanthe 70 bps increase in average TAMAR, limiting the impact of higher market rates on funding costs.

Foreign currency deposits amounted to US$1.3 billion, increasing 1.5% QoQ and 0.9% YoY.

Total Assets were AR$9,114.6 billion as of September 30, 2026, decreasing 1.3% QoQ and 8.4% YoY. The sequential performance mainly reflected: i) a 9.3%, or AR$201.0 billion, decrease in the public sector investment portfolio and repo transactions reflecting asset and liability management decisions following the reduction in institutional deposits, partially offset by: ii) a 17.1%, or AR$43.1 billion, increase in the corporate notes investment portfolio. In addition, iii) the loan portfolio (net of provisions) increased 1.3%, or AR$ 58.1 billion, driven by 13.4%  increase in US dollarâdenominated loans partially offset by a 1.7%   decline in peso-denominated loans, as the Company prioritized disciplined origination and attractive risk-adjusted returns over volume, while iv) cash and due from banks remained broadly stable declining 1.0%, or AR$ 14.1 billion, reflecting lower regulatory liquidity needs at quarter-end. The leverage ratio (Assets to Shareholders' Equity) was 7.3x, decreasing 10 bps QoQ, from 7.4x as of June 30, 2026, and 60 bps YoY, from 7.9x as of September 30, 2025. The average leverage ratio in 3Q26 was 6.9x, stable compared with 2Q26 and 3Q25.

Total Loans amounted to AR$4,624.0 billion as of September 30, 2026, increasing 0.9% QoQ and 1.8% YoY and 155.5% since March 31, 2024. Loan growth since March 31, 2024, has significantly outpaced the industry's 142% increase, while remaining in line with the industry on a YoY basis. Net loans amounted to AR$ 4,383.0 billion as of September 30, 2026, increasing 1.3% QoQ and 1.1% YoY.

The sequential performance was primarily driven by a 13.4% increase in U.S. dollar loans, mainly to corporate clients in export-oriented sectors, which continued to lead economic activity, while pesoâdenominated loans decreased 1.7% reflecting soft loan demand and a disciplined origination strategy focused on attractive risk-adjusted returns.

By segment, quarterly performance was driven by commercial loans, which increased 4.2%, while retail loans declined 5.1%. Lending activity gained momentum toward quarter-end, with total loans increasing 3.7% in September compared to August. Retail loan origination also picked up, with origination volume in September 20% higher than in August. On a YoY basis, commercial loans grew 24.6%, while retail loans declined 19.4%, reflecting the disciplined approach to retail origination maintained since early 2025.

Common Equity Tier 1 Ratio (CET1) was 13.5% as of September 30, 2026, declining from 14.2% in the prior quarter but remaining 30 basis points higher than a year earlier. The sequential decline primarily reflects higher RWA density, driven by an increase in loans and an increase in market risk associated with the expansion of the corporate notes portfolio.

#5468. What does 007 mean? The 00 license to kill, explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Here's what 007 means, how James Bond's double-0 code number and fictional license to kill work in Ian Fleming's novels and films, and how real U.K. law compares

The number 007 is a job code, not a name. It is James Bond's service number. It tells the reader which section Bond belongs to and what that section authorizes him to do. That is why the question "what does 007 mean" has a precise answer, and that answer starts in the original novels.

Bond is the fictional MI6 officer created by the British novelist Ian Fleming. MI6 is the common name for the Secret Intelligence Service, the U.K.'s foreign intelligence agency. Fleming introduced his agent in the novel Casino Royale, published in 1953. Eon Productions released its first Bond film, Dr. No, in 1962, with Sean Connery in the lead role. The code number moved with the character from page to screen.

The number has two parts. The double zero marks a special section, and the final digit identifies one officer within it. In Fleming's fiction, the prefix carries an authority that ordinary officers do not hold. It is the authority to kill in the line of duty, known in shorthand as the license to kill. Both the section and the license are inventions of the stories, not features of the real MI6.

This guide works through the code one piece at a time. It covers how the prefix is read, how Bond earned it in the original novel and how the 2006 film of the same name retold that moment. It looks at the other double-0 agents who appear on screen and at the film that handed the 007 number to someone new. It also explains the real U.K. law that comes closest to a license to kill, and why that law is something else entirely. The final slide turns to Fleming's wartime work in British naval intelligence and the 1989 film that borrowed the phrase for its title.

Each slide stands on its own, so readers can start with whichever part of the 007 question they need.

007 is James Bond's service number, the code that identifies him inside MI6 in Ian Fleming's spy novels. The double zero places him in a special section, and the closing seven singles him out as one agent within it.

The code works like an address. The first two characters point to the unit. The last character points to one officer inside that unit.

That makes 007 a designation rather than a name. It describes a position within an organization, and Bond is the man who fills it. Both the officer and his section exist only in fiction, not in the real MI6.

The number arrived on the page with the character in Casino Royale, Fleming's first Bond novel. Dr. No, the first Eon Productions film, later carried both to cinemas with Sean Connery in the role.

Fleming never gave a documented reason for choosing seven. No statement from the author explains why Bond received that digit rather than another. Theories about its origin circulate, but none rests on anything Fleming verifiably said or wrote.

The digit's job inside the stories is clearer than its origin. It tells one double-0 officer apart from the others in the same section. Nothing in the code itself says more than that.

In Ian Fleming's James Bond novels, the double-0 prefix marks an officer of the double-0 section. Officers in that section are authorized to kill in the line of duty. "License to kill" is the shorthand for that authority.

The prefix and the license work as a pair. The double-0 number is the marker. The authority to kill is what that marker signals.

The phrase describes a power rather than a formal rank or job title. It compresses what the prefix permits into three words.

The authority is tied to the line of duty. In the fiction, it covers what a double-0 officer does on assignment for the service.

Fleming introduced the idea in Casino Royale, the novel that launched the series. In that book, Bond reflects on his double-0 status and on what the authority to kill means for him. The license enters the series in the same book as the character himself.

The double-0 section carries over into the Eon Productions films. On screen, as in the novels, the license works as a plot device.

Both the section and its powers are story devices. Fleming built them into his invented version of MI6. They exist only on the page and on screen.

James Bond earns his double-0 prefix in Ian Fleming's 1953 novel Casino Royale by killing two people on assignment. The 2006 film of the same name tells that origin story differently, with new targets and new circumstances.

Bond does not start out as a double-0 officer. Casino Royale treats the prefix as a status that must be earned, and the novel names two specific kills as the qualification.

The first kill takes place in New York. Bond's target there is a Japanese cipher expert, a specialist in codes.

The second takes place in Stockholm, the Swedish capital. That target is a Norwegian double agent, someone who appears to serve one side while secretly working for another.

The two kills span two countries, the U.S. and Sweden. Both targets come from the intelligence trade itself. One deals in codes, and the other in divided loyalty. Neither is a soldier or a common criminal. Bond's qualifying work is aimed at the people who make up the spy business.

The 2006 film, starring Daniel Craig, reworks this backstory. It shows Bond's promotion in a black-and-white opening sequence. The monochrome sets those scenes apart from the color footage that follows. It marks them as the step that comes before the rest of the story.

The sequence shows Bond killing two men. One is Dryden, a section chief, whom Bond confronts in Prague. The other is Fisher, Dryden's contact. Both men belong to the spy world, as the novel's targets do. These two deaths replace the novel's kills and earn the screen Bond his double-0 number.

The film keeps the novel's count of two kills but changes the people involved. In the book, the targets are a cipher expert and a double agent. In the film, they are a section chief and his contact. The shape of the origin survives the adaptation, while its details belong to each version alone.

James Bond is not the only officer with a double-0 number in the Eon Productions films. Three others appear on screen: 006 in GoldenEye (1995), 009 in Octopussy (1983) and 004 in The Living Daylights (1987).

All three carry the same double zero as Bond. Only the last digit changes from one officer to the next. That detail shows that 007 is one numbered post among several. It is not a label reserved for one man.

The 006 designation belongs to Alec Trevelyan. Sean Bean plays him in GoldenEye. Here the number comes with a full character name and a named actor. That ties the 006 post to a specific person in the story rather than leaving it as a digit.

Agent 009 appears in the opening of Octopussy. He is already dead when the audience first sees him. He is also disguised as a clown.

Agent 004 appears in the opening of The Living Daylights. He is killed during a training exercise.

The two films use these officers in a similar way. In each, the other double-0 agent appears in the opening sequence rather than later in the story. Neither survives that sequence. The audience meets him only briefly, and his number matters more than his character.

Taken together, the three films sketch the double-0 section as a working unit with several members. On screen, Bond is one numbered officer within that group, and his place in it is 007.

In No Time to Die, the 2021 Bond film, the 007 designation belongs to someone other than James Bond. Bond has left the service, and an officer named Nomi, played by Lashana Lynch, carries the number.

The story turns on that change in Bond's status. He is no longer working for MI6, the Secret Intelligence Service, when the events of the film take place. His exit leaves the code number open, and another officer holds it.

The detail shows how the number works inside the fiction. The 007 code is tied to a post in the double-0 section, not to one particular man. When an officer leaves, the post remains, and so does its number.

The film links two characters to the same three digits. Bond is the character audiences have connected with the number since Ian Fleming's novels. Nomi is the officer who holds it while the film's events unfold.

That arrangement treats 007 as a working designation that MI6 assigns. It is not a personal name that retires when one officer walks away.

The license to kill is not real. MI6 has no double-0 section, and none of its officers holds a standing license to kill. Both exist only in Ian Fleming's novels and the films adapted from them.

MI6 is the Secret Intelligence Service. In the stories, it employs James Bond under the number 007. In reality, it has no numbered section of officers authorized to kill.

The closest real-world comparison is a piece of legislation, not a code number. Section 7 of the U.K. Intelligence Services Act 1994 lets the Secretary of State authorize certain acts outside the British Isles. These are acts that would otherwise break U.K. law.

The purpose of that authorization is protection at home. Staff who carry out an authorized act abroad are shielded from liability in the U.K. for that act.

Section 7 is sometimes nicknamed the "James Bond clause." The nickname borrows from the fiction. It does not describe what the law permits.

Section 7 is not a license to kill. It gives no officer a personal, standing authority to take a life. The power to authorize sits with the Secretary of State, not with any individual officer.

The difference from the fiction lies in where the authority comes from. In Fleming's stories, the double-0 prefix itself marks an officer authorized to kill in the line of duty. The authority travels with the officer's number.

Under the 1994 act, nothing travels with a number. The provision addresses whether staff face liability under U.K. law for an authorized act abroad. It does not create a class of officers set apart for lethal work.

For readers asking whether the license to kill is real, the answer has two parts. The double-0 license is an invention of the stories. The nearest real law works as a legal shield, not a grant of lethal power.

Ian Fleming, the novelist who created James Bond, worked in British naval intelligence during World War II. The phrase most closely tied to Bond's double-0 status later became the title of a 1989 Bond film, Licence to Kill.

Fleming's wartime post was real intelligence work. His spy fiction came afterward. Bond did not appear in print until several years after the war ended.

The order of events separates fact from invention. Fleming's naval service is part of the historical record. The double-0 section he later wrote about is not. Its authority to kill exists only in the novels and the films adapted from them.

The name of his hero came from a different field altogether. Fleming borrowed the name James Bond from an American ornithologist. That James Bond wrote a field guide to the birds of the Caribbean. The fictional spy and the real bird expert share a name and nothing else.

Fleming wrote the Bond novels at Goldeneye, his home in Jamaica. The house shares its name with the 1995 Bond film GoldenEye. The film's title capitalizes the second E. The Caribbean runs through both details. The ornithologist's field guide covered the region's birds, and the novels were written on one of its islands.

Licence to Kill starred Timothy Dalton as Bond. It was the 16th Bond film made by Eon Productions, the production company behind the main Bond film series.

The title keeps the British spelling, licence. In U.S. English, the same word is spelled license. Both spellings refer to the same authority attached to the double-0 prefix.

The story turns the phrase around. In Licence to Kill, Bond acts without official sanction. The title names an authority the service grants, and the plot follows Bond working outside it. A film named for the license shows its hero without the official backing that gives the double-0 number its meaning in the stories.

#5467. Corma raises $125M to train cybersecurity-optimized foundation models

Corma.ai Ltd., a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for cybersecurity teams, has raised $125 million in funding.

NEA led the Series A round. Corma stated today that returning backers Khosla Ventures, Coatue and Sequoia Capital chipped in as well. The company is now valued at $1 billion.

Corma, which has offices in San Francisco and Tel Aviv, says competing AI models are often better at launching cyberattacks than fixing them. The company recently conducted a test in which it asked several large language models to hack a simulated corporate network. They succeeded at installing a malicious file across 85% of the test runs. In contrast, the models found only 12% of the malicious files that they themselves installed.

According to Corma, the gap between LLMs’ offensive and defensive capabilities can give hackers an edge over cybersecurity teams. That’s the issue the company is tackling with its cybersecurity-optimized AI models. Corma says that the algorithms can speed up some breach response workflows by a factor of 100 while reducing the associated costs.

The company benchmarked one of its models against the competition using an evaluation called DefenseBench V5. The test measures two metrics: how reliably a model performs defensive cybersecurity tasks and how fast it completes them. Corma says that its model outperformed GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and several other cutting-edge LLMs.

The company’s algorithms find breaches by analyzing data from other cybersecurity tools. Corma can ingest telemetry generated by firewalls, network monitoring software and a range of other applications. The company says that its models not only find threats but also generate remediation guidance for each one.

Automating breach response tasks is difficult because it requires LLMs to filter numerous false positives and duplicate alerts. Moreover, models often have access to only partial information about breaches. Many companies discard cybersecurity logs after a relatively short amount of time to reduce data storage costs.

Corma says that its algorithms can perform breach investigations on a fully autonomous basis. If human input is needed, they alert a relevant member of the cybersecurity team. It’s also possible to manually steer Corma’s models via a Slack chatbot. An administrator could, for example, ask Corma to double-check whether a recent effort to remove malware from a compromised server was successful.

“Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” said Corma co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alon Pluda.

Corma will use its newly raised funds to buy more infrastructure and enhance its AI models.

#5465. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”

That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
