#5464. Is James Bond a code name? The films point to one man and a handed-down number

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Is James Bond a code name? See how the fan theory holds up against Fleming's novels and 10 moments in the Eon films, from Dr. No to Skyfall

"Bond, James Bond" sounds like a personal name, spoken by one man about himself. Sean Connery first delivered the line at a casino table in Dr. No (1962), the first film in the Eon Productions series. George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Daniel Craig and other actors later played the same MI6 agent. Each brought a different face and manner, yet the films kept the same name.

That gap sits behind a long-running fan question: is James Bond a code name? The theory holds that "James Bond" is an identity handed from one agent to the next, much like a 00 number. If true, it would explain why the hero's face changes while his job and employer stay the same. The producers have not confirmed the idea as official continuity.

The question shapes how the whole series reads. Under the code-name theory, the films become a relay of different men sharing one cover identity. Without it, they follow one character played by a succession of actors. The two readings give different answers about which events carry over and whose past belongs to whom.

The films supply evidence on both sides. In On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), Lazenby's Bond turns to the camera and says, "This never happened to the other fellow." M and Q also recur under the same titles while the actors change, a pattern fans fold into the theory. Other scenes point the opposite way. In For Your Eyes Only (1981), Moore's Bond visits the grave of Tracy, the wife from the Lazenby film. Casino Royale (2006) restarts the story with Craig earning his 00 status. Skyfall (2012) takes him to his family estate in Scotland and establishes that his parents are dead.

The books set a baseline of their own. Ian Fleming introduced the character in his 1953 novel Casino Royale and wrote him as a single man. The code-name idea does not come from Fleming.

The 10 slides below walk through that record, from Fleming's page to the Craig era. A central distinction runs through them: the number versus the name. In the films, the 00 prefix marks a licence to kill, and other agents carry other numbers. The name James Bond belongs to one man in each version of the story.

The James Bond code name theory holds that "James Bond" is a name MI6 assigns to whichever agent holds the 007 post, not the name of one man. It is a fan explanation for the series' changing lead actors. The producers have not confirmed it as official continuity.

The idea answers a practical question that faces any long-running film series. The Eon Productions films have recast their lead several times, from Sean Connery to Daniel Craig. The series rarely explains a recasting on screen. A new face appears in the tuxedo, and the story moves on.

Time is the other problem the theory tries to solve. Read as one unbroken career, the films would follow a single field agent across several decades of missions. A rotating name removes that strain.

In its usual form, the theory treats "James Bond" as a working identity, similar to a cover legend in espionage. Each new holder takes on the name, the number and the reputation attached to them. The previous agent retires, dies or drops out of the record. Colleagues inside MI6 know a handover took place. Enemies in the field may not.

That structure also sets the test the theory has to pass. If the name belongs to a post, the films should treat Bond's personal history as disposable. A new holder would have no reason to grieve a predecessor's wife. He would not return to a predecessor's childhood home or carry a predecessor's old wounds. Any scene that ties the name to one specific life works against the theory.

The reverse test matters too. A scene that acknowledges a change of actor gives the theory something to stand on. So does a scene that treats Bond's job as larger than the man doing it. The films contain moments of both kinds, spread across different eras and different leads.

The question therefore comes down to what appears on screen. The code name theory is a way of reading the films, not a rule written into them. Each era of the series can be checked against it on its own terms.

Dr. No, released in 1962, was the first film in the Eon Productions series, and it cast Sean Connery as James Bond. At a casino table, Connery's Bond introduces himself with the line "Bond, James Bond."

The line gives the surname first, then the full name. That is how a person states his own name. Nothing in the wording presents it as a rank, a title or an assignment.

The setting points the same way. A casino table is a social space, not an MI6 briefing room. Bond gives his name there as any guest at the table might, rather than reciting an official designation.

The scene matters for the code-name theory. Any case that "James Bond" is a cover identity has to account for the character's first screen introduction. In Dr. No, the name arrives as a personal introduction from the man himself.

Dr. No is also the starting point for every later continuity question. As the first Eon film, it is the earliest screen evidence of how the series treats the name. Every later film in the series, with each new lead actor, follows from this one.

Ian Fleming created James Bond in Casino Royale, published in 1953, and wrote him as one specific man. Nothing in Fleming's novels presents the name as a title passed from agent to agent.

Fleming was a British journalist who had served in naval intelligence. During World War II, he worked as an assistant to the U.K.'s Director of Naval Intelligence. That background informs the codes, briefings and field operations in his books.

The name has a documented origin. Fleming borrowed it from James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote Birds of the West Indies. Fleming wanted a plain, unremarkable name for his hero. He took it from a real person rather than inventing a cover identity.

Casino Royale sends Bond to a French resort on an MI6 assignment. His target is Le Chiffre, a Soviet-linked operative who has lost money he does not control. Bond's job is to beat him at baccarat and leave him unable to cover the losses.

The novel also explains how Bond got his 00 prefix. He tells an ally that he earned it by killing two people on assignment. One was a Japanese cipher expert in New York. The other was a Norwegian double agent in Stockholm. In Fleming's telling, the number reflects a record of specific acts by one agent.

Fleming kept writing the same character across 12 novels and two short story collections. Some of that work appeared after his death in 1964. Characters such as M and the CIA's Felix Leiter recur, and later books refer back to earlier missions.

The most detailed biography arrives in You Only Live Twice, published in 1964. After Bond is presumed dead, M writes an obituary of him for The Times. It sets out his parents, childhood, schooling and naval career. That record describes a single person with a single life story.

The code-name theory concerns the films, where a series of actors stepped into the role. Readers of the books meet one James Bond, written by one author over roughly a decade. Any case for a shared code name has to rest on what the movies added, not on Fleming's source material.

In the opening of On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), George Lazenby's Bond turns to the camera and says, "This never happened to the other fellow." Fans cite the line as support for the theory that James Bond is a code name.

Lazenby followed Sean Connery, who had played Bond since the series began. That made Lazenby the first actor to take over a role audiences knew from only one face. Placing the line in the opening means the film addresses the recasting almost as soon as Lazenby appears.

Bond speaks the line to the camera, not to another character. That makes it a direct aside to the audience. For a moment, Bond steps outside the story and acknowledges the people watching it.

One reading treats "the other fellow" as a reference to Connery. On that view, the joke concerns the casting change, not anything that happens inside MI6. The film signals that it knows a new actor is playing a familiar character.

Code-name theorists read the same words another way. If "James Bond" were a title passed between MI6 agents, the other fellow could be an earlier agent who held it. The line would then be an in-story remark about a predecessor, not a joke about an actor.

The words alone do not decide between those readings. The line names no one. It says nothing about MI6 assigning names, and it does not mention a 00 number or a handover.

The rest of the film complicates the code-name reading. On Her Majesty's Secret Service is the film in which Bond marries Tracy. A later film returns to that marriage as part of Bond's own past, with a different actor in the role.

The producers at Eon Productions have not confirmed the code-name theory as official continuity. That leaves the line open to both readings, with no official answer attached.

For Your Eyes Only (1981) shows Roger Moore's Bond at the grave of his wife, Tracy. Bond married Tracy in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), a film that starred George Lazenby. The scene presents two actors as one man with a single shared past.

That detail bears directly on the code-name theory. Under that theory, "James Bond" would be a title passed from one MI6 agent to the next. A new agent who inherited the name would have no personal reason to visit another man's wife.

To absorb the scene, the theory would have to treat the successor as a man who took on his predecessor's grief along with his name. Nothing in the scene suggests that. Moore's Bond visits the grave as a widower, not as a colleague paying respects.

The grave scene only works if Moore's Bond is the same person who married Tracy. The film asks the audience to accept that his history carries over. A different actor lived through that history on screen.

Moore's first outing as Bond came in Live and Let Die (1973), four years after On Her Majesty's Secret Service was released. He reached the scene at Tracy's grave eight years after that debut.

The wedding film and the graveside film sit 12 years apart. Across that span, the actor playing Bond changed. The character's widowhood did not.

That gap shows how the series treats its own record. The marriage belongs to the character, not to the actor who performed it. A recast did not erase it.

The scene gives the series a direct continuity link between actors. It ties a later Bond to an event from Lazenby's film. It does not, however, give an in-story reason for why Bond looks different.

That leaves viewers with a fixed point rather than a full answer. The face changed between 1969 and 1981. The marriage, and the loss behind it, stayed attached to the same man.

M and Q return throughout the Bond films, but the actors who play them change over time. Supporters of the code-name theory treat that turnover as a sign the series handles key roles as posts that different people can fill.

M is the head of Bond's service and the figure who sends him on his assignments. Q runs the department that supplies his equipment. On screen, both characters are known by a single letter rather than a full name. A letter reads more like a job title than like a person's identity, and that is the detail the theory leans on.

Judi Dench played M from GoldenEye (1995) through Skyfall (2012). Her run covers 17 years. It also straddles Casino Royale (2006), the film that restarted the series with a new origin story for Bond. The same actor therefore held the role of M on both sides of that reset. The character stayed in place even as the series began Bond's story again.

Skyfall also shows the M title changing hands inside the story itself. Dench's M dies in that film. Gareth Mallory, played by Ralph Fiennes, then takes over the post. Here the films treat M openly as an office that one person leaves and another fills.

The code-name theory builds on this kind of continuity. If a letter-based title can move from one actor to the next, the argument goes, the name James Bond might work the same way. On that reading, each new Bond actor would be playing a new agent who inherits the name along with the job.

The comparison has a limit. M and Q are presented as designations tied to a position inside the service. James Bond is presented as a personal name, the one he gives when he introduces himself. Mallory keeps his own name when he becomes M. A new face behind a single-letter title shows that the office can change hands. It does not show that a man's own name can.

The M and Q pattern is consistent with the code-name theory, but it does not establish it.

Casino Royale (2006) restarted the James Bond film series with Daniel Craig in the lead. The film shows Bond earning his 00 status, telling his origin as a new story rather than continuing an old one.

That structure matters for the code-name theory. A code name implies a line of agents. Each would take the identity from the agent who held it before him. The newest holder would arrive with a predecessor's history already attached.

A reboot works differently. It sets the earlier films aside and starts the same character's life again from an earlier point. Nothing is inherited. The earlier adventures no longer form part of his record.

Craig's Bond is not presented as a recruit stepping into an established identity. He is James Bond at the start of his career, before he holds a license to kill. His promotion to 00 status is the event the story builds from.

That sequence runs against the code-name reading. Under the theory, the name would come with the 007 post. In Casino Royale, the order is reversed. The man already has the name, and he has to earn the number. The promotion confers the 00 prefix, not the identity.

The film's title also signals a fresh start. Casino Royale shares its name with Ian Fleming's first Bond novel. By borrowing that title, the 2006 film returns to the character's starting point instead of picking up from the most recent adventure.

The reboot leaves one loose thread. Judi Dench, who first played M in GoldenEye (1995), stays in the role for Casino Royale. The same actor in the same part sits on both sides of the restart.

The film does not explain that overlap. It also does not present Craig's Bond as the agent from the earlier films. The casting carries over, while the story begins again.

Skyfall (2012) takes Bond to his family estate in Scotland and establishes that his parents are dead. Those two details give the name James Bond a personal history. A code name passed between agents would carry no such history.

The estate shares its name with the film. Skyfall is not an MI6 safe house or a cover identity. It is the Bond family's property, and the film presents it as the place Bond comes from.

That detail cuts against the code-name theory. The theory holds that "James Bond" is a title handed from one agent to the next. A title does not come with a family home. It does not come with a mother and a father either.

Skyfall attaches both to the name. The man called James Bond in this film is the son of a specific family. The house in Scotland belongs to that family. For the theory to hold, that history would have to belong to someone other than the agent using the name. The film gives no sign of a split like that.

The family link also changes what the surname means. If the estate belongs to the Bond family, then "Bond" came to him through his parents, not through an MI6 posting. In this film the name is inherited at birth rather than issued with a job.

The film's title points in the same direction. Rather than naming a villain, a weapon or a mission, Skyfall takes its name from a private house. That choice ties the title to Bond's own past rather than to his work.

The film belongs to the Daniel Craig run of the series, which began with a fresh origin story. Where that story showed his promotion to 00 status, Skyfall reaches further back, to the family behind the agent.

The evidence has limits. Skyfall describes the Craig-era Bond only. It does not connect its family history to the versions played by earlier actors. On its own terms, the film shows that within one continuity, James Bond is a real name with a family behind it.

In the Bond films, the 00 prefix marks an agent with a license to kill. Bond is not the only agent who holds one, so the number works as a post within MI6 rather than a personal name.

GoldenEye (1995) shows this through 006, an agent played by Sean Bean. He and Bond are both 00 agents in the same service. Their numbers sit one apart. The designation is a slot that MI6 fills, and the film gives it to a different man with a different face.

Octopussy (1983) does the same with 009. His appearance shows that the series put other licensed agents on screen 12 years before GoldenEye. Across the two films, the 00 roster includes men besides Bond, and each holds his own number.

That pattern bears directly on the code name debate. A number that several agents can hold works the way fans imagine the name James Bond works. The films treat 007 as a designation an agent is assigned. They treat James Bond as the man who holds it.

Casino Royale (2006) adds a related detail. The film shows Bond earning his 00 status. He is already in MI6's service when the number arrives. He has the name before he has the number. The number is something MI6 grants. The name is something he already carries.

The name follows a different pattern from the number. Within each version of the series, the character called James Bond is one person. He carries his own history and his own relationships. The 00 prefix describes what he is licensed to do. The name describes who he is.

This separates two ideas the code name theory tends to merge. The films do contain a handed-down role, and it is the number. A viewer looking for something passed between agents can find it in the 00 designations themselves, which more than one officer can hold. The name James Bond stays attached to one man in each version.

Eon Productions, the company run by Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, has never formally declared a single continuity for the James Bond films. No official statement confirms that "James Bond" is a code name. None lays out a timeline that links every film.

That leaves the films as the record. Eon has produced the series since Dr. No in 1962. What appears on screen is the main guide to how Bond's history fits together.

On screen, the evidence points in two directions. Some films carry one man's past across different actors. Others restart the story with a new origin.

The cross-actor links rest on specific scenes. For Your Eyes Only (1981) shows Roger Moore's Bond at the grave of Tracy. Bond married her in On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969), when George Lazenby held the role. The scene treats both actors as the same person with a shared past.

Casino Royale (2006) breaks that chain. Daniel Craig's Bond earns his 00 status in that film. His career starts over rather than continuing from earlier entries.

The reboot did not replace everyone. Judi Dench played M from GoldenEye (1995) through Skyfall (2012). That span means the same actor held the role on both sides of the 2006 restart. A recurring character can carry over even when Bond's own story begins again.

Skyfall (2012) then gives the Craig version a family estate in Scotland and parents who have died. Those details tie the name to an individual with a birth family, not to a title handed between agents.

The 00 number works differently. Other agents in the films hold numbers such as 006 and 009. That pattern marks the number as an assignment. The name stays attached to one man in each version.

Without a formal statement from the producers, the code-name idea remains a fan theory. What the films show is one man's story running across several actors, followed by a reboot that started it again.

#5462. How Bond's rights passed from Ian Fleming to Amazon MGM Studios

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Who owns James Bond? Rights to 007 are split among Ian Fleming's estate, Danjaq and Amazon MGM Studios, shaped by decades of deals and legal disputes

James Bond is one character with several owners. The books that introduced him belong to one company. The films are controlled by others. For years, a third party also held a claim to some of his best-known enemies. Anyone asking who owns James Bond is really asking about a set of separate rights. Those rights have been bought, sold, contested and divided many times.

The story begins with Ian Fleming, the British author who created Bond on the page. His literary rights sit with Ian Fleming Publications. The screen rights followed a different path. In the 1960s, producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman set up Danjaq as a holding company to control the film franchise. A related company, Eon Productions, makes the movies.

That arrangement did not stay fixed. Saltzman sold his stake to United Artists in 1975. The sale turned a Hollywood studio into a partner in the film rights. The studio's share later sat with MGM, which also distributes the films in the U.S.

A separate fight ran alongside the main franchise. Filmmaker Kevin McClory spent years in a legal battle over the story behind Thunderball. He won rights tied to its story elements, including the criminal organization SPECTRE and its leader, Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Those rights made room for a Bond film outside the official series, Never Say Never Again, released in 1983. MGM and Danjaq later acquired the McClory interests and ended the dispute.

Amazon $AMZN is the newest name in that chain. The company announced a deal to buy MGM in May 2021 and completed it in March 2022. With MGM came the studio's stake in the films. In February 2025, Amazon MGM Studios reached an agreement with Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, the longtime Eon producers. Under it, Amazon took creative control of the franchise. Broccoli and Wilson remain co-owners of the Bond intellectual property through Danjaq.

The 10 slides that follow take these ownership events one at a time. They cover the author, the companies, the studio sales, the legal battle and the most recent deal. Each explains who holds which piece of 007, how it changed hands and who now shapes the character's future on screen. They are a selection of the main moments, not a complete legal history of the franchise.

James Bond began as a character in a book, not a film. British author Ian Fleming introduced him in Casino Royale, a spy novel published in the U.K. in 1953. Every later claim to the 007 rights traces back to that novel and the books that followed it.

Fleming wrote the manuscript in early 1952 at Goldeneye, his house on the north coast of Jamaica. The London publisher Jonathan Cape released it in April 1953. Bond arrived as an established agent, with the 007 designation already assigned to him.

The plot is compact. Britain's Secret Service sends Bond to a casino in Royale-les-Eaux, a fictional resort town in northern France. His target is Le Chiffre, an agent working for the Soviet Union who has lost money he cannot account for. Bond's task is to beat him at baccarat and leave him ruined.

Fleming drew on his own career for the setting. During World War II, he served in British naval intelligence. He worked as personal assistant to Admiral John Godfrey, the director of naval intelligence. That experience gave the book its attention to tradecraft, office politics and the mechanics of espionage.

The character's name has its own origin. Fleming borrowed it from James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote a field guide to the birds of the West Indies. Fleming wanted a name that sounded plain, and the bird expert's name suited that purpose.

Casino Royale was the first of 12 Bond novels. Fleming also wrote Bond short stories, collected in For Your Eyes Only in 1960 and in Octopussy and The Living Daylights, published after his death. Fleming died in 1964. His final novel, The Man with the Golden Gun, appeared the following year.

The novels supplied the characters, titles and plots that producers later adapted for the screen. Film titles such as Dr. No, Goldfinger and Thunderball come directly from Fleming's books. That literary source is the starting point for every rights question that followed, from the books themselves to the films and the disputes over them.

The rights to Ian Fleming's James Bond novels belong to Ian Fleming Publications, the company that represents the author's estate. The company was previously known as Glidrose.

Both names refer to the same rights holder. Glidrose is the older name. Ian Fleming Publications is the name the company uses today.

This ownership covers Bond on the page. Fleming's novels are the original source of the character, and the literary rights attach to those books.

The films are a separate matter. The movie series has its own chain of owners. Danjaq LLC holds the film franchise, and Eon Productions makes the films.

That split is why the question of who owns James Bond has more than one answer. A question about the novels points to Ian Fleming Publications. A question about the movies points to Danjaq, Eon and the studio partners that have held a share of the film rights over the decades.

The two sides of Bond have also followed different histories. The film rights have passed through several hands. The literary rights have stayed with the company tied to Fleming's estate, under its old name and its current one.

Studio deals involving MGM concern the film franchise. On their own terms, they are not transactions over Fleming's books.

Danjaq LLC is the holding company behind the James Bond film franchise. Producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman set it up in the 1960s to hold their rights to the 007 movies.

Broccoli, known as Cubby, was an American producer who wanted to bring the books to the screen. Saltzman, who was born in Canada, had secured an option on most of Fleming's novels before the two men teamed up. Their partnership paired Broccoli's interest in the books with Saltzman's option.

The company's name comes from its founders' wives. It joins the first names of Dana Broccoli and Jacqueline Saltzman.

Danjaq's role is ownership rather than filmmaking. It holds the franchise's rights. Eon Productions, a separate company, handles the production of each film.

That split matters for anyone tracing who controls Bond on screen. The character began in Ian Fleming's novels, and the books remain a separate property. Danjaq's interest covers the film franchise, not Fleming's writing.

United Artists was tied to the franchise from the start. The studio financed and distributed Dr. No, the first Eon Bond film, in 1962.

Danjaq has not held the film rights alone for most of its history. After Saltzman sold his stake to United Artists in 1975, Danjaq and the studio shared the film rights. That studio interest later sat with MGM, which distributes the films in the U.S.

Broccoli kept his interest in Danjaq after Saltzman's exit. Of the two families in the company's name, only the Broccolis remained. His daughter, Barbara Broccoli, and his stepson, Michael G. Wilson, went on to lead Danjaq and Eon in later decades. Wilson is the son of Dana Broccoli from an earlier marriage. That makes him Barbara Broccoli's half-brother.

Danjaq remains the vehicle for the family's stake. Under a February 2025 agreement, Amazon $AMZN MGM Studios took creative control of the films. Broccoli and Wilson stayed co-owners of the Bond intellectual property through Danjaq.

Eon Productions is the company that makes the official James Bond films. It handles the filmmaking itself, while the related holding company Danjaq controls the film rights those movies depend on.

Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman formed Eon in London in 1961. Its first Bond film, Dr. No, was released in 1962 with Sean Connery as 007. That film adapted Fleming's 1958 novel of the same name. Eon has remained a British company through every film in the series since.

Eon carries out the practical work of producing a Bond film. That work covers developing scripts, hiring directors, casting actors and running the shoot. The company has long based its productions at Pinewood Studios, west of London. Pinewood's 007 Stage was built for The Spy Who Loved Me, which came out in 1977. The stage burned down in 1984. It was rebuilt and renamed the Albert R. Broccoli 007 Stage.

The division between Eon and Danjaq separates making the films from owning them. Eon is the name audiences see in the opening credits. Danjaq is the entity that holds the rights behind those credits.

Control of Eon's productions passed to a new generation in the 1990s. Barbara Broccoli, Albert's daughter, and Michael G. Wilson, his stepson, took over as the lead producers. GoldenEye, released in 1995 with Pierce Brosnan in the role, was the first Bond film they produced together. Albert R. Broccoli died the following year, in 1996.

Broccoli and Wilson also oversaw the reboot that began with Casino Royale in 2006. That film adapted Fleming's first Bond novel and introduced Daniel Craig as 007.

The most recent Eon production is No Time to Die, released in 2021. It was Craig's fifth and final appearance as Bond. It is also the 25th film in Eon's official series. That count leaves out Bond films made by other companies.

Harry Saltzman sold his share of the James Bond film franchise to United Artists in 1975. From then on, Danjaq and United Artists shared the film rights to 007.

Saltzman had built the series with Albert R. Broccoli. The two producers set up Danjaq in the 1960s as the holding company for the films. Eon Productions, their production company, made the movies themselves.

United Artists was already part of the story before the sale. The studio released Dr. No in 1962, the first film in the Eon series. It went on to distribute the Bond films that followed through the rest of the 1960s and into the 1970s.

The 1975 deal changed that relationship. United Artists was no longer only the company that put the films in theaters. It now held part of the rights to the character on screen, alongside Danjaq.

Broccoli kept his position through Danjaq. Saltzman's departure ended the arrangement in which two independent producers jointly controlled the franchise.

The change showed up on screen in the credits. Saltzman and Broccoli had shared producer credit on every Eon Bond film since Dr. No. Their last joint production was The Man with the Golden Gun, released in 1974 with Roger Moore as Bond. The next entry, The Spy Who Loved Me, came out in 1977 and named Broccoli as its sole producer.

The structure set in 1975 still frames Bond franchise ownership. One side is a producer-owned company, Danjaq. The other is a studio stake that has moved through later corporate deals.

The Danjaq side has stayed in the Broccoli family. Barbara Broccoli, Albert R. Broccoli's daughter, and Michael G. Wilson, his stepson, are co-owners of the Bond intellectual property through the company.

The sale involved only the films. Saltzman's stake did not touch the James Bond novels, which sit outside Danjaq's holdings. Those books are controlled by Ian Fleming Publications, the company that represents Fleming's estate.

Kevin McClory won a share of the rights to story elements from Thunderball after a long legal fight. Those elements include SPECTRE, the criminal organization Bond confronts across several stories, and its leader, Ernst Stavro Blofeld.

The dispute fell outside the usual split of Bond ownership. Most of the character's story material traces back to Ian Fleming's novels. Ian Fleming Publications holds the literary rights, and Danjaq controls the film side. The Thunderball material did not fit neatly into that arrangement.

McClory's claim centered on the story behind Thunderball rather than on Bond as a whole. He did not gain control of the character or of the wider film series. His rights were tied to specific elements of that one story.

SPECTRE gave Bond a recurring, organized enemy rather than a single villain in each adventure. Blofeld runs SPECTRE, which made him the villain most closely tied to that recurring threat.

That overlap created a practical problem. Two separate parties held claims touching the same villains and the same plot material. Any producer who wanted to use SPECTRE or Blofeld had to account for McClory's position.

The outcome of the legal fight left a portion of Bond's story world outside the control of the main film rights holders.

Never Say Never Again is a 1983 James Bond film made outside Eon Productions' official series. It exists because Kevin McClory held rights to the Thunderball story material. Those rights let a rival production bring Bond to the screen without Danjaq or Eon.

The film retells the plot of Thunderball, which Eon had already adapted for the screen in 1965. In both versions, the criminal organization SPECTRE steals nuclear weapons and holds the world to ransom. The 1983 film kept that core premise and reworked many of the details around it.

Sean Connery returned to play Bond. He had starred in six Eon films, starting with Dr. No in 1962 and ending with Diamonds Are Forever in 1971. The title nods to Connery's earlier vow never to play Bond again. Never Say Never Again was his last film as 007.

Jack Schwartzman produced the film, and McClory received an executive producer credit. Irvin Kershner, who had directed The Empire Strikes Back, directed it. Warner Bros. distributed the film in the U.S.

The cast surrounding Connery was largely new to the franchise. Klaus Maria Brandauer played the villain Largo, and Max von Sydow played Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Kim Basinger played Domino $DPZ, and Barbara Carrera played the assassin Fatima Blush. Edward Fox played M, Bond's superior.

Several familiar parts of the Eon formula are absent. The film does not open with the gun-barrel sequence that begins Eon's entries. It also does not use the James Bond Theme. Michel Legrand wrote the score instead.

The release put two competing Bond films in cinemas in the same year. Eon released Octopussy, starring Roger Moore, a few months before Never Say Never Again arrived. Audiences in 1983 could see two different actors play the same character in two unrelated productions.

Never Say Never Again is not counted among Eon's official Bond films. It showed what split ownership of 007 meant in practice: a second producer, a second studio and a second Bond on screen.

MGM and Danjaq bought out the Thunderball rights held by Kevin McClory's interests. The purchase ended a long dispute over who could put SPECTRE and Ernst Stavro Blofeld on screen.

Those rights grew out of McClory's earlier legal fight over the story elements of Thunderball. SPECTRE is the criminal organization in that story. Blofeld is the villain who leads it.

The two buyers already controlled the official Bond film business. Danjaq is the holding company that Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman set up in the 1960s to control the film franchise. MGM is the studio partner in the film rights, and it distributes the Bond films in the U.S.

Before the buyout, the McClory rights sat outside that ownership structure. That gap allowed Never Say Never Again to reach cinemas in 1983 without Eon Productions, the company that makes the official films.

The acquisition closed that gap. It placed SPECTRE and Blofeld with the same owners as the rest of the Bond film rights. It also removed the outside claim that had made a Bond film beyond Eon's series possible.

Amazon $AMZN became a part-owner of the James Bond films when it completed its purchase of MGM in March 2022. MGM's stake in the 007 film franchise transferred with the studio. That put Amazon on the studio side of Bond's film ownership, opposite Danjaq LLC.

The acquisition took about 10 months from announcement to completion. Amazon announced in May 2021 that it would buy MGM. The studio now sits inside the company as part of Amazon MGM Studios.

Amazon bought MGM's position in Bond, not the whole franchise. The film rights have long been split between a Hollywood studio and Danjaq, the holding company Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman created to control the films.

The studio's share dates to Saltzman's decision to sell his stake to United Artists. United Artists then held the film rights jointly with Danjaq. It later became part of MGM. That chain of ownership is how a piece of 007 ended up with Amazon.

Danjaq was not part of the sale. Neither was Eon Productions, the related company that makes the films. Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, co-owners of the Bond intellectual property through Danjaq, kept their position after Amazon took over MGM. The franchise gained a new studio partner. The holding company on the other side stayed the same.

Distribution came with the purchase as well. MGM distributes the Bond films in the U.S. The studio that releases 007 movies to American audiences therefore became part of Amazon.

Amazon's ownership began after Daniel Craig's run as Bond had ended. No Time to Die, released in 2021, was his fifth and final film in the role. When the MGM deal closed, no Bond film had followed it.

Owning MGM did not, on its own, give Amazon creative control of Bond. That came later, through a separate agreement with Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

In February 2025, Amazon $AMZN MGM Studios reached an agreement with Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson that gave Amazon creative control of the James Bond film franchise. The pair kept their co-ownership of the Bond intellectual property, which they hold through Danjaq.

Broccoli and Wilson have family ties to the franchise's founding producer. Barbara Broccoli is the daughter of Albert R. Broccoli, who co-founded Danjaq with Harry Saltzman. Michael G. Wilson is Albert R. Broccoli's stepson. Wilson also co-wrote several Bond screenplays in the 1980s, including For Your Eyes Only and Licence to Kill. Through their stake, the Broccoli family still holds an interest in the film rights.

The agreement split two roles that had sat together for decades: owning the 007 film rights and deciding what reaches the screen. Before the deal, Broccoli and Wilson held creative authority over the series. They exercised it through Eon Productions, the company that makes the films. After the deal, that authority belonged to Amazon MGM Studios.

Ownership did not shift in the same way. The agreement changed who runs the series. It did not move Broccoli and Wilson's Danjaq stake to Amazon.

Amazon MGM Studios is Amazon's film and television division. Its interest in Bond came through the MGM acquisition, which brought the studio's share of the film rights. The February 2025 agreement added creative control to that existing stake.

The deal followed the end of one Bond era. No Time to Die, released in 2021, was Daniel Craig's fifth and final film as Bond. Decisions about what follows it now rest with Amazon MGM Studios.

That leaves a layered answer to who owns James Bond. Ian Fleming Publications holds the rights to Fleming's novels. Danjaq holds Broccoli and Wilson's share of the film property. Amazon MGM Studios holds the stake that came with MGM, along with creative control of the films.

#5461. Tech Moves: Wizards of the Coasts names president; new execs at Skydance, Pulumi, Marchex and Syndio

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:24 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:04 am

— Dan Ayoub, the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games. Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said. “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”

Earlier in his career, Ayoub spent more than a decade at Microsoft, primarily with its 343 Industries video game studio, now called Halo Studios.

— Farah Ali has joined the media company Skydance as vice president of engineering, based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. She previously spent a decade at Electronic Arts over two stints, most recently as vice president of AI transformation and technology.

Ali has also served as an affiliate professor at the University of Washington, teaching courses in software entrepreneurship, and as a technical advisor for Madrona Venture Labs. She was co-founder and chief technology officer of FreightWeb, a Seattle-based logistics technology startup.

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth.

— Irene Chang has joined Pulumi as chief revenue officer. The Seattle startup automates cloud infrastructure tasks such as managing networks and databases, optimizing costs and ensuring compliance.

Chang said Pulumi’s culture and product won her over. “We automate deployments so teams can provision resources in seconds and scale from simple apps to enterprise architectures without losing control or compliance,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

Chang was previously Postman’s VP of corporate sales for the Americas and before that held VP roles at Cloudflare.

Pulumi is No. 15 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Marchex, the Seattle-based, publicly traded call and conversation analytics company, has named Travis Fairchild as president. The news was disclosed in an SEC filing. Fairchild was previously with Marchex for 18 years in strategy and business development roles.

He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

— General Fusion has named David Janashvili as chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company is developing fusion energy devices and became the first fusion venture to go public, through a SPAC. It trades on Nasdaq as GFUZ.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.

— Gravity Payments has appointed CEO Tammi Kroll as chairman of its board of directors while she continues to lead the digital payments company.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

Kroll joined the company in 2015 as CTO, chief operating officer and chief information officer. She took over as CEO in 2022 after founder Dan Price resigned while facing assault and reckless driving charges. That case and a second were dropped, and Price maintained his innocence.

— Syndio, a Seattle-based pay equity startup, has two more leadership changes following the addition of seven new executives in April:

Syndio is No. 45 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Seattle-based real estate brokerage Redfin has named Andy Swanton as general manager of rentals. He returns to the company after a short stint in 2022 as VP of properties. Swanton has also worked for Opendoor and BYD.

— Seattle cybersecurity company ExtraHop has appointed Rupert Clayson as head of sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). The company reports growth in sectors including financial services and energy, and offers defense against AI-assisted security attacks. Clayson, who is based in London, joined from TeamViewer and was previously with Fortinet.

— POSaBIT Systems, a Seattle-based company providing point-of-sale and payments technology for the cannabis industry, has named Emily Eagon as CFO. Eagon joined POSaBIT last year as vice president of finance and has more than 25 years of experience in finance and accounting roles, including leadership at Verdigris and predictis.

— Benjamin Mullins has returned to Amazon as head of program management for the Devices Brand Studio. Mullins spent four years with Prime until 2019, when he left for a role at Oracle. He then joined Meta, where he was head of product for Reality Labs.

— Debra Bouchegnies has announced she is retiring from the University of Washington’s CoMotion Labs at the end of the year. Bouchegnies is CoMotion’s associate director of marketing and has been with the program since 2018. A replacement has not been named.

— Aman Dhingra has been appointed to the Technology Alliance board of directors. Dhingra has been with McKinsey & Co. for 17 years and serves as a partner.

#5458. Nvidia's board isn't considering bringing Jensen Huang back, is focused on investigation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A petition to reinstate the former CEO has drawn nearly 180,000 signatures as the board continues its investigation

Nvidia $NVDA's board is not weighing a return by Jensen Huang to the CEO post and is concentrating on an inquiry into his conduct, according to CNBC, which cited a source with knowledge of the situation.

The board has retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run an inquiry into whether Huang’s conduct put national security or corporate secrets at risk.

An online petition pushing the board to restore Huang to the job is approaching 180,000 signatures, according to CNBC. Backers include Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

President Donald Trump said Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO and that he thought Huang had learned a “big lesson.”Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said in a Monday interview with CNBC that Huang had not raised the idea of returning when they spoke.

Huang resigned last week amid reports that he had been unfaithful with at least two women, and the campaign to bring him back has since drawn support from tech executives. U.S. officials suspect one of the women, Alice Huang, of relaying information to China's intelligence services. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.

The board opened an independent investigation on Nov. 8, the day Huang admitted infidelity in a note to employees. After Huang resigned on Thursday, it named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO.

Gerstner and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, both Nvidia shareholders, wrote a letter Friday urging the board to weigh all options, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang." The letter stopped short of demanding that he be brought back right away.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a dramatic shake-up at Nvidia on Sunday and said the board should seek its next CEO from beyond Nvidia's own ranks. He said he wants answers from the board and outside counsel within 10 days.

The board said Friday that it is selecting a search firm. "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC. The spokesperson characterized talk of specific names for the job as premature.

U.S. lawmakers plan to probe the national security ramifications of Huang's affair as well as his ties to Trump and the president's Cabinet, according to CNBC.

Nvidia will release results for its fiscal third quarter on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

#5457. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5456. Nvidia debuts new Rubin HPC chip, scientific research libraries

Nvidia Corp. today introduced a set of offerings designed to speed up scientific research across a range of fields.

The lineup is headlined by Rubin HPC, an upcoming graphics card with significantly more cores than the company’s current flagship chip. It’s joined by over a half-dozen software tools geared towards scientists and engineers. The technologies made their debut at the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago.

Nvidia’s flagship Rubin graphics processing unit features 898 Tensor cores, transistor clusters specifically optimized for large language models. It also includes over 28,000 CUDA cores. Those circuits can run not only LLMs but also other workloads such as scientific simulations.

The Rubin HPC (pictured), the upcoming chip that Nvidia previewed today, will feature over 50,000 CUDA cores. It will also ship with a new iteration of NVLink, the interconnect that Nvidia’s GPUs use to exchange data with central processing units. The current version of the technology can move 3.6 terabits per second per graphics card.

Nvidia stated that Rubin HPC will also include a “sparse data acceleration” feature. Sparse data is the technical term for datasets that contain a large number of zeros. Many scientific projects generate such data, particularly in fields such as biology and astrophysics. A telescope, for example, might use zeros to represent sections of space without any visible stars.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

Nvidia plans to ship Rubin HPC in 2028. In the meantime, customers can speed up their scientific workloads using the software tools that debuted alongside the chip today.

Nvidia ships its GPUs  with a collection of libraries called CUDA-X that is designed to ease scientific research projects. The company’s SC26 announcement introduced several new additions to the suite.

Astrophysicists are gaining access to cuPhoton.xBeam, a library that makes it easier to analyze data from the Event Horizon Telescope network. It’s a collection of observatories used study black holes. According to Nvidia, cuPhoton.xBeam can perform data analysis tasks that historically took a month in eight minutes. It’s rolling out alongside cuPhoton.xLens, a library for simulating the plasma that fusion reactors use to generate electricity.

On the biology research side, Nvidia is open-sourcing cuSpa. It speeds up cell polygon calculations, which are used to study the structure of cells and the manner in which they interact with one another. Plus, an existing cellular analysis tool called rapids-singlecell is now available to Nvidia users in a containerized format.

Nvidia’s new biology research tools are joined by an AI bundle called Nemotron for Science. It’s built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open-source LLM the company introduced last month. The model features 124 billion parameters and activates about a tenth of them at any given time. It’s partly based on Mamba-2, a more hardware-efficient alternative to the ubiquitous Transformer model architecture.

Nemotron for Science pairs the LLM with a set of pre-packaged post-training workflows. Researchers can use them to optimize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specific scientific tasks. Additionally, Nvidia has added in nearly 50,000 chemistry-related questions. They can be used to post-train AI models and evaluate the capabilities of models that have already gone through the process.

“Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries,” Buck said.

Quantum computers rely on a conventional processor to manage their qubits. Nvidia provides a set of software tools called CUDA-Q that makes it easier to link quantum hardware to its GPUs and CPUs. The company today expanded the suite with new building blocks for developing quantum software and an algorithm that can mitigate qubit errors.

Nvidia is teaming up with IBM Corp. and the U.S. Energy Department’s Fermilab to create a “modular quantum codesign platform”. It will combine the chip giant’s DGX B200 systems with quantum hardware from IBM. According to the companies, the goal is to create an environment that researchers can use to develop new qubit error correction algorithms and other quantum software.

#5455. The U.S. will tighten AI chip restrictions after Nvidia's Jensen Huang saga put the spotlight on a loophole

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A new rule follows weeks of scrutiny of chip exports, and as Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim final rule that will require licenses to export advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. The rule also restricts remote access to U.S. chips through data centers overseas.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the bureau said in a statement. It said the Treasury Department and the National Security Council wrote the rule and directed its release.

Under the rule text, a license will be required to send chips to data centers that supply significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5. Data centers, foreign foundries and chip exporters must perform due diligence on customers' direct or indirect ownership or control. Data centers already providing such computing power must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date or face future export restrictions. Commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers and social media companies, are exempt.

The five-country requirement applies in addition to existing license requirements, the rule says. It does not apply to chips destined for companies headquartered in the United States, or with a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. Commerce will review applications case by case. The rule describes the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.

The rule also formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, which it says was never enforced.

The rule takes effect on its publication in the Federal Register, with comments due 60 days after. It had not been posted as of 9 a.m. ET Monday.

Nvidia $NVDA stock slid by as much as 2.9% on Monday, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost up to 5.5%.

The rule is meant to limit Chinese companies' access to advanced AI chips. It comes as President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday in Shenzhen, and as pressure grows on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to tighten export controls.

The rule follows weeks of scrutiny of chip exports. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week and acknowledged a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is suspected of spying for China. Megaspeed is accused of illegally shipping export-controlled chips into China and has denied wrongdoing. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, has asked Jensen Huang to testify on Dec. 3 and Lutnick on Dec. 10. Lutnick has agreed to appear.

Before the rule, U.S. export controls covered the physical transfer of chips but not remote access to them, Cassia King, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, said last week.

#5454. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

#5453. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5452. AAA sees fewer Thanksgiving travelers as gas prices hit records and airfares climb 17%

Free daily briefing on global business news.

AAA projects 81.5 million Thanksgiving travelers, down 0.1% and ending a three-year streak of record holiday travel

AAA projects 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, 0.1% fewer than last year, as record gas prices and higher airfares weigh on trips.

The forecast covers Tuesday, Nov. 24, through Monday, Nov. 30. The projection is about 121,000 fewer than the 81.6 million who traveled last year, AAA said.

"After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year," Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA Travel, said in a statement. "But travelers won't notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels."

AAA projects 72.9 million people will travel by car, down 200,000 from 73.1 million last year. The group tied the drop in part to record gas prices. August, September and October each set a monthly record at the pump, and November could do the same. No Thanksgiving Day national average has topped $4 a gallon, and the highest was $3.58 in 2022.

About 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights, a 0.2% decrease from last year, AAA said. Roundtrip domestic flights reserved for the holiday run 17% above year-ago prices, with the typical ticket costing $800. Buses, trains and cruises are expected to carry 2.6 million people, up 4.1%.

Gas prices were just above $4 a gallon on Nov. 9, with AAA's measure of the national average at about $4.01. AAA data show no November before 2026 had a nationwide average above $4. Prices have dropped since last week but still sit above year-ago levels.

AAA prepared its forecast the week of Oct. 12. A nationwide FAA ground stop last Friday ran past the four-hour mark and snarled air travel through the weekend, according to The Washington Times. AAA spokesperson Aixa Diaz said the stop should not meaningfully dent holiday trips unless a repeat occurs, according to The Washington Times. Diaz said people planning holiday trips rarely stay put without a major disruption, according to The Washington Times.

INRIX, a transportation data provider, expects Tuesday and Wednesday to be the busiest days on the road as people head out, AAA said. Sunday and Monday should be busiest for the return. Congestion in New York, Washington, Los Angeles and Boston could be more than double normal levels, according to INRIX.

#5451. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”
