#5450. Who does James Bond work for? MI6, the Secret Intelligence Service

Free daily briefing on global business news.

MI6 vs. MI5 explained in 10 points, from James Bond's fictional employer to the headquarters, legal powers and ministerial oversight of each British agency

James Bond, the spy Ian Fleming created, is written as an officer of a real government agency. That agency is MI6, formally the Secret Intelligence Service, often shortened to SIS. Fleming's novels usually call Bond's employer simply the Secret Service. The films settled on MI6. The 00 section and its license to kill belong to fiction, not to the real service.

Much of the confusion comes from a second agency with almost the same shorthand name. MI5, formally the Security Service, works inside the U.K. Its remit covers counter-espionage, counter-terrorism and protective security at home. MI6 looks outward and gathers foreign intelligence. The two numbers sit one digit apart, but the jobs behind them point in opposite directions.

That divide between foreign and domestic work sits at the center of the MI6 vs. MI5 question. It also means a fictional MI6 officer chasing villains through London is working on another agency's ground. Inside the U.K., that territory would properly fall to MI5 or the police.

The two agencies share a single origin. Both trace back to the Secret Service Bureau, founded in 1909. The bureau split into home and foreign sections. The numbered names came from War Office military intelligence designations. For most of their history, neither service rested on statute. MI5 gained a statutory basis through the Security Service Act 1989. MI6 followed with the Intelligence Services Act 1994. That law also brought public government acknowledgment of the service.

The differences run through the structure of each organization. MI5 reports to the Home Secretary. MI6 reports to the Foreign Secretary. The two work from separate London headquarters: MI6 at Vauxhall Cross and MI5 at Thames House on Millbank. MI6's chief is known as "C." Fleming modeled M on that tradition. MI5's head holds the title Director General. Their powers differ too. MI5 officers cannot make arrests. Police carry out arrests in MI5 cases.

The 10 slides that follow take one angle each. They cover the agencies' shared beginnings, the laws that govern them, ministerial oversight, their buildings and their chiefs. They also explain the limits on MI5's powers and how the Bond films have put MI6 on screen.

James Bond is written as an officer of MI6, the agency formally called the Secret Intelligence Service, or SIS. MI6 gathers foreign intelligence for Britain. Bond's fictional career belongs to that outward-facing remit.

Bond is not a real person. He is a character created by Ian Fleming, and no actual officer stands behind the name. The organization Fleming placed him in is real.

The novels and the films label that organization differently. In Fleming's books, Bond's employer is usually called the Secret Service. The films use MI6.

Those labels point to a single agency. The Secret Service of the novels, the MI6 of the films and the Secret Intelligence Service of formal usage all describe the same foreign-facing body.

MI5 is a different organization. Its formal name is the Security Service. It handles domestic security rather than foreign intelligence. Bond is not written as an MI5 officer.

Some of Bond's best-known trappings have no real-world equivalent. His 007 designation places him in the 00 section, and that section is fiction.

The same goes for the license to kill. MI6 officers do not hold a literal license to kill. The phrase belongs to the stories, not to the real service.

The short answer to who James Bond works for is MI6. The fuller answer is the Secret Intelligence Service, the formal name of the agency that Fleming's Secret Service stands in for.

MI5, formally known as the Security Service, protects the U.K. from threats at home. Its remit covers three areas: counter-espionage, counter-terrorism and protective security within the U.K.

The two names describe one organization. Security Service is the official title. MI5 is the widely used shorthand.

Counter-espionage means detecting and disrupting spying. For MI5, the target is foreign intelligence activity aimed at the U.K. and carried out on British soil. The task is defensive. The goal is to stop secrets from being stolen at home, not to collect secrets overseas.

Counter-terrorism is the second strand of the remit. Here the concern is terrorist violence planned or carried out inside the U.K. MI5's role is to identify those threats and investigate them.

Protective security is the third strand. It covers measures that make people, information and sites harder to attack or compromise. Counter-espionage and counter-terrorism deal with threats that already exist. Protective security aims to reduce exposure before a threat takes shape.

All three functions point inward. None of them involves gathering intelligence abroad. That domestic focus is what separates the Security Service's work from foreign intelligence gathering.

The line between Britain's two best-known intelligence agencies is drawn by geography. MI6 gathers intelligence abroad, while MI5 protects security inside the U.K.

MI6, formally the Secret Intelligence Service, faces outward. Its business is information about other countries and about threats that take shape beyond Britain's borders.

MI5, formally the Security Service, faces inward. Its work is defensive, and it is carried out at home rather than overseas.

The gap is one of purpose as well as place. Foreign intelligence means finding out what is happening in other parts of the world. Domestic security means guarding the country against threats that reach it.

The two shorthand names make the agencies sound like numbered branches of one organization. They are separate bodies with separate jobs. Each has its own legal basis, its own chief and its own minister.

Location usually settles which of the two agencies is responsible. Intelligence gathered in other countries belongs to MI6. Protecting the U.K. from threats at home belongs to MI5.

MI5 and MI6 share a single ancestor: the Secret Service Bureau, founded in 1909. The bureau split into a home section and a foreign section. Those two halves grew into the agencies known today as MI5 and MI6.

The home section dealt with matters inside the country. The foreign section looked outward. That division gave each future agency its basic direction long before either carried its modern name.

The home section is the root of MI5, now formally the Security Service. The foreign section is the root of MI6, now formally the Secret Intelligence Service. The modern split between domestic security and foreign intelligence follows the same line the bureau drew.

The shorthand names came from the War Office. MI5 and MI6 began as military intelligence designations within that department. The "MI" in each name stands for military intelligence. The number identified the section.

The formal titles leave that heritage behind. Neither "Security Service" nor "Secret Intelligence Service" contains the word "military." The popular names still carry the old War Office label.

The phrase "Secret Service" also lives on in fiction. Ian Fleming's novels usually use it for James Bond's employer.

MI5 was placed on a statutory footing by the Security Service Act 1989. MI6 gained the same footing through the Intelligence Services Act 1994, which also brought the British government's public acknowledgment of the service.

A statutory basis means an act of Parliament sets out an agency's existence and role in law. Before 1989, no act of Parliament did that for MI5. Before 1994, none did it for MI6.

Both services descend from the Secret Service Bureau of 1909. Measured from that date, MI5 operated for 80 years before a statute defined it. MI6 operated for 85 years before the same happened.

The two laws arrived five years apart. The domestic Security Service was written into law first. The foreign-facing Secret Intelligence Service followed.

Each agency has its own statute rather than a shared one. The Security Service Act 1989 is MI5's law. The Intelligence Services Act 1994 is MI6's. The separate statutes match the split between a service that works at home and one that gathers intelligence abroad.

The 1994 act did two jobs for MI6. It wrote the service into law. It also marked the point at which the government publicly acknowledged that MI6 existed. Until then, the state the service worked for gave no official public confirmation of it.

That second change separates the two laws. The 1989 act gave MI5 a legal footing. The 1994 act gave MI6 both a legal footing and official public recognition. For 85 years, the real agency behind the fictional James Bond had no official public existence.

MI5 and MI6 answer to different cabinet ministers. The Security Service, known as MI5, reports to the Home Secretary. The Secret Intelligence Service, known as MI6, reports to the Foreign Secretary.

Each reporting line matches the agency's remit. MI5's work on counter-espionage, counter-terrorism and protective security takes place within the U.K. Those are domestic matters. The Home Secretary is the cabinet minister responsible for home affairs.

MI6 gathers foreign intelligence. Its work concerns other countries rather than threats inside the U.K. That outward focus lines up with the Foreign Secretary's brief. The Foreign Secretary handles the U.K.'s dealings with the rest of the world.

The split between the two ministers mirrors the split between the two services. The ministers' job titles offer a quick way to tell the agencies apart. Home points to MI5. Foreign points to MI6.

The same structure shows where James Bond would sit if his job were real. Bond is a fictional character, written as an officer of MI6. A real officer in that role would work for a service that answers to the Foreign Secretary, not the Home Secretary.

MI6, formally the Secret Intelligence Service, has its headquarters at Vauxhall Cross in London. MI5, formally the Security Service, is based at Thames House on Millbank, also in London.

Each address belongs to a different job. Vauxhall Cross houses the service that gathers foreign intelligence. Thames House houses the service responsible for security inside the U.K.

One agency works abroad and the other works at home. Even so, both main bases sit in the British capital. The split between the two services is a matter of remit, not of where their headquarters stand.

The buildings also offer a quick way to tell the services apart. A reference to Vauxhall Cross points to MI6. A reference to Thames House or Millbank points to MI5.

The chief of MI6 is known as "C," a tradition that began with Mansfield Smith-Cumming. MI5 is led by a Director General. The two services give their heads different titles.

Smith-Cumming signed documents in green ink. The single letter "C" did not stay with him. It passed to the post itself, and whoever runs the Secret Intelligence Service is known by it.

The letter works as a title rather than a name. It identifies the office, not the individual who holds it. A reader who sees "C" in a reference to British intelligence is looking at a job title, not a person's name.

MI5 uses a more conventional label. Its head is the Director General, a title that describes the job in ordinary administrative terms. Coverage of the Security Service's leadership uses that title rather than a code letter. The Director General heads the agency responsible for counter-espionage, counter-terrorism and protective security within the U.K.

Ian Fleming drew on the "C" tradition when he created "M," Bond's superior in the novels. M is a fictional character. The single-letter title, however, borrows from real practice at MI6. It gives Bond's boss the same initial-only identity that the real chief of the foreign intelligence service carries.

Fleming's novels usually call Bond's employer the Secret Service. The films use the name MI6. In both versions, M heads the fictional counterpart of the real agency led by C.

The borrowing runs in one direction. Fleming modeled M on C, not on the Director General of MI5. That fits the fiction as a whole, in which Bond serves the foreign-facing service rather than the domestic one.

The titles also offer a quick way to tell the agencies apart. A reference to "C" points to MI6, the Secret Intelligence Service, which gathers foreign intelligence. A reference to the Director General points to MI5, the Security Service.

MI5 officers do not have the power to arrest anyone. When a Security Service case reaches the point where a suspect must be detained, police officers make the arrest.

That limit applies across MI5's work. An officer on a counter-terrorism or counter-espionage case cannot personally take a suspect into custody, however far the investigation has gone.

The result is a case shared between two bodies. MI5 works on the threat itself. Police handle the arrest that follows. The detention happens under police authority, not the agency's own.

This separates the real MI5 from the image of an intelligence officer who both uncovers a plot and seizes the people behind it. In MI5's case, those are two different jobs. Two different organizations hold them.

It also marks a clear boundary around what the Security Service is. MI5 is an intelligence and security agency, not a police force. Its officers investigate threats. The power to arrest stays with the police.

The James Bond films place their hero inside MI6, the Secret Intelligence Service. GoldenEye (1995) and later films in the series show the agency's real headquarters at Vauxhall Cross in London.

The building on screen is not an invented office. Vauxhall Cross is where the real MI6 is based.

GoldenEye was released the year after the Intelligence Services Act 1994. That law placed MI6 on a statutory basis. It also brought the government's public acknowledgment of the service.

Judi Dench played M, the head of the service in the films. The character's title traces back to Ian Fleming, who modeled M on the tradition of "C." C is the title used by the real chief of MI6. That tradition began with Mansfield Smith-Cumming, who signed documents in green ink. On screen, the chief is M. In reality, the chief is C.

The films use the name MI6 for Bond's employer. Fleming's novels usually called it the Secret Service.

Parts of the screen job have no real counterpart. The 00 section is fiction. No MI6 officer holds a real license to kill.

Geography marks another gap between the films and reality. MI6 gathers foreign intelligence and reports to the Foreign Secretary. When a film sends Bond after a threat inside the U.K., that work would properly fall to MI5 or the police.

MI5, formally the Security Service, covers that domestic ground. Its remit is counter-espionage, counter-terrorism and protective security within the U.K. It reports to the Home Secretary rather than the Foreign Secretary. Its headquarters is Thames House on Millbank, London. Its head holds the title Director General.

Arrests mark a further difference. MI5 officers do not have arrest powers. Police make the arrests in MI5 cases. A domestic case resembling a Bond plot would close with police detaining a suspect, not an MI6 officer.

#5449. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5448. Proposed DHS rule would end deference to prior H-1B approvals. Here are 4 effects

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A proposed DHS rule would end USCIS deference to past approvals. Four effects workers and employers should plan for on H-1B renewals.

For a foreign professional on an H-1B visa, a renewal has usually meant building on a decision the government already made. The immigration officer who reviews an extension has started from the worker's last approval and leaned toward it, rather than judging the job and the employer from a blank page. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed taking that starting point away. Nothing has changed yet for anyone filing today, and the existing deference rules govern every petition until a final rule is issued. The public can comment on the proposal until Nov. 13, according to IANS, and the proposal is not yet law. Workers and their employers can use the time before a final rule to prepare for renewals that would have to stand on their own record.

Most of the change would land on workers from one country. DHS estimates the rule would reach about 208,000 petitions each year, and in fiscal 2024 Indian-born professionals received about 79% of the approvals for workers continuing in H-1B jobs, according to IANS. Indian workers and the companies that employ them would therefore face most of any added scrutiny of extensions. For those workers, a renewal that once rested on the last approval would become a new test of whether the job and the employer still qualify.

Mantra Law Office, an immigration law firm, laid out what could happen to H-1B renewals once U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services no longer gives weight to its own past decisions, from more paperwork for companies to less certainty for workers. These effects form a sequence. Each one follows from the one before it, beginning with an officer who is free to judge a renewal from scratch. The cost of that sequence won't be spread evenly. Many renewals may go through much as they do now, while the cases an officer singles out for a closer look can stall. The gap between the typical case and the unlucky one matters for each of the effects that follow.

The proposal changes where an officer starts a renewal, not what an H-1B worker has to prove. Today an officer reviewing an extension begins by leaning toward the earlier approval. Under the proposed rule, officers would lose the duty to start from that approval and could reassess a worker's eligibility independently, according to Mantra Law Office. The worker's history would still count. "This proposal would not prohibit USCIS officers from considering a prior approval where relevant," DHS said, as reported by IANS. An earlier approval would become one piece of evidence that an officer can weigh or set aside. A clean record would help a worker, but it would no longer guarantee the result.

Today an officer needs a reason before taking a second look at a case that was already approved. Under the existing standard, an officer can depart from the earlier decision only on finding that it rested on a material error, that the facts have materially changed, or that new information has come to light. If none of those is present, officers treat the questions the earlier approval answered as settled. The proposal would remove the need for any such finding. An officer could reopen questions that a previous officer already answered, even when nothing about the worker or the job has changed.

Without deference as the starting point, the outcome of a renewal would depend more on the officer who reviews it. Two officers looking at the same file would have more room to reach different decisions. How closely they examine a case would depend more on who opens it. A worker should treat the next renewal as a case to be made again rather than as a formality, even with the same employer and in the same job.

Every question an officer reopens is one the worker's file would have to answer again.

Officers who review an H-1B renewal without leaning on the last approval are likely to ask workers and employers for more evidence. An officer who starts fresh has to settle questions that the earlier approval once answered, such as whether the job still qualifies for the H-1B category and whether the employer still meets the requirements. The Department of Homeland Security anticipates that dropping the deference requirement could lead to more requests for evidence, according to Mantra Law Office. Such a rise would follow from the fresh reviews, because an officer who must judge every element again may ask for whatever the earlier file once settled. For a worker, a request for evidence means the petition isn't decided on what was filed, and the case stays open until the officer receives more.

Nobody knows how large any increase might be, because the DHS expectation has no number attached and no result has been measured yet. Officers could send requests in a handful of renewals or in a large share of them. That unknown is the real burden for workers, who can't tell in advance whether their renewal will be approved as filed or held for questions. The practical response is to stop treating the last approval as proof and to file as though a request is coming, with the case for eligibility already documented.

Each request has to be answered with documents, and those answers add up to a heavier filing burden.

Under the proposal, an employer filing an H-1B extension would have to make the case for the job again rather than rely on the fact that an officer approved it before. Employers may need fuller proof that the job and the employment relationship still fit the visa category, according to Mantra Law Office. An extension would then turn on what the company can show about the job today, not on a decision made years earlier. Closer reviews and more evidence requests leave employers with one sensible response, which is to answer an officer's likely questions in the original filing instead of waiting to be asked.

Most of the added proof concerns how the employer has set up the job, not the worker's degrees or experience. The company may have to show what the role is, what the worker does in it and how the company stands as the worker's employer, and the company keeps the records on each of those points. A short job description that won approval the first time may need to be rewritten in fuller detail so that it can justify a renewal without help from the earlier decision. For the worker, the outcome of a renewal therefore rests heavily on how carefully the employer describes and documents the role.

The earlier approval still belongs in the file as supporting evidence. Officers would not be barred from considering prior approvals when they are relevant, so employers have good reason to include them. An old approval can back up a renewal, but it cannot replace current proof that the job still qualifies.

The safest renewal is one an employer prepares to pass even if the officer has never seen the first approval.

With closer reviews, more requests for evidence and heavier paperwork, a worker filing to renew an H-1B can no longer count on how long the case will take or how it will end. Mantra Law Office writes that added scrutiny and possible requests for evidence raise burdens and make plans for continued employment less predictable. The uncertainty concerns the timeline and the outcome, not the worker's right to keep working once status ends. NIH says in guidance from 2021 that an officer does not have to approve an on-time extension before the worker can stay on the job. A wait with no decision date is harder to plan around than a known deadline, because the worker and the employer cannot settle their plans until an answer arrives.

That protection has a firm limit. In the same 2021 guidance, NIH says a worker may keep working up to 240 days past the end of status. When an officer slows a decision with added scrutiny and requests for evidence, each extra week of review uses part of that period. A fixed limit and a review of unknown length fit poorly together, because the slower the decision, the less of that cushion the worker has left.

Filing early is the one part of the process a worker controls. The 240-day protection applies only if USCIS receives the petition, with fees, before status expires, according to NIH guidance from 2021. With closer scrutiny likely, a worker who files late would give up the one protection that makes a long review bearable. A worker who files well ahead lets more of the review happen before status runs out, which leaves more room before day 240 if an officer pulls the case aside for questions.

If the proposal becomes final, a renewal will no longer rest on the last approval, and filing early will become the worker's main safeguard.

#5447. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5446. How the U.S. Emergency Alert System gets warnings to your TV, radio and phone

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How the U.S. Emergency Alert System works, from the agencies that run it to the codes, phone alerts and tests that get warnings to the public

A tornado warning from a National Weather Service forecast office can reach a car radio, a cable TV channel and a smartphone. That reach depends on shared digital codes, a federal gateway run by FEMA and legal obligations that bind broadcasters and cable systems. The Emergency Alert System carries warnings over radio, TV and cable. Wireless Emergency Alerts carry them to phones.

Knowing how the U.S. Emergency Alert System works explains why its messages look and sound the way they do. The two-tone sound heard during a broadcast alert is called the attention signal. A digital header sent with the alert carries instructions for receiving equipment. Those instructions identify the type of event, the counties affected and the time window the warning covers. Phone alerts take a different route from TV and radio alerts. They reach handsets by cell broadcast rather than by text message. Phone users can switch off some categories of alert, but not Presidential alerts.

The system's predecessors date to the Cold War. CONELRAD began in 1951, the Emergency Broadcast System replaced it in 1963 and the Emergency Alert System took over in 1997. Today the system carries a wide range of messages, including tornado warnings, flash flood warnings and AMBER alerts for abducted children. Federal, state, local, tribal and territorial agencies can all send messages through FEMA's gateway, but only after they are approved as senders.

The network has weak points. In January 2018, a false ballistic missile alert reached phones and broadcasts in Hawaii. Retracting it took 38 minutes, according to the FCC. The episode exposed the system's reliance on authorized senders getting messages right. It also depends on people having a working device turned on and nearby when a warning goes out.

The 10 slides that follow break the system into its working parts. They cover the three federal bodies that share responsibility for it and its history since 1951. They also explain which media providers must carry alerts, the SAME code carried in broadcast warnings and the relay chain that moves national messages from station to station. The remaining slides look at IPAWS and the Common Alerting Protocol, Wireless Emergency Alerts on cellphones and the National Weather Service's role. They close with the weekly, monthly and nationwide tests that check equipment and the limits that remain.

No single agency owns the Emergency Alert System. Three federal bodies run it jointly: the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Weather Service.

Each agency covers a separate function. The FCC sets and enforces the rules. FEMA operates the national alerting infrastructure. The National Weather Service supplies weather warnings. One alert can involve the work of more than one of these agencies before it reaches the public.

The Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, is the regulator. It writes the rules that govern how the EAS operates, and it enforces them. Those rules apply to radio and TV broadcasters, cable systems, satellite radio and TV providers, and wireline video providers. Each of these participants must carry alerts and keep EAS equipment. They must also run weekly and monthly tests.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, handles the national layer. It operates the national alerting infrastructure, and it is the agency that can trigger a national-level alert. FEMA designates the Primary Entry Point stations that receive national alerts first. Those stations pass the message on to other stations in a daisy chain.

FEMA also runs the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, known as IPAWS. Authorized federal, state, local, tribal and territorial agencies use it to send one message over several channels. Those messages are written in the Common Alerting Protocol, an XML-based format.

The National Weather Service, or NWS, issues the system's weather-related alerts. Its forecast offices originate warnings such as tornado warnings and flash flood warnings. Those warnings feed both the EAS and Wireless Emergency Alerts, which reach phones by cell broadcast. NOAA Weather Radio is a related channel for weather warnings.

A flash flood warning shows how the roles fit together. An NWS forecast office issues it. Broadcasters and cable systems carry it under rules the FCC writes and enforces. A national-level alert takes a different route, starting with FEMA and the Primary Entry Point stations it designates.

The Emergency Alert System replaced the Emergency Broadcast System in 1997. The Emergency Broadcast System had itself replaced CONELRAD, a Cold War warning system that began in 1951.

That sequence makes today's system the third national broadcast warning system the U.S. has used. CONELRAD came first. It started in 1951, in the early years of the Cold War.

The Emergency Broadcast System took over from CONELRAD in 1963. CONELRAD had been in service for 12 years.

The Emergency Broadcast System had a much longer run. It stayed in place for 34 years before the Emergency Alert System replaced it in 1997.

The two earlier systems covered 46 years in total, from CONELRAD's launch to the arrival of the Emergency Alert System.

The Emergency Alert System is the system in use today. The name of the national warning system has changed twice since 1951. Its purpose has stayed the same: getting official warnings to the public through broadcast channels.

Radio and TV broadcasters, cable systems, satellite radio and TV providers, and wireline video providers are the required participants in the Emergency Alert System. Each one must carry alerts and keep EAS equipment in place to receive them.

The obligation has two parts. A participant needs working equipment that can pick up an incoming alert. It also has to pass that alert along to its own audience. Owning the gear without airing the message does not meet the requirement.

The Federal Communications Commission sets these obligations and enforces them. The same agency writes the rest of the system's rules. Individual companies do not decide on their own whether to take part.

These categories cover the main ways people receive radio and TV at home or in the car. A person watching a satellite channel and a person listening to a local radio station are both reached through participants held to the same requirement.

Participants also serve as the links in the alert chain. A national alert passes from station to station in a daisy chain, with each participant's equipment receiving the message and delivering it to its own audience. State and local plans set out how alerts move between participants in each area.

The equipment requirement comes with a testing requirement. Every participant must run weekly and monthly tests. Those checks show whether its equipment can still receive an alert and pass it along.

Mobile phones are not on this list. Warnings reach phones through Wireless Emergency Alerts, a separate channel with its own rules. A household that relies only on a phone gets alerts through that system rather than through broadcast, cable or satellite participants.

Every Emergency Alert System message starts with a digital header built on Specific Area Message Encoding, known as SAME. The header tells receiving equipment who sent the alert, what kind of emergency it describes, which counties it covers and how long it applies.

SAME is data rather than speech. It travels as a coded signal at the front of an alert, ahead of the audio message or on-screen text that the public hears and reads. Broadcast and cable equipment reads that code before anything else in the alert.

The first field is the originator code. It identifies the type of sender behind the alert. Equipment down the line can then tell where a warning came from. A weather warning from the National Weather Service and a message from a local emergency agency carry different originator codes.

A three-letter event code follows. It names the hazard in compact form. TOR, for instance, stands for a tornado warning. With a separate code for each type of event, equipment can tell a tornado warning apart from other alerts without anyone listening to the audio.

Location codes come next. SAME uses FIPS codes, which identify individual counties. An alert can list several of them. A flash flood warning for two neighboring counties, for example, would carry two FIPS codes. That lets a warning name a specific area instead of an entire state.

The header also carries a time window. That field sets the period during which the alert is in effect.

The part of an alert meant for human ears begins with the attention signal. It combines two tones, one at 853 Hz and one at 960 Hz, sounded together. The combined sound marks the start of the spoken or written warning.

Every SAME message closes with an end-of-message code, NNNN. That code tells receiving equipment the alert is over.

The header and the tones do different jobs. The digital codes tell machines how to identify and sort an alert. The two tones tell people to stop and pay attention.

A national alert enters the Emergency Alert System through Primary Entry Point stations, which FEMA designates. From those stations, the message moves outward from one station to the next in a daisy chain until it reaches local audiences.

FEMA operates the national alerting infrastructure and can trigger alerts at the national level. Primary Entry Point stations are where such a message first lands. FEMA decides which stations fill that role. Those stations receive the national alert before any other station in the broadcast chain.

The relay works by handing the message along. One station carries the alert, and the next station picks it up and passes it on. Each handoff extends the warning into another station's coverage area. A message that starts at the entry points can spread across the broadcast network this way.

Under this structure, a station does not need its own direct connection to FEMA to carry a national alert. It needs only to receive the message from the station ahead of it in the chain. The trade-off is dependence on the links upstream. A station farther down the line can relay an alert only after the stations before it have passed the message along.

The national entry points handle only the first stage. State and local plans decide how an alert moves within a particular area. Those plans set up the local relay paths that carry a message the final distance to the stations serving a given community.

This station-to-station relay is the broadcast side of national alerting. Alerts on phones travel through a separate channel, Wireless Emergency Alerts, rather than being handed from one radio or TV station to the next.

The full route has three layers. A national message starts at the FEMA-designated entry stations and moves through the daisy chain. It then follows the local relay arrangements that each state and locality has set up.

IPAWS, FEMA's Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, is the gateway that lets an approved agency write one warning and send it over several alerting channels. The Common Alerting Protocol, or CAP, is the shared message format that makes this single-entry approach work.

The gateway is open to agencies at every level of government. Federal, state, local, tribal and territorial authorities are all eligible. A county emergency office and a federal agency can reach the public through the same system. Once a warning enters IPAWS, it follows the same route whatever the size of the agency that wrote it.

Access is not automatic. An agency must be approved before it can send alerts through IPAWS. That approval step controls who can put a message into the national alerting infrastructure, which FEMA operates. It also means every message in the gateway comes from an agency that has already been cleared to send.

CAP is an XML-based format. XML is a text-based markup language that computers can read and process. A CAP message packages a warning as structured data rather than free-form text. Each piece of information sits in a defined place within the message. Details such as the type of event, the area affected and the time the warning expires each have their own labeled field.

That common structure is what lets one message travel to more than one channel. Every approved sender uses the same format. An alerting official writes the warning once and submits it to IPAWS. The gateway then handles distribution. The message does not have to be rewritten for each outlet. Broadcast equipment and phone networks draw on the same core content. A warning on a TV screen and one on a cellphone therefore describe the same event for the same place.

IPAWS grew out of a 2006 executive order. The system that came from it sits between the agencies that write warnings and the channels that deliver them to the public.

Wireless Emergency Alerts, the phone-based layer of U.S. public warning, began in 2012. The messages reach mobile phones through cell broadcast technology rather than as ordinary text messages.

That difference shapes how the alerts behave. A text message is addressed to one phone number and delivered to that number alone. Sending a warning that way would require a list of every number in an affected area. Cell broadcast skips that step. One message goes out from cell towers to the compatible phones connected to them in the area being warned.

For the person holding the phone, that means there is nothing to sign up for. The sender never needs to know who is in the area or what their phone number is. A compatible phone that is switched on and connected to the network can display the alert.

Wireless Emergency Alerts are one of the channels that IPAWS, FEMA's Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, can reach. An agency must be approved as a sender before it can issue one. That rule applies to federal, state, local, tribal and territorial agencies alike.

Wireless Emergency Alerts fall into three categories. Presidential alerts are reserved for national emergencies and are issued at the direction of the president. Imminent Threat alerts cover hazards that put lives or property at risk. Tornado warnings and flash flood warnings issued by National Weather Service forecast offices fall into this group. AMBER alerts concern child abductions.

The categories follow different rules on the user's side. People can opt out of Imminent Threat and AMBER alerts in their phone's settings. They cannot opt out of Presidential alerts.

Phone alerts work alongside the broadcast side of the Emergency Alert System rather than replacing it. The same warning about a tornado or a missing child can appear on a television screen, interrupt a radio program and light up a phone. A person away from a TV or radio can still get the warning on a phone. Someone without a phone can still hear it on air.

National Weather Service forecast offices originate many of the warnings that reach the public, including tornado warnings and flash flood warnings. Those warnings feed both the Emergency Alert System and Wireless Emergency Alerts. One forecast office's decision can therefore reach broadcast audiences and phones.

A weather warning starts with meteorologists, not with broadcasters or phone carriers. The forecast office responsible for the threatened area decides that a warning is needed and issues it. From there, the warning moves outward through several channels at once.

Weather is the National Weather Service's share of federal alerting. The meteorological judgment behind a tornado or flash flood warning comes from the weather service. The agencies that write the rules and operate the national alerting infrastructure do not make that forecast call.

On the broadcast side, a weather warning enters the Emergency Alert System. Radio and TV stations, cable systems, satellite providers and other required participants can then pass it to their audiences. That route puts a weather alert onto TV screens and radio speakers. A flash flood warning takes the same broadcast route as a tornado warning.

On the wireless side, the same warning can reach phones as a Wireless Emergency Alert. A person who is not watching TV or listening to the radio can still receive it. That includes someone who is outdoors or away from a television when the forecast office issues the warning.

NOAA Weather Radio is a related channel for these warnings. It belongs to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the parent agency of the National Weather Service. Listeners hear it through a dedicated weather radio receiver rather than an ordinary broadcast station.

Together, these routes give a single weather warning more than one path to the public. Someone who misses a broadcast alert may still get the message on a phone or a weather radio.

Every participant in the Emergency Alert System must run required weekly and monthly tests. The U.S. has also held nationwide tests, starting with the first nationwide EAS test on Nov. 9, 2011.

The routine tests fall on the outlets that carry alerts to the public. Broadcasters, cable systems, satellite providers and wireline video providers must all keep EAS equipment. The weekly and monthly schedule gives that equipment a trial run between real emergencies.

A test checks the system at a moment when no one is in danger. Gear that sits idle until a crisis could fail without anyone noticing. A regular schedule gives an outlet the chance to find a fault before a tornado warning or an AMBER alert has to pass through the same equipment.

Nationwide tests work at a different scale. A routine test at one station confirms that its own setup works. A nationwide test sends a single message meant to reach audiences across the whole country. It shows whether the system holds together as a national network, not only whether its separate parts function.

The Nov. 9, 2011 test took place before Wireless Emergency Alerts existed. WEA, the system that delivers alerts to phones, began in 2012. As a result, that first nationwide test covered TV, radio and cable audiences but not phones.

Later nationwide tests added phones. The tests on Sept. 20, 2018, and Oct. 4, 2023, involved WEA alongside the EAS. On both dates, the test message was meant to reach mobile phones as well as people watching TV or listening to the radio.

Adding phones to a test widens what it checks. The broadcast portion shows whether stations and cable systems pass a message down the line. The WEA portion shows whether the same alert reaches the devices people carry with them.

A test message that appears on a screen or plays over a speaker is a check of the system, not a warning of real danger. The weekly and monthly tests cover individual outlets, while the nationwide tests cover the network as a whole.

The Emergency Alert System depends on two things: people need a working device that is switched on and nearby, and authorized senders have to get the message right. Hawaii's false ballistic missile alert on Jan. 13, 2018, showed what happens when the second condition fails.

That morning, a warning of an incoming ballistic missile went out to people across Hawaii. It reached them on their phones and through broadcast outlets. No missile was on the way.

Taking the message back proved harder than sending it. The FCC investigated the incident and found that the retraction took 38 minutes.

The episode showed a trade-off built into the alerting chain. The technology moved the false alert quickly. It reached the same broad audience a real warning would have reached. Speed and reach are the purpose of the system. They also mean a mistake travels as fast as an accurate alert does.

Sender approval does not remove this risk. Federal, state, local, tribal and territorial agencies must be approved before they can send through IPAWS, FEMA's alerting gateway. Approval decides who may issue a warning. Getting each message right still falls to the sender.

The device condition is just as basic. A warning carried over radio and television reaches only people who have a set turned on. A Wireless Emergency Alert reaches only phones that are powered on and connected to a cell network. The owner also has to be close enough to notice it. Someone asleep with a phone switched off, or away from any screen or speaker, can miss an alert entirely.

These limits do not change the system's basic design. Broadcasters, cable providers, satellite services, phones and weather radio each give a warning another route to the public. That overlap raises the odds a message gets through. It cannot make up for an inaccurate sender or an audience with no device on hand.

#5445. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5444. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.
