#5443. How the Ford Bronco went from compact 4x4 to full-size SUV and back

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Ford Bronco generations span six numbered versions since 1966. This guide explains each one, plus the Bronco II, Bronco Sport and Bronco Raptor, as the nameplate turns 60

Ford $F revealed the first Bronco in August 1965 as a 1966 model, which puts the nameplate's 60th anniversary in 2025. Over those six decades, the name has gone on very different vehicles. A compact off-roader, a full-size sport utility vehicle and a current family of off-road models have all carried the Bronco badge.

The story does not run in a straight line. Ford launched the Bronco as a small 4x4 built for rough terrain. Later versions shared their underpinnings with the F-Series pickup and grew much larger. Ford dropped the name after the 1996 model year and handed the full-size SUV role to the Expedition. The Bronco then stayed off the market for more than two decades. It returned for the 2021 model year as an off-road-focused SUV once more.

Tracing the Ford Bronco generations in order shows how one nameplate tracked the changes in Ford's truck and SUV lineup. The Bronco began in a small class of compact utility vehicles. It then became a large SUV tied to Ford's full-size pickup line. Its size and styling changed several times during the full-size years. The current model returned to the off-road purpose of the first one.

The history also has practical value. A Bronco from the late 1960s and one from the early 1990s share a name, but they are very different vehicles. Anyone shopping for a classic or used example needs to know which version is which. Body styles, dimensions and platforms changed from one era to the next. Related models add more room for confusion. The Bronco II and the Bronco Sport carry the name but sit outside the main line of numbered generations.

This guide covers all six numbered generations in order, from the original compact 4x4 to the current model. It also explains the related vehicles that wear the Bronco name. One section covers a 1994 news event that put a Bronco on live U.S. television. Each section can be read on its own, in any order.

The first-generation Ford $F Bronco was a compact, short-wheelbase off-roader that Ford built to compete with the International Harvester Scout and the Jeep CJ. It was sold for the 1966 through 1977 model years. Four-wheel drive came standard on every first-generation example.

Its two rivals came from different backgrounds. The Jeep CJ descended from the military Jeep of World War II. The CJ initials stood for Civilian Jeep. Ford had a direct link to that wartime vehicle. The company built Jeeps under contract during the war, alongside Willys-Overland. International Harvester, a Chicago-based maker of farm equipment and trucks, introduced the Scout in 1961. The Bronco gave Ford its own entry in that small four-wheel-drive segment.

Donald N. Frey was the product manager behind the project. The vehicle that emerged was a dedicated compact off-roader rather than a shortened version of a bigger truck. That sets the first Bronco apart from the full-size, pickup-based Broncos that came after it.

The Bronco rode on a 92-inch wheelbase. Wheelbase is the distance between the front and rear axles. A short one lets a vehicle turn more tightly. It also lowers the chance of the underbody scraping as the vehicle crests a steep rise. Both traits help on narrow, uneven trails.

Ford fitted coil springs to the front suspension and leaf springs at the rear.

Ford kept the same basic body for all 12 model years. A 1977 Bronco shares its core shape with a 1966 example. The first generation never got a full redesign during that run.

The first engine offered was a 170-cubic-inch inline-six. Ford added a V8 later in the production run. That gave buyers a choice between six and eight cylinders in the same compact body.

The second-generation Bronco, built on a different platform, replaced it for the 1978 model year.

The first Ford $F Bronco was sold in three body styles. Buyers could choose a wagon with a full roof, a roadster with no roof or a half-cab pickup with a roof over the front seats only.

All three shared the same short-wheelbase chassis and the same front end. The differences sat behind the front seats, in how much of the vehicle was covered and what the rear space was meant to carry.

The wagon was the closed version. Its roof covered both the passenger area and the cargo space behind it. That gave occupants and anything stowed in back protection from rain and cold. The top could also be removed, so wagon owners had an open-air option without buying a separate model.

The roadster went the other way. It came with no roof at all, leaving the cabin open to the weather. That made it the most stripped-down of the three and the closest in layout to the open utility vehicles of the period.

The half-cab split the difference. A short roof sheltered the driver and front passenger and ended just behind the front seats. That partial roof is where the name half-cab comes from. Behind the seats, the body stayed open as a small cargo bed. In practice it was a compact four-wheel-drive pickup built on the Bronco's short chassis.

Ford did not keep all three for long. The roadster and the half-cab were dropped after a few years. The wagon carried on through the end of the first generation in 1977. For the later years of that run, it was the only Bronco body style Ford sold.

Ford also layered trim packages on top of those body styles. The Sport and Ranger trims added extra equipment and dressier appearance details to what started as a basic utility truck. These packages changed how the Bronco was finished inside and out. The body underneath stayed the same.

Ford later reused the Ranger name for its compact pickup truck, a separate vehicle from the Bronco.

The second-generation Ford $F Bronco, sold for the 1978 and 1979 model years, moved the SUV onto the full-size F-Series pickup platform. The result was a much larger vehicle built to compete with the Chevrolet Blazer and the Dodge Ramcharger.

That change ended the Bronco's life as a compact off-roader. The original model had been sized to take on the International Harvester Scout and the Jeep CJ. Its replacement belonged to a different class of truck, with a bigger cabin and a chassis shared with Ford's full-size pickups.

Chevrolet set the template for that class. It launched the full-size K5 Blazer for the 1969 model year on its pickup truck underpinnings. Dodge followed with the Ramcharger for 1974. Both offered far more interior room than the first-generation Bronco.

Ford had planned a bigger Bronco earlier in the decade. The 1973 oil crisis and the fuel concerns that followed pushed the program back. The larger truck did not reach showrooms until the 1978 model year.

Building on the F-Series platform let Ford share much of the Bronco's front-end structure and styling with its pickups. From the front, the Bronco closely resembled an F-150 of the same years. The difference came behind the doors, where a shorter body ended in a tailgate instead of a cargo bed.

The rear section of the roof could be removed. That design kept some of the open-air appeal of the original Bronco. With the top in place, owners had a closed cabin for bad weather. The rear window in the tailgate could also be lowered into the gate.

Every second-generation Bronco used a V8 engine. A 351-cubic-inch V8 was standard, and a 400-cubic-inch V8 was the larger option. Ford offered no six-cylinder engine, a break from the first generation.

Trim levels ranged from the basic Custom to the more comfortable Ranger XLT.

The second generation lasted just two model years, the shortest run of any numbered Bronco generation. Ford replaced it for 1980 with a redesigned version that remained a full-size truck.

Ford $F made the Bronco smaller and lighter for the 1980 model year, in part to improve its fuel economy. The third-generation Bronco kept its full-size F-Series roots in a more efficient package and stayed in production through the 1986 model year.

The redesign tracked the truck underneath it. Ford introduced a new F-Series pickup for 1980, the seventh generation of that line, and the Bronco moved onto the updated platform. The SUV and the pickup shared their front-end styling. That kept the Bronco visually tied to Ford's pickups.

Fuel costs formed the backdrop. The second-generation Bronco, sold for 1978 and 1979, was a large truck sold just as fuel prices began to climb. The 1979 oil shock followed the Iranian Revolution. It pushed U.S. gasoline prices higher and brought shortages and long lines at filling stations in some areas.

Federal rules also changed. The Energy Policy and Conservation Act of 1975 created the Corporate Average Fuel Economy program, known as CAFE. Its standards for light trucks took effect with the 1979 model year. That put SUVs such as the Bronco under federal fuel economy targets for the first time.

Ford trimmed the Bronco rather than giving up its full-size format. The third generation kept the two-door body and a removable rear roof section. Buyers still had an open-air option. The cabin and cargo area remained larger than those of the original compact Bronco from the 1960s.

The styling changed during the run. For 1982, Ford moved its blue oval emblem onto the grille of its pickups and the Bronco. It replaced the block "FORD" lettering that earlier trucks carried across the front.

The full-size Bronco also gained a smaller sibling during this period. Starting with the 1984 model year, Ford sold the Ranger-based Bronco II in the same showrooms. The full-size truck kept its place in the lineup.

The third-generation design ran for seven model years, far longer than the two-year run of the model it replaced. Ford followed it for 1987 with a fourth generation that restyled this design instead of starting from scratch.

The Bronco II was a separate, smaller Ford $F SUV built on the Ranger compact pickup. Ford sold it for the 1984 through 1990 model years. It shared the Bronco name but was not a numbered generation of the full-size Bronco, which stayed in Ford showrooms alongside it the entire time.

Ford built the Bronco II to fill a gap in its own lineup. By the early 1980s, the full-size Bronco rode on F-Series underpinnings. It had grown well beyond the compact proportions of the 1966 original. Ford had no smaller utility vehicle to sell next to it.

The Ranger supplied the foundation. Ford launched that compact pickup for the 1983 model year. The Bronco II borrowed its chassis and front-end design. The result was a short, two-door utility vehicle with a fixed steel roof and a rear liftgate. It was much shorter than the full-size Bronco.

The compact SUV segment was filling up at the same time. Chevrolet introduced the S-10 Blazer for 1983, built on its own small pickup. Jeep followed with the unibody Cherokee for 1984. The Bronco II reached buyers in the same model year as that Jeep.

Power came from V6 engines. The first models used a 2.8-liter V6. Ford moved to a 2.9-liter V6 for 1986. Four-wheel-drive versions used Ford's Twin-Traction Beam front suspension, the same design found on four-wheel-drive Rangers of the period. Ford also added a two-wheel-drive Bronco II for 1986.

Ford assembled the Bronco II at its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. The model offered only two doors throughout its seven-year run. No four-door body was ever added.

Ford replaced the Bronco II after the 1990 model year with the Explorer, which arrived for 1991. The Explorer kept a Ranger-derived foundation but added a four-door body, the configuration the Bronco II never had. Ford also offered a two-door Explorer for buyers who preferred the shorter layout. The Bronco II name did not return after that changeover.

The fourth-generation Ford $F Bronco, sold for the 1987 through 1991 model years, updated the third-generation truck rather than replacing it. Ford revised its styling to match the F-Series pickups of the period.

The update kept the Bronco visually tied to the full-size pickup line it had been built from since 1978. When the look of Ford's F-Series trucks changed, the Bronco's appearance changed with them. The SUV and the pickup kept a shared family resemblance.

The underlying package carried over from the 1980–1986 Bronco. Ford had already made that truck smaller and lighter than the 1978–1979 version. The fourth generation kept that size instead of starting from a clean sheet.

That makes the boundary between the third and fourth generations mostly a matter of appearance. The truck underneath stayed in the same family. For anyone sorting through used or classic examples, the revised styling is what separates a 1987–1991 Bronco from the full-size version that came just before it.

The run lasted five model years. That was longer than the two-year second generation. It was shorter than the seven-year third generation that preceded it.

For most of those years, the full-size Bronco shared Ford showrooms with the smaller Bronco II. The two trucks carried the same badge but sat on different platforms.

The fourth generation ended after the 1991 model year. A redesigned fifth-generation Bronco replaced it for 1992.

The fifth-generation Ford $F Bronco covered the 1992 through 1996 model years, and Ford redesigned it alongside the F-Series pickups it was selling at the time. Ford retired the Bronco name after the 1996 model year.

That shared redesign kept the full-size Bronco closely tied to Ford's pickup line. From 1978 onward, every full-size Bronco had been built on F-Series foundations, and this generation followed the same approach. Its front-end styling matched the F-Series trucks of the same model years.

The basic layout did not change. The full-size Bronco remained a two-door SUV through its final model year. Ford's lineup already included a four-door option by then. The Explorer, a midsize SUV that replaced the Bronco II for the 1991 model year, was offered with four doors as well as two.

Ford sold the fifth generation in several trim levels, including XLT and Eddie Bauer. The Eddie Bauer version carried the name of the outdoor clothing brand founded in Seattle. Ford used the same tie-in on the Explorer and later the Expedition.

Ford introduced the Expedition for the 1997 model year as its new full-size SUV. It took over the role the Bronco had filled in Ford's lineup. The Expedition shared its underpinnings with the redesigned F-150 that Ford launched for the same model year.

The new SUV's body differed from the Bronco's in two ways. The Expedition had four doors and an available third row of seats. The full-size Bronco never offered either.

The Expedition also became the basis for a luxury model. Lincoln launched the Navigator for the 1998 model year on the same foundation. It was Lincoln's first SUV. The Expedition remains in Ford's lineup today.

The Bronco name then stayed out of Ford's lineup for 24 model years, from 1997 through 2020. It returned for the 2021 model year with an all-new design.

On June 17, 1994, a white 1993 Ford $F Bronco driven by A.C. Cowlings was at the center of a televised police pursuit in Los Angeles involving O.J. Simpson. Simpson rode in the vehicle as police followed it across Southern California freeways.

The pursuit came after Simpson failed to turn himself in to police that day. He had been charged with murder in the deaths of his former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman. Both had been found dead outside her Los Angeles home earlier that month.

Cowlings was a longtime friend of Simpson. The two played football together at the University of Southern California and later with the Buffalo Bills. The Bronco in the pursuit belonged to Cowlings. Simpson owned a separate white Bronco of his own.

The chase moved at low speed. Patrol cars trailed the Bronco in a long column rather than trying to force it off the road. News helicopters tracked it from overhead. Bystanders gathered on overpasses and along the route to watch it pass.

Television networks broke into scheduled programming to carry the pursuit live. NBC was airing Game 5 of the NBA Finals between the New York Knicks and the Houston Rockets that night. The network shifted part of its coverage to the pursuit.

The pursuit ended at Simpson's home in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. He surrendered to police there later that evening.

Simpson's criminal trial followed. Jury selection began in the fall of 1994, and the trial ran through much of 1995. A jury acquitted him of both murders on October 3, 1995.

Within the Bronco's own history, the vehicle in the pursuit was a fifth-generation model. That generation was the full-size version Ford sold for the 1992 through 1996 model years. It was also the last version of the original Bronco before Ford retired the nameplate after 1996.

Ford $F revealed the sixth-generation Bronco on July 13, 2020, and it went on sale for the 2021 model year.

The new Ford Bronco comes in two body styles, a two-door and a four-door. The two-door rides on a shorter wheelbase. That gives it proportions closer to the compact Bronco Ford launched in the 1960s. The four-door has a longer body with rear doors and more room for passengers and cargo.

Both versions have a removable roof and removable doors. With those pieces off, the Bronco can be driven with an open cabin. The doors are frameless, which means the side glass is not surrounded by a metal window frame. Ford designed the roof and doors to come off as part of the factory vehicle, not as an aftermarket conversion.

The styling draws directly on the first-generation Bronco. Round headlights, a flat hood and a boxy, upright body recall the shape of the 1966 original.

Ford builds the Bronco at its Michigan Assembly Plant in Wayne, Michigan. The SUV uses body-on-frame construction. In that traditional truck layout, the body is mounted on a separate ladder-type chassis. The layout is common among vehicles built for heavy off-road use.

The Sasquatch package is one of the Bronco's main off-road options. It is aimed at buyers who plan to take the SUV onto rough trails. It fits larger off-road tires along with other trail-focused hardware. The name refers to the large, hairy creature of North American folklore.

Ford also equips the Bronco with a terrain management system it calls G.O.A.T. Modes, short for Goes Over Any Type of Terrain. The driver selects a mode to match the surface, such as sand, mud or rock. The system then adjusts the vehicle's settings for those conditions.

The Bronco competes most directly with the Jeep Wrangler. Both are sold in two-door and four-door forms, and both offer a removable roof and doors.

The Bronco Sport arrived for the 2021 model year as a smaller, separate model sold alongside the Bronco. The Bronco Raptor, a performance off-road version of the Bronco, followed for the 2022 model year.

The two models turned one nameplate into a family of vehicles in different sizes and with different levels of capability. Ford $F introduced the Bronco Sport at the same July 2020 event where it unveiled the new two-door and four-door Bronco. The Bronco Sport reached dealers in late 2020, months before the first Bronco deliveries in 2021.

The Bronco Sport is built differently from the Bronco. It uses unibody construction, in which the body and frame form a single structure. It shares its underpinnings with the Ford Escape compact crossover. The Bronco uses a separate body-on-frame design, the layout traditionally used for pickups and dedicated off-roaders.

Production is split between two countries. Ford builds the Bronco Sport at its Hermosillo plant in Mexico. The Bronco is assembled at Michigan Assembly Plant in Wayne, Michigan.

The Bronco Sport borrows several ideas from its larger sibling. Both offer G.O.A.T. Modes, Ford's name for selectable drive settings matched to conditions such as mud, sand or snow. The letters stand for "Goes Over Any Type of Terrain." The Badlands trim is the most off-road-focused version of the Bronco Sport.

The Bronco Raptor sits at the other end of the range. Ford Performance, the automaker's performance division, developed it. It is based on the four-door Bronco and adds wider fenders and larger tires than other versions of the SUV.

The Raptor name came from the F-150 pickup. Ford introduced the F-150 SVT Raptor for the 2010 model year as a factory-built truck designed for high-speed desert driving. The Bronco Raptor carries that badge over from Ford's full-size pickup to its body-on-frame off-road SUV.

The two additions give the Bronco name a wider spread than it had in its first life. Across the original 1966 to 1996 run, the only other vehicle to carry the name was the Ranger-based Bronco II.

#5442. ‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am

Editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter. The company was not involved in this story.

Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

“So you want an internship this summer?” he asked Miya McClain, as she remembers it.

She was Miya Sneed then, 18 and homesick at Mills College in Oakland, Calif. She had come home to speak for Technology Access Foundation, the Seattle nonprofit where she had gone from knowing nothing about computers to building software and leading a team of student interns. Earlier in the luncheon program, she had shown the crowd a scheduling system she built for TAF.

Microsoft had planned the offer in advance and already had her resume, but she had no idea what was coming. A Seattle Times photographer caught the look of shock on her face, and the photo ran the next day on the front of the newspaper’s business section.

That internship, the first of two, led to a full-time job at Microsoft after college. She spent eight years there before moving into product leadership roles at Nordstrom, Cisco and Smartsheet. Today McClain is senior vice president of product management at SumerSports, a sports analytics company.

“Most of my jobs came through connections with TAF,” she said, crediting the organization for repeatedly “opening doors I didn’t even know could be opened.”

That’s the path Trish Millines Dziko had in mind when she left Microsoft 30 years ago to start TAF with her partner, Jill Hull Dziko: teach kids of color to work with technology, and get them hired by tech companies.

But about eight years in, she saw a problem. TAF’s interns were thriving, she said, but many couldn’t get into college computer science or engineering courses because their high schools had already steered them into lower-level math and science.

To change that, TAF would need to reach students by sixth grade, inside the schools.

So TAF went into public education. The organization, which marked its 30th anniversary Oct. 1, now co-manages a public middle and high school in Federal Way, Wash., and coaches teachers in other public schools.

“No matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills. They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

Executive director, Technology Access Foundation

Working with entire schools, rather than kids who signed up for a tech program, changed the goal, too. The focus now is on skills students can use in any field, whether or not it’s tech.

Students learn science, technology, engineering and math through projects that combine subjects and put classroom lessons to use. In 2020, for example, two students at TAF’s Federal Way school turned a gardening robot into a model 3D printer using a cake-frosting syringe, a threaded rod and a motor, as GeekWire reported at the time.

“What we want to make sure is, no matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills,” Millines Dziko said. “They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

The shift has cost TAF money. The organization has missed out on larger funding opportunities, Millines Dziko said, because it isn’t focused solely on tech and isn’t growing as fast as some funders would like. In the early 2010s, as education philanthropy flowed to charter schools, TAF couldn’t raise enough to open the additional schools it had planned.

“But we stuck with what was true, and what works for our kids,” she said, “and we’re still here.”

Millines Dziko grew up in New Jersey, raised by a single mother who cleaned floors for a living. She told the Seattle P-I in 1995 that she believed she’d been placed in a lower-level math class because of her race. She took summer-school classes to work her way into honors.

She studied computer science at Monmouth College on a basketball scholarship and began working at Microsoft in 1988 as the first tester on SQL Server. “She was always a force to be reckoned with,” said Bob Muglia, the longtime Microsoft executive who hired her, speaking with GeekWire at the organization’s 30th anniversary party in October. His foundation now supports TAF.

She later moved into a diversity role and took over Microsoft’s high school internship program, making it technical and filling it almost entirely with Seattle kids of color. When she pushed the company to reach students earlier, she said, “the attitude was, it’s not broken, so let’s not fix it.”

Then her partner, Jill Hull Dziko, a social worker in Seattle Public Schools’ behavior-disorder classrooms, brought seven or eight middle schoolers to campus. They were rowdy on the shuttle ride over and went silent when they walked into a room of high school interns testing a new handheld computer.

On the way back, Millines Dziko recalled, they were saying, “I want to be an engineer. I want to do what they did.”

She left Microsoft in August 1996 and put $150,000 of her own money into TAF. If she didn’t help others, she told the P-I the next year, her late mother “would want me to have my butt kicked.”

TAF set up in a Columbia City storefront next to a Taco del Mar. When they first opened the door, she said, they could see the basement through the subfloor, and the staff wired the network themselves. The first students started after-school classes in 1997, training for paid summer internships.

McClain joined the second class as she entered ninth grade, along with her older sister. Millines Dziko taught them to take apart a computer and write their first programs. “She’s encouraging, but she’s also very strict,” McClain said. “We all got jobs that summer, so obviously she taught us something.”

In 2000, TAF started a program for younger students called TechStart. At the anniversary party in October, Sherry Williams, TAF’s executive director of operations, who joined in 1997 as its fourth employee, told the crowd about a young girl who was afraid of math. The girl’s mother brought her every afternoon, and the girl kept working at it.

One day she walked in wearing a T-shirt that said “I love math.”

“Although her school wasn’t serving her, in our after-school program, she was being served,” Williams said. “And she knew she could do anything after that.”

TAF opened a public school, TAF Academy, with Federal Way Public Schools in 2008. Mike Miles, one of its first ninth-graders, went reluctantly. The school looked way too small, he told the Federal Way Mirror the following year. “I didn’t want to have six kids in my class, but my parents made me go anyway.”

He was ahead in math, and the new school couldn’t offer the class he needed, so he spent his first year in the back of the room teaching himself from a textbook.

The next year, TAF arranged for him to take math at another public school down the street. Looking back as a parent, he said in a recent interview, he appreciates that the school was willing to “swallow your pride a little” and acknowledge that it couldn’t give him what he needed. He got the math education there, and where he is today, he said, is “better than what I ever could have expected.”

Miles, now 32, graduated in 2012 with TAF Academy’s first class, earned a business degree at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and leads data teams at a cybersecurity startup in the Washington, D.C., area.

He remembers sitting in a circle in social studies, discussing the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed Black teenager in Florida, and learning to keep disagreements from turning into “a shouting match,” a skill he relies on in his work now.

Federal Way wasn’t the original plan. TAF spent two years designing a school for Seattle Public Schools, and in 2006 it proposed one for Rainier Beach High School, first as a replacement for the school and then as an academy inside the building.

Many students and teachers saw it as a takeover. Teachers worried the academy would drain resources from the existing school, and families objected that the district had discussed the proposal for a year without telling them. At a packed community meeting that November, there was shouting, and the PTSA president walked out with dozens of students, The Seattle Times reported.

“It was just the dumbest and the most frustrating thing I had ever been through,” Millines Dziko said in a recent interview. “I said we’re done, no more.”

Federal Way Superintendent Tom Murphy read about it, called her and came up to Seattle to meet. After a couple of hours, she said, he told her, “You belong in Federal Way.” TAF is now working with its fifth superintendent there, she said.

The lowest point, she said, came around 2012, when TAF had to lay off staff for the second time. Education philanthropy was pouring into charter schools, a planned expansion into Renton had stalled for lack of money, she said, and TAF had just moved into a new building.

She recalled seeing reports that only a small share of major philanthropic funding went to nonprofits led by people of color, and she started asking herself a question. “Is me being a leader of this organization gonna hold us back from getting funding? Would it be better if we had someone who was white to lead the organization?”

She talked it over with Williams and Zithri Saleem, two of her top leaders, and “we almost went down that road,” she said. But she reconsidered. “That’s not the answer either,” she said. Instead, TAF had to “get out there and show them,” and find other people interested in its work.

Seattle came back around after Denise Juneau became superintendent. In 2020, the school board approved a TAF partnership at Washington Middle School in the Central District. Three years later, facing a budget shortfall, the district cut it, as GeekWire reported at the time. “It’s solely about money,” Millines Dziko told The Seattle Times then.

Asked whether she could see herself working with Seattle Public Schools again, she said, “No.” The district has “way too many problems,” she said, and dealing with them “takes our energy away from places where we could be having impact.”

In 2024, TAF was among the nonprofits chosen in MacKenzie Scott’s open call, after a process that included peer review. TAF expected $1 million and got $2 million. “It wasn’t the money; it was the belief in our work,” Millines Dziko said.

TAF used $500,000 for operating needs it had been saving for and put the rest in a certificate of deposit, she said.

TAF reported about $4 million in revenue and $5 million in expenses in its Form 990 for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025, and ended the year with about $11.4 million in net assets. Millines Dziko said the organization’s annual budget is now close to $7 million, and its fundraising team raises about 93% of it, mostly through grants.

TAF Academy had been recognized for test-score gains. It was named a School of Distinction in 2012 for improvement in middle-school reading and math. In 2016, the district cited three consecutive years of recognition as one reason for merging it with Saghalie Middle School. The combined school, TAF@Saghalie, opened in 2017, and TAF co-manages it with the district.

TAF@Saghalie’s four-year graduation rate for the class of 2025 was above 88.5%, compared with 82.6% statewide, according to state data. On state tests in 2024-25, 17% of the school’s low-income students who took the tests in grades 6–8 and 10 met the English language arts standard and 11% met the math standard, compared with 30% and 15% for low-income students in the same grades across Federal Way Public Schools.

Millines Dziko argues that standardized tests don’t measure what matters. They assume every student had a teacher who covered everything on the exam, she said, and “they demean kids,” charting their academic course as early as third grade.

TAF trains teachers to track each student’s growth and is building its own way to document it. Teachers score students from 1 to 4 against standards, backed by photos of projects and samples of student work. The data lives in the modern version of SQL Server, the Microsoft database Millines Dziko was hired to test in 1988.

The system is in the third year of a pilot. Only selected teachers are participating, and TAF is still working out how much time teachers can spend documenting students’ work while teaching, she said. TAF is bringing in an evaluator from the University of Washington Bothell to review the pilot, she said.

Millines Dziko’s goal is for every district in the country to use it, and for standardized tests to “go out the window,” with the money states spend on them going to teacher training instead. “I believe it will,” she said.

Miles liked the project-based learning but said he found gaps in his preparation when he got to college. “I took physics at TAF Academy, took physics in college, and I was not prepared,” he said. What he got in return, he said, was “a different way of thinking.”

TAF looked like a program for teaching technical skills, he said, but “they taught kids how to be people.” He tries to pass that on to his son, he said, including putting others first and using his gifts to help others.

TransformED, TAF’s teacher-coaching program, places a full-time coach in a partner school for five years. It works with five schools now and plans to add 10 more over five years, at about $200,000 per school per year, Millines Dziko said. In September, TAF hired a former Atlanta principal, Donya Loyd Kemp, to lead it, as GeekWire reported.

Millines Dziko is wary of the rush to bring AI into classrooms. Students can use it to find sources, she said, but then they have to investigate those sources themselves. “It should be used as a tool to gather quickly, so I can now use most of my time doing the thinking.”

Millines Dziko said the region’s tech companies should invest in public schools as a way to attract and keep families here, not just with donated products and the occasional volunteer day. “That’s performative,” she said.

What she wants are lasting relationships, like the ones TAF has with smaller companies that come back to its schools every year to give students real problems to solve. As for the big tech companies, “I need them to be more about pouring into instead of extracting out of,” she said.

Millines Dziko turns 70 in July. For the past year and a half, she said, Williams and Joshua Halsey, TAF’s executive director of education, have taken on more of the leadership, freeing her to spend more time raising money and building relationships.

She doesn’t expect to stop working, she said, predicting that she’ll never retire.

At the 30th anniversary party, she hugged about three-quarters of the room, by her count. Looking around at her former students, many with kids of their own, it hit her.

“This is 30 years, man, and look at y’all,” she said, recalling the moment later. “Y’all are good.”

#5440. Why the Supreme Court denies most petitions and what happens to the rest

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A guide to how the Supreme Court chooses which cases to hear, from certiorari petitions and the rule of four to circuit splits, the cert pool and unexplained denials

The U.S. Supreme Court sets its own agenda. A party that loses in a lower court can ask the justices for review, but it has no right to receive it. Most of those requests are turned away, usually through a single line on an order list with no reasons given. The cases that make it through become the ones that produce rulings on federal law for courts across the country.

That control over the docket comes from both legislation and the Court's own practices. Congress made most of the Court's appellate work discretionary with the Judiciary Act of 1925. A 1988 law later removed most of the mandatory appeals that remained. The justices filled in the details through written rules and internal routines that have built up over decades.

Knowing how the Supreme Court chooses which cases to hear explains why some legal questions get a national answer while others stay unsettled for years. It also explains why a refusal to hear a case is not a ruling on its merits. A denied petition leaves the lower court's decision in place, but the denial itself sets no precedent.

The selection process runs through several stages and a specialized vocabulary. Law clerks screen petitions for a writ of certiorari, many of them through a shared arrangement called the cert pool. The Chief Justice circulates a list of petitions for discussion, and the justices vote in a private conference. Four votes are enough to add a case to the docket. Conflicts among the federal appeals courts, known as circuit splits, are among the grounds the Court's own rules name for granting review. The Solicitor General, who represents the federal government before the Court, can also influence which cases advance, sometimes at the justices' invitation.

This list covers 10 of the steps and concepts that govern case selection. It is a selection, not a complete account of the Court's docket. The entries move from the mechanics of a cert petition through the rule of four, the other reasons listed in Rule 10 and the role of friend-of-the-court briefs. Later entries turn to denials, relists and dissents from denial. The final entry covers the routes that bypass ordinary certiorari, including disputes between states and emergency applications. Each entry stands on its own. Readers can start with whichever question brought them here.

Most cases reach the U.S. Supreme Court through a petition for a writ of certiorari, a formal request asking the justices to review a lower court's decision. The Court has no obligation to grant it. Review depends on the justices' discretion, not on a right held by the parties.

The petition comes from the side that lost below. That party, called the petitioner, argues that the case deserves the attention of the nation's highest court. The opposing party, the respondent, can file a brief in opposition urging the justices to leave the lower-court ruling in place.

The word itself is Latin. Certiorari is usually glossed as "to be more fully informed." The name reflects what the writ does. A higher court calls up the record of a case so it can examine what happened below. Lawyers and court watchers often shorten the term to "cert," and the Court speaks of granting or denying cert.

The Court's own rules spell out the discretionary nature of the process. Supreme Court Rule 10 states that review on a writ of certiorari is not a matter of right but of judicial discretion. A petitioner who believes the lower court decided the case wrongly has no guarantee of a hearing. The petition has to persuade the justices that the case warrants a place on their docket.

A petition follows a set format under the Court's rules. Rule 14 requires the questions presented for review to appear first, expressed concisely. Those questions frame what the justices would decide if they granted review. The petition must also include an appendix with the opinions and orders issued by the lower courts in the case.

Deadlines apply as well. Under Rule 13, a petition is generally due 90 days after the lower court enters its judgment. If a party asked the lower court for rehearing in time, the clock instead runs from the date that request is denied. A justice can extend the deadline by up to 60 days. The application for more time goes to the justice assigned to the circuit where the case arose.

Cost does not have to block a filing. Under Rule 39, a petitioner who cannot afford the Court's fees can ask to proceed in forma pauperis, a status that waives them. Many petitions from prisoners arrive this way.

Four of the nine Supreme Court justices must vote to grant a petition for review. A majority is not required. A minority of the bench can put a case on the Court's docket.

The rule of four is a practice the justices follow among themselves. It does not appear in the Constitution, and no federal statute imposes it. It governs the justices' internal votes rather than anything a litigant can invoke or enforce.

The threshold sits one vote below a majority of a full nine-member Court. In practice, a group of justices who think a legal question deserves an answer can move a case forward without persuading a fifth colleague. The case then gets a full hearing even if most of the Court would have passed on it.

The vote takes place in private. The justices do not usually announce who voted to grant review. When the Court accepts a case, the public record typically shows only that the petition was granted. The tally behind it stays out of view.

A grant moves the case onto the Court's merits docket. The parties file full briefs on the legal question, and the case is usually scheduled for oral argument. Deciding a case follows a different rule from accepting one. A ruling on the merits requires a majority of the justices who take part.

That difference has consequences. On a full bench, four justices can bring a case in, but four votes cannot decide it. If the participating justices split evenly, as can happen after a recusal, the lower court's judgment stands. A ruling by an equally divided Court sets no national precedent.

A grant also says nothing about the final outcome. A vote to hear a case reflects a judgment that the question merits the Court's attention. It is not a vote on who should win. Justices who voted to grant review can land on opposite sides of the decision. The Court sometimes affirms the very ruling it agreed to review.

The Court can also step back after granting. It occasionally dismisses a case as improvidently granted, a disposition often abbreviated as DIG. That can happen when briefing or argument exposes a problem that keeps the Court from reaching the question it meant to decide.

A circuit split happens when two or more federal courts of appeals answer the same question of federal law in different ways. Supreme Court Rule 10(a) names that kind of conflict among the appeals courts as a reason the justices may agree to hear a case.

The U.S. has 13 federal courts of appeals. Twelve of them are regional circuits. These are the First through Eleventh circuits, each covering a group of states or territories, plus the D.C. Circuit in the nation's capital. The 13th is the Federal Circuit. It does not cover a region. It hears appeals on specialized subjects, such as patent cases, from across the country.

Each regional circuit sets precedent for the federal trial courts inside its borders. A ruling from the Ninth Circuit, which includes California, binds federal district judges in that circuit. It does not bind judges in the Fifth Circuit, which includes Texas. Those judges follow their own circuit's precedent. The appeals courts are also free to disagree with one another.

That structure is where splits come from. When circuits split, the same federal statute or constitutional provision can mean one thing in one part of the country and something else in another. A person's rights, a company's legal obligations or the outcome of a criminal case can then depend on geography. Within the court system, only the Supreme Court can settle the disagreement nationwide. Its rulings on federal law bind every lower federal court.

Lawyers who file petitions often try to show that a split exists. A genuine conflict gives the justices a reason for review that their own rules recognize. Petitions and legal commentators also describe splits by their size. A shallow split may involve only a few circuits. A deep split involves several circuits lined up on each side of the question.

A split does not guarantee that the Court will take a case. The justices sometimes let a disagreement continue so that more appeals courts can weigh in before the question reaches them. Legal writers often call that process percolation.

Supreme Court Rule 10 names several grounds for review beyond conflicts among federal appeals courts. They include an important federal question the Court has not settled and a sharp departure from accepted judicial procedure. A lower-court ruling that conflicts with the Supreme Court's own decisions is another.

Rule 10 places all of these grounds under a single standard. The rule says a petition for a writ of certiorari will be granted only for "compelling reasons." The listed grounds are examples of reasons the justices may treat as compelling. They are not a checklist that guarantees a hearing.

The first ground concerns unsettled law. A state court of last resort or a federal court of appeals may decide an important question of federal law that the Supreme Court has never resolved. The rule describes this as a question that has not been, but should be, settled by the Court. The word "important" carries weight here. A novel question alone does not meet the standard.

The second ground concerns how a case was handled. A federal court of appeals may depart far from the accepted and usual course of judicial proceedings. It may also approve such a departure by a lower court. Rule 10 treats either situation as a reason the Court may step in. The rule ties this ground to the Court's supervisory power.

The third ground protects the Court's own precedent. A state court or federal appeals court may decide an important federal question in a way that conflicts with relevant Supreme Court decisions. Review may follow in that situation. Lower courts are bound to apply the Supreme Court's rulings. This ground gives the justices a way to address departures from them.

Rule 10 also states that its factors are neither controlling nor fully measuring the Court's discretion. The justices can grant review in a case that fits none of the listed grounds. They can also deny review in a case that appears to fit one.

The rule closes with a caution for litigants. A petition that claims only that a lower court made erroneous factual findings is rarely granted. The same is true of a petition that claims only that a lower court misapplied a properly stated rule of law.

The cert pool is a shared screening system, begun in 1972, in which participating justices' chambers divide the work of reviewing petitions. A law clerk writes one memo on each petition. The memo recommends that the Court grant review, deny it or ask for the Solicitor General's views.

Justice Lewis Powell proposed the arrangement, and Chief Justice Warren Burger supported it. Before the pool existed, each chamber read every petition on its own. Thousands of petitions reach the Court each year. Splitting the load meant a petition could be summarized once for the participating justices rather than separately in each chamber.

Inside the pool, petitions are assigned among the participating chambers. The clerk who draws a case prepares a single memo. That memo then circulates to every justice in the pool.

The memo lays out the facts of the dispute and the rulings in the lower courts. It also sets out the questions the petitioner wants the justices to answer. It then assesses whether the case is a suitable candidate for review.

Each memo closes with one of those three recommendations. A call for the Solicitor General's views asks the federal government to file a brief before the justices decide.

Law clerks are typically recent law school graduates. Most have already clerked for a judge on a lower federal court. Each associate justice can hire up to four clerks.

A pool memo is a starting point, not the final word. Justices often have their own clerks review the shared memo and add notes that reflect that chamber's priorities. The decision on whether to hear a case still belongs to the justices themselves.

Not every chamber takes part. Justice John Paul Stevens stayed out of the pool, and his clerks screened petitions for him. Justice Samuel Alito later withdrew from it. Justice Neil Gorsuch also does not participate. The Alito and Gorsuch chambers review petitions on their own. Petitions get a separate read in those chambers in addition to the pool memo.

A cert petition reaches the justices' private conference only if it appears on the discuss list, which the Chief Justice circulates. Any justice can add a petition to that list. Petitions that never make the list are denied without discussion.

The discuss list is a second filter on top of the earlier screening. By the time a conference arrives, the justices' chambers have already reviewed the pending petitions. The list narrows that pool to the ones at least one justice thinks the full Court should talk through.

The Chief Justice drafts the list but does not have the final say over what reaches the table. A justice who wants the Court to consider a petition can add it without anyone else's agreement.

Petitions left off the list never receive a conference vote. They are denied automatically. The petitioner gets the same brief denial as a party whose case was debated at length. The set of excluded petitions is often called the "dead list."

The conference itself is closed. Only the nine justices attend. No clerks, secretaries or other staff are in the room. The most junior justice takes notes and answers the door if a message arrives. Discussion moves in order of seniority, starting with the Chief Justice.

The calendar shapes the workload. Petitions keep arriving during the Court's summer recess, and they build up. The justices take up that backlog at the "long conference," held in late September. It comes shortly before the new term opens on the first Monday in October. The long conference handles far more petitions than a typical conference during the term.

The results of each conference become public through order lists, which the Court releases after the justices meet. An order list records which petitions were granted and which were denied. It also carries other procedural orders in pending matters. The Court posts its order lists on its website, where lawyers, journalists and litigants check them for news about specific cases.

The Solicitor General represents the federal government before the Supreme Court. If the government is not a party but has a stake in a case, the justices can issue a call for the views of the Solicitor General, or CVSG.

The office sits inside the Department of Justice. Congress created it in 1870, in the same law that established the department. The president nominates the Solicitor General, and the Senate confirms the nominee. The Solicitor General also argues some of the government's cases before the justices in person.

The job includes a screening role on the government's side. When a federal agency loses in a lower court, the Solicitor General decides whether the government will ask the Supreme Court for review. As a result, the government does not petition on every loss. It brings only the cases its lawyers judge worth the Court's time.

Petitions the Solicitor General files on the government's behalf are granted at a much higher rate than other petitions. The office is sometimes called the "tenth justice." Lincoln Caplan used that phrase as the title of his 1987 book about the office.

A CVSG works differently. In these cases, the government stands outside the dispute. The parties might be two companies, or a private plaintiff and a state. The case may still turn on a federal statute or a federal regulation, or on a question that affects how federal agencies operate. The Court asks the Solicitor General to file a brief setting out the government's position.

That brief usually tells the justices whether the government thinks the petition should be granted or denied. It can also address the underlying legal question. The justices are not bound by the recommendation, but it carries weight in their decision.

A CVSG also adds time to the process. The Court generally holds the petition while it waits for the government's brief. A case that draws a CVSG stays undecided until that filing arrives.

Outside groups can weigh in before the Supreme Court decides whether to take a case. Under Supreme Court Rule 37, a friend-of-the-court brief may be filed either supporting or opposing a petition for a writ of certiorari. Its formal Latin name is an amicus curiae brief.

The filers are not parties to the lawsuit. They are organizations, governments or individuals with a stake in the legal question the petition raises. Common filers include states, trade associations, labor unions, advocacy groups and academics who study the area of law involved.

At the petition stage, an amicus brief does not argue the full merits of the dispute. Its job is narrower. It tries to show the justices that the question deserves a national answer, or that it does not.

A brief supporting review might describe how a lower-court ruling affects businesses, agencies or courts that had no part in the original case. It can point to people and institutions outside the courtroom who live under the ruling. A brief opposing review might argue that the issue is too narrow or too rare to need the Court's attention.

That focus matches what the Court says it wants from amicus filers. Rule 37 describes a helpful amicus brief as one that raises relevant matter the parties have not already brought to the Court's attention. The rule adds that a brief which does not serve that purpose burdens the Court. Such filings are not favored.

Rule 37 also sets a disclosure requirement. A brief must state whether counsel for a party wrote it in whole or in part. It must also identify anyone other than the amicus, its members or its lawyers who paid for its preparation or submission. That puts the brief's authorship and funding on the public record.

Amicus briefs carry no vote and bind no one. Review still depends on the justices' own decision to grant it, and an outside filing cannot stand in for that. What a cert-stage brief can add is context the petition alone may not supply. That context might include the range of institutions a ruling reaches or the other settings where the same question is arising.

When the Supreme Court denies a petition for certiorari, it almost never explains why. A denial also does not mean the justices agree with the lower court's ruling. It means only that the Court has chosen not to hear the case.

A denial leaves the lower-court ruling in force, and the parties remain bound by it. Other courts cannot treat the denial as an endorsement of the ruling below or as Supreme Court precedent.

Justice Felix Frankfurter made this point in Maryland v. Baltimore Radio Show in 1950. In a separate opinion, he wrote that a denial carries no expression of opinion on the merits of the case. Lawyers and judges still read denials that way.

A denial can rest on reasons that have nothing to do with the legal question. A case may have procedural problems, such as an issue that was not properly raised in the lower courts. Its facts may make it a poor vehicle for deciding a broader question. The justices may also prefer to let an issue develop further before stepping in. The Court rarely says which reason applied.

Relisting is a separate step. The Court sometimes relists a petition, which places it on the agenda for a later conference instead of resolving it at the first one. A relist can mean a justice wants more time to study the case or is drafting a separate writing. It is not a promise of a grant. Some relisted petitions are granted, and others are denied.

Justices who disagree with a denial can say so publicly. A dissent from denial of certiorari explains why a justice believes the Court should have taken the case. A statement respecting denial lets a justice comment without dissenting. Such statements sometimes flag a question the Court could address in a future case. Neither type of writing sets precedent. Both become part of the public record and can show where individual justices stand.

The Court also has a middle path between granting and denying. In a GVR — grant, vacate and remand — the Court grants the petition, vacates the lower-court judgment and sends the case back. The lower court then reconsiders the case, most often in light of a new Supreme Court decision. The Court often holds petitions that raise issues similar to a pending case, then disposes of them once it rules. A GVR does not decide who wins. The lower court can reach the same result after taking a fresh look.

Not every case reaches the Supreme Court through an ordinary cert petition. Original jurisdiction, mandatory direct appeals, certiorari before judgment and emergency applications each follow their own path to the justices.

Original jurisdiction comes from Article III of the Constitution. It covers cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and cases in which a state is a party. In these matters, the Supreme Court acts as the trial court rather than as an appeals court.

Disputes between states form the core of this docket. Federal law makes the Court's jurisdiction over controversies between two or more states exclusive. No other court can hear them. Many of these suits involve state boundaries or the division of rivers and other shared water supplies.

A state cannot simply file such a suit and expect a trial. It must first ask the Court for leave to file a complaint, and the justices can refuse.

The justices do not take testimony themselves. In many original cases, the Court appoints a special master to gather evidence and hear arguments. The special master then writes a report with recommendations. The parties can file exceptions to that report. The justices make the final decision.

A small set of direct appeals remains mandatory. The best-known category involves rulings from three-judge district courts, which Congress requires in some redistricting challenges. The losing side can appeal straight to the Supreme Court. The Court must decide these appeals, though it can resolve some of them summarily without oral argument.

Supreme Court Rule 11 creates another shortcut, called certiorari before judgment. It lets the Court take a case while it is still pending in a federal appeals court. That skips the intermediate appellate ruling entirely. The rule allows it only when a case is of such imperative public importance that it justifies departing from normal appellate practice.

Emergency applications travel a separate track altogether. A party might ask the Court to stay a lower-court order or to pause a policy while litigation continues. Each application goes first to the justice assigned to the circuit where the case arose. That justice can act alone or refer the request to the full Court.

These emergency rulings often come without full briefing or oral argument. This part of the Court's work is often called the shadow docket.

#5439. Constellation Space launches its platform for managing fleets of satellites with AI tools

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Alan Boyle on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:10 amNovember 12, 2026 at 9:11 am

Seattle-based Constellation Space is rolling out its flagship software platform, which uses machine learning to streamline operations for fleets of satellites and the ground networks that serve them.

“We build models in-house for things like weather, attenuation, signal jamming, demand … and synthesize all of that to help operators understand what their ground contact plan looks like in the future, and how to optimize their fleets,” CEO Kamran Majid told GeekWire.

The Constellation Platform is tailor-made for a growing number of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit. Keeping track of thousands of satellites — and the best opportunities for downlinking data from each of those satellites — is becoming an increasingly complicated task.

Constellation Space, which was founded last year, draws upon Majid’s experience as a NASA engineering intern and as a software engineer working on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.

“At Starlink, I saw firsthand how manual mission-control processes break down as constellations scale,” he said. “I started Constellation to help smaller teams get ahead of link failures instead of spending their time rebuilding pass plans and recovering from outages.”

Majid’s fellow co-founders include chief technology officer Raaid Kabir, a veteran of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, and Omeed Tehrani and Laith Altarabishi, who were previously software engineers at Capital One. “We’re a team of six people right now,” Majid said.

One year into its existence, Constellation Space has already gained traction. Several months ago, the startup said it raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Y Combinator, Nvidia, OpenAI, Samsung Next and other investors.

Majid said an early version of the Constellation Platform has attracted more than 10 customers, including Amazon Web Services. It’s also used by more than 20 academic institutions. “Our annual contract value this year is $2.25 million,” he said.

The platform combines forecasts for factors affecting satellite transmissions — including space situational awareness, weather conditions, signal-to-noise ratios, signal jamming and bandwidth demand — to predict how many gigabytes of data can be transmitted during a given pass. Operators can then use that data to optimize transmission settings and schedules.

Its machine-learning model is pre-trained on data from a global network of sensors. Once it’s deployed, the model adapts to each fleet’s specific hardware and ground stations. Constellation Space says satellite operators can boost downlinked data per pass by as much as 36%.

Majid said the journey from SpaceX to startup has been “really interesting.”

“The mindset is very similar,” he said. “I was previously an engineer. Now I’m finding myself in more of a business role. The mindset is just ‘first-principles thinking’ about everything. Eliminate all the requirements that don’t make sense before you even start to think about solving the problem. Those core tenets have stayed as we’ve progressed as a venture, and I think that’s been really important to our success so far.”

Setting up the startup in the Seattle area, where more than half of the world’s satellites are built, has also been interesting.

“We are a Y Combinator company, so we were in San Francisco for a couple of months, and there was a lot of pressure from the community in SF to have everyone be in San Francisco. We definitely felt that a little bit,” Majid said.

“But operating in the satellite sector of the space industry, Seattle is becoming more and more of a hub for the space industry in general,” he said. “Space companies are either completely moving here, opening up headquarters here, or just branching out here. It’s that, mixed in with Seattle just being known as a tech hub — and also, we all love Seattle.”

#5438. ‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center plan draws Eastern Washington protests

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon’s plans to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.

Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Big tech is shady. No more data centers” and “Water for life, not data,” according to the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin and its photos of the event.

The majority of the roughly 56 public comments were opposed to or had concerns about data center development, including worries about groundwater supplies, effects on agriculture and wildlife, and a lack of transparency, the Union-Bulletin reported. Supporters pointed to potential benefits from job creation and economic development.

The meeting highlighted continued resistance to data centers from communities concerned about higher electricity bills, depleted freshwater supplies and other environmental and social repercussions. Over the past year, tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft have pledged to limit those impacts and invest in host communities, but those commitments have not ended the opposition.

Elected officials are increasingly considering legislation and local ordinances to set standards and require greater transparency — an approach some tech leaders say could help address public concerns.

“There is a role for good laws, and if laws emerge that require that everybody do this work in a responsible way, I think that might be part of the solution,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, recently told reporters at a company event.

Commissioners in Western Washington’s Skagit County last month adopted significant restrictions on data center development. The facilities are prohibited in unincorporated areas, with some exceptions, and new caps on size and electricity usage will limit the technology to small-scale operations.

The planned Walla Walla County campus is one of two projects that would mark Amazon’s first large-scale data center developments in its home state. The second is in West Richland, part of the Tri-Cities. Amazon already operates smaller data centers in Washington.

The Walla Walla County campus would occupy roughly 134 acres at Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. Its three proposed single-story data center buildings would create about 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

According to a company fact sheet, the campus would use roughly 14 million gallons of water from the public utility to cool its equipment during its first year of operation. Amazon says it is working with the port to build a system that would replace the utility-supplied cooling water with nonpotable water drawn from the Columbia River. Wastewater from the campus “will meet industrial reuse standards,” the company said.

The campus would also use about 6 million gallons of utility-supplied water annually for employee needs.

Amazon’s fact sheet says the company will cover the electricity costs associated with the data center and that the “expenses aren’t added to the bills of local residents or businesses.”

The company is also working with partners to develop a nuclear power plant using small modular nuclear reactors near the Tri-Cities. The proposed plant could begin operating in the 2030s and “will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said.

Despite Amazon’s assurances, many attendees at Monday’s meeting called for a one-year, countywide moratorium on new data center development, the Union-Bulletin reported. Commissioner Bertha Clayton said she would consider a pause on new applications to give officials time to draft an ordinance to better regulate the developments.

Clayton said zoning changes adopted now would be unlikely to affect the current phase of Amazon’s project. The other two commissioners have previously said they do not support a moratorium, according to the Union-Bulletin.

The proposal is undergoing an environmental review under Washington’s State Environmental Policy Act, or SEPA. The review will assess potential environmental impacts and identify measures to address them. It will also determine whether the project requires a more detailed environmental impact statement.
