#5437. From maintenance windows to DNS faults: 10 causes of a bank app outage

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 causes of a bank app outage, from bad software updates to cloud failures and cyberattacks, explain why your banking app sometimes stops working

A banking app is a window, not a vault. The screen on a phone shows balances and sends payment instructions, but almost none of the actual work happens there. Each tap starts a request that travels through a chain of systems, and the bank controls only part of that chain.

The chain has several layers. The app on the phone talks to the bank's servers through application programming interfaces, or APIs, which pass requests back and forth in a structured format. Those servers draw on the core banking system, the ledger of record for accounts, balances and transactions. Around them sit outside vendors that handle tasks such as identity checks, one-time passcodes and fraud screening. Many banks also rent computing capacity from cloud providers or run their own data centers. Card payments and transfers move over shared payment networks the bank does not run. Connecting all of it is the public internet, which depends on the Domain Name System and on routing protocols to deliver traffic to the right place.

A fault in any one of those layers can produce the same result for the customer. The app freezes on a loading wheel, rejects a login or shows a generic "something went wrong" message. From the outside, a broken card network and a failed server update can look identical. That is one reason a bank app outage can be hard to diagnose, both for customers and for the bank's own engineers working to restore service.

Banks cause some outages on purpose. They take systems offline to install security patches or upgrade software, often at hours when fewer people are using them. Other outages come without warning: a release with a bug, a rush of customers on payday, a hardware failure in a data center or an attack meant to overwhelm servers. Some are partial. A customer may see a balance but be unable to move money.

The slides that follow explain 10 distinct causes of banking app problems, from scheduled maintenance to cyberattacks and aging infrastructure. Each one describes how the mechanism works and what it tends to look like on a customer's screen. They are a selection of mechanisms rather than a complete list, and they are not ranked.

Scheduled maintenance is downtime a bank chooses. Banks switch systems off on purpose to apply security fixes, upgrade software or migrate data to new platforms, and they often warn customers days ahead.

Not every change can be made while a system is running. Updating a database structure, replacing hardware or switching to a new version of core software can require pausing new transactions. A short pause keeps records consistent. It prevents a payment from being half-recorded in the old system and half-recorded in the new one.

Banks usually book this work for overnight hours or early weekend mornings in their home time zone, when activity is lightest. For a bank with customers abroad, a quiet 2 a.m. window at home can land in the middle of the working day somewhere else.

Planned work does not always switch off the entire app. A bank may leave balances and transaction history on screen while it pauses transfers, bill payments or new account applications. This setup is known as read-only mode, because data can be viewed but not changed. At other times, login itself is disabled, and the app shows a message that service is temporarily unavailable.

Notices typically appear in several places. Common channels include a banner inside the app, a message on the bank's website, an email to customers and posts on the bank's social media accounts. Some banks also run a dedicated service status page that lists current and upcoming disruptions. Many notices give a start time and an expected end time for the window.

A maintenance window can run longer than announced. If an upgrade step fails, engineers may need to reverse the change and restore the earlier version before services return. That recovery work stretches the outage past the time customers were told to expect.

For customers, the practical effect comes down to timing. A transfer or bill payment started just before a window opens may wait in a queue until systems come back online. A posted notice is often the quickest way to tell planned downtime apart from an unexpected failure.

A bank's core banking system is its master record of accounts, balances and transactions. When that core fails or slows down, the app cannot show or move money, even if the app itself is working normally.

A core system does more than store numbers. It opens and closes accounts, posts deposits and withdrawals, calculates interest, applies fees and tracks loan repayments. It is the official record of how much money each customer has.

The mobile app keeps little of that data on the phone. When a customer opens it, the app sends a request through the bank's servers and connecting software to the core. It then displays whatever comes back. The same core typically serves online banking, branch terminals, ATMs and call center staff. That shared dependence offers one clue to a core problem. Several channels tend to fail at the same time, not just the app.

Many cores do not finalize every transaction the instant it happens. Some work is posted in batches, often in an end-of-day run that brings the books into line. Between runs, a bank may track activity in a separate layer. That layer records pending items and adjusts the available balance a customer sees. If it falls out of step with the ledger, the gap shows up on the customer's screen.

The symptoms are often subtle. A balance may look stale, or stop updating after a purchase. A transaction can sit as pending longer than usual, appear twice, or vanish and return. Transfers may be accepted on screen but held before they move. In a deeper failure, the app may show an error in place of a balance. It may also switch to a view-only mode that hides payment options.

A core is hard to switch over to a backup. A website can run on many identical servers, and traffic can shift to a healthy one. A ledger must stay consistent. Two copies cannot both accept transactions without risking conflicting balances. Before a backup takes over, the bank has to confirm that every recorded transaction has carried across.

That caution also shapes recovery. After service returns, staff may need to reconcile transactions that arrived during the disruption. Balances can look wrong for a while as that work finishes, even though the app appears normal again.

A bank app can break the moment new code goes live. A faulty release can stop logins, block payments or scramble what appears on screen, whether it is pushed to the bank's own servers or to the app on customers' phones.

Two kinds of release matter here. Server-side changes update the systems the app talks to behind the scenes. A bank can deploy them at any time, and every customer feels the effect at once. It does not matter which version of the app sits on a given phone. A bug introduced this way can reach the whole customer base within minutes.

App releases work differently. A new version of an iPhone or Android app goes out through Apple $AAPL's App Store or Google $GOOGL Play. Each person installs it on their own schedule unless automatic updates are switched on. As a result, one customer can have a working app while another, on a newer or older version, sees errors. Support teams often ask which version a customer is running for this reason.

Not every bad deployment involves broken code. A configuration error can do similar damage. Examples include a wrong setting, a timeout set too short or a database address pointing to the wrong place. Changes like these are small and quick to make. That speed also makes them easy to get wrong.

When a release goes wrong, the usual first response is a rollback, which restores the previous working version. Server-side rollbacks can be fast if the team planned for them. App rollbacks are harder. A developer cannot simply pull a version back off phones that have already installed it. The fix usually arrives as another update.

Database changes complicate matters further. If a release altered how data is stored, reverting the code may not reverse that change. The older code may then fail to read the newer data format.

Engineering teams use several practices to limit the damage. A staged rollout sends a change to a small share of users first, then widens it if error rates stay normal. Google Play supports staged rollouts by percentage of users. Apple offers a phased release that spreads automatic updates over seven days.

Feature flags let a team ship code with a new function switched off. The team can then turn it on, or off again, without publishing a new release. Canary deployments route a slice of server traffic to the new version while the rest stays on the old one.

Testing catches many problems before launch, but a test environment is not an exact copy of production. Real customer data, real traffic and the wide variety of phones in use can expose bugs that tests missed.

For customers, timing is the clue. Problems that appear right after an app update, or that affect only people on one version, point toward a bad release. A wider system failure tends to hit everyone regardless of version.

A bank app can slow down or fail when too many customers use it at once. Predictable peaks such as paydays, benefit payment dates, tax deadlines and holiday shopping can push demand past the capacity a bank's systems were built to handle.

Many of these spikes follow the calendar. Direct deposits often post early in the morning, and many customers open their apps soon after to check that the money arrived. Government benefit payments also arrive on fixed dates. In the U.S., the federal income tax filing deadline usually falls in mid-April. In the U.K., the online deadline for Self Assessment returns is Jan. 31. Tax payments cluster around both deadlines.

Heavy load shows up first as slowness. Each server can only handle so many open connections and database queries at the same time. Once those limits are reached, new requests wait in line. If they wait too long, they time out, and the app displays a generic error.

Some banks use autoscaling, which adds server capacity automatically as traffic rises. It has limits. New servers take time to start, and a sudden spike can outrun them. Autoscaling also tends to cover the front-end layer that handles app requests, not every system behind it. A database or core ledger with fixed capacity can become the bottleneck. Extra front-end servers can then send it even more requests.

To protect those downstream systems, banks use rate limiting and queueing. Rate limiting caps how many requests a system accepts in a given period and turns the rest away. Customers often see this as a "try again later" message. Queueing holds requests and processes them in order. That can delay a transfer without losing it.

The app may still open normally while transactions fail. Balances and recent activity can be served from a cache, a stored copy of recent data that is cheap to deliver. A payment or transfer has to reach the systems that actually move money. Those are the systems under the most strain during a surge.

Retries can make a surge worse. When an app is slow, customers tap refresh or try a payment again, and software may also retry failed requests on its own. Each attempt adds load, a pattern engineers call a retry storm. Many apps space out automatic retries, a technique called exponential backoff, to limit the effect. Banks also load-test their systems and plan capacity around previous peaks. A peak larger than any seen before can still exceed that plan.

A bank app can go dark when the computing infrastructure underneath it fails. Banks host their services in their own data centers, on outside cloud platforms or on a mix of both. A power, hardware or network fault in any of those places can take the app down with it.

A data center is a building filled with servers, storage and networking equipment. It depends on a steady supply of electricity, cooling and network connections. Facilities usually carry backup batteries and generators to ride through a grid failure. If a cooling system breaks or a switch to backup power fails, servers may shut down to protect themselves. Every service running on that hardware stops with them.

Cloud providers such as Amazon $AMZN Web Services, Microsoft $MSFT Azure and Google $GOOGL Cloud rent this kind of capacity to customers. They divide their infrastructure into geographic regions. Each region contains several separate facilities, often called availability zones, with their own power and networking. A bank that spreads its app across multiple zones can usually survive the loss of one. A fault that hits an entire region is harder to escape. The same is true of a shared service the provider runs across regions.

Redundancy is the standard defense. A bank may copy data continuously to a second site and keep standby systems ready to take over. That handoff is called failover. It does not always work cleanly. A backup site may lack the capacity to carry full traffic. Data may not have finished copying when the primary site goes down. A bank also has to confirm that balances are consistent before it resumes moving money. That check can stretch out recovery.

Shared dependence creates a different kind of risk. When many companies rely on the same provider, one fault can disrupt unrelated businesses at once. A customer may find a bank app, a streaming service and an airline website failing on the same morning. That pattern often points to shared infrastructure rather than any single company's code.

Many banks run hybrid setups. They keep core records in their own data centers while running the app's front end, analytics or customer messaging in the cloud. Each link between those environments is another point of failure. If the connection between the cloud-hosted app and the bank's on-premise systems breaks, the app may open but fail to load accounts.

To a customer, a hosting outage looks like most other failures — a spinning wheel, an error message or a blank screen. Status pages run by the bank or by the cloud provider are often where an infrastructure problem is first confirmed.

A banking app relies on outside companies for jobs such as identity verification, one-time passcode delivery, fraud screening and account data aggregation. When one of those vendors fails, customers can lose access to login or a single feature, even while the bank's own systems run normally.

These connections run through application programming interfaces, or APIs. An API is a defined way for one piece of software to request data or an action from another. The banking app sends a request to a vendor's API, waits for a reply and then decides what to show the customer. If the reply never comes, arrives late or returns an error, the app has nothing useful to display.

Login is one place where this dependency becomes visible. Many banks send a one-time passcode by text message or email as a second step after a password. That message usually passes through a messaging provider and then a mobile carrier before it reaches the phone. A delay anywhere in that chain can mean the code expires or never arrives. The customer then cannot finish signing in.

Identity checks are another pressure point. Opening an account or adding a new device can trigger a check with an outside identity verification service. Some of these services compare a photo of an ID document with a selfie. If the service is unavailable, the app may stall at the verification step or ask the customer to try again later.

Fraud screening works in the background. Some banks pass login attempts or transactions to an outside fraud detection system that scores the risk before approval. When that scoring service times out, the bank has to decide whether to block the activity or let it through without a score. A bank configured to default to caution blocks it. The customer sees that as a refusal or an error message.

Data aggregation links run in the other direction. Budgeting apps, lenders and investment platforms often connect to bank accounts through an aggregator that pulls balances and transaction history. When the aggregator's connection breaks, the outside app shows stale data or asks the user to reconnect. The bank's own app may show the same account correctly the whole time.

The common thread is a split between where the failure happens and where the customer notices it. The bank's servers and ledger can be healthy while the broken part belongs to a different company. That split can also slow the repair. Bank support staff may be able to confirm the problem, but restoring service depends on the vendor.

Card payments and bank transfers travel over networks that sit outside a bank's own systems. When a card network, a payment processor or a transfer system has a fault, payments can fail even while the bank app opens and shows balances normally.

A single card tap or swipe passes through several separate parties. The merchant's terminal sends the transaction to the merchant's payment processor and acquiring bank. From there, it travels over a card network such as Visa $V or Mastercard $MA. The network routes it to the issuing bank, which holds the cardholder's account and decides whether to approve the payment.

That approval step is called authorization. It takes seconds and confirms that the account exists and has enough funds or available credit. Settlement comes later. It is the process in which money actually moves between the banks involved, usually in batches. A fault at the authorization stage shows up at once as a declined card. A fault at the settlement stage may surface later, as a transaction that stays pending longer than expected.

Each link in that chain is a possible point of failure. The location of the fault shapes who is affected. A processor problem can stop one group of merchants from accepting cards while shops using a different processor carry on. A card network problem can hit cardholders at many banks at the same time. An issuer problem is limited to that bank's own customers.

Bank transfers run on separate rails. In the U.S., many direct deposits, bill payments and account-to-account transfers move over the Automated Clearing House network, known as ACH. In the U.K., the Faster Payments system carries near-instant transfers between accounts at participating banks. If one of these systems slows or stops, a transfer submitted in the app may be accepted but not arrive on time.

Payment network disruptions therefore often look like an app failure. The app may log in, display balances and let a customer start a payment. The problem appears only at the final step, as a decline, an error message or a transfer stuck in processing. That error shows up inside the bank's app, even when the fault sits with a network several steps away.

Banks cannot repair an outside network themselves. They can pause affected features, post service notices and use backup routes where those exist. Card networks also offer a fallback called stand-in processing. When an issuer's systems cannot be reached, the network can approve or decline transactions on the issuer's behalf. It does so within limits the issuer has set in advance.

A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack floods a bank's systems with junk requests until real customers can't get through. Banks may also take their own apps offline on purpose to contain a suspected breach. Either way, the customer is locked out, but the cause behind the error screen is very different.

The "distributed" part is what makes these attacks hard to stop. The traffic does not come from one computer. It arrives from thousands of machines at once. Those machines usually belong to a botnet — a network of hijacked devices that an attacker controls remotely. Infected home routers, security cameras and other internet-connected gadgets often serve as recruits. Their owners rarely know it.

Attackers aim at different layers of a bank's setup. Some attacks try to saturate the network connection itself with sheer volume. Others target the protocols computers use to open connections, using up a server's capacity to track them. A third kind mimics ordinary app behavior, such as repeated login attempts or balance requests. That last type is harder to spot because each request looks legitimate on its own.

Banks defend against floods mainly by filtering traffic before it reaches their servers. Specialist mitigation services route incoming traffic through scrubbing centers. Those systems drop requests that match attack patterns and pass clean traffic onward. Content delivery networks spread load across many locations, so no single site absorbs the full flood. These tools reduce the damage. A large or novel attack can still slow an app or knock it offline for a time.

Intent and composition separate an attack from a legitimate rush of customers. A payday spike is real people trying to complete real tasks. A DDoS flood is manufactured traffic built to exhaust resources, and most of it never completes a transaction. On the customer's screen, though, both show up as the same stalled loading wheel.

Not every cyberattack outage comes from a flood. A bank that detects a possible intrusion, such as malware on internal systems or unauthorized access, may deliberately shut down online and mobile services. Isolating affected systems stops an attacker from moving further. It also protects customer data while investigators work. Ransomware, which encrypts files and demands payment for their release, can force the same kind of shutdown.

Outages tied to a breach tend to last longer than flood-driven ones. A DDoS attack usually ends when the traffic stops or is filtered out. An intrusion requires forensic work before anything comes back online. Restoring service means confirming the attacker is gone, checking that data has not been altered and rebuilding systems from clean backups.

A DDoS attack on its own does not mean customer accounts have been accessed. The goal of a flood is disruption, not theft. Attackers sometimes use one as cover for other activity, though. Banks therefore continue to investigate after the traffic subsides. A bank's official website and verified social media accounts are where it confirms what kind of incident occurred.

A bank app can be running normally and still be unreachable if the Domain Name System fails to resolve its address. Internet routing errors that send traffic the wrong way have the same effect. In both cases the fault sits between the phone and the bank, not inside either one.

The Domain Name System, or DNS, works like the internet's directory. An app does not reach a server by its name alone. It first asks a DNS resolver to translate a hostname, such as the address of the bank's API, into a numeric IP address. If the bank's authoritative DNS servers go down, or a DNS provider the bank relies on has a fault, that lookup fails. The app then shows a connection error even though the servers behind the name are healthy.

DNS answers are also cached for a set period, known as the time to live. Caching can make a fault uneven. Some users keep working from a stored answer, while others whose cached answer has expired cannot connect. The same mechanism can slow a fix. A corrected record takes time to replace the old one across resolvers.

Routing is a separate layer. The Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, is the system large networks use to tell one another which IP addresses they can reach and by which path. A mistaken or withdrawn BGP announcement can make a bank's addresses vanish from parts of the internet. Traffic can also be steered down a path that leads nowhere. BGP depends heavily on trust between networks. One network's misconfiguration can therefore spread well beyond the network that made it.

Expired certificates and domains cause a related kind of failure. Banking apps connect over encrypted connections that use Transport Layer Security, or TLS, which depends on a valid digital certificate. If that certificate lapses, the app's security checks reject the connection. A lapsed domain registration can break the name entirely.

These faults often hit some customers and spare others. A problem at one internet service provider, one mobile carrier or one region's DNS resolver can leave everyone else unaffected. That is why switching from home Wi-Fi to mobile data sometimes brings a banking app back. The switch sends requests through a different network and often a different resolver. Outage reports during these events can cluster by provider or location rather than spreading evenly across a bank's customers.

Many banks run modern mobile apps on top of systems built decades earlier, joined by layers of connecting software. Those links between old and new are often fragile. That makes every change riskier and every failure slower to diagnose.

Technical debt is the term software engineers use for the accumulated cost of shortcuts and aging design. Ward Cunningham, a programmer, coined the metaphor in the early 1990s. Like financial debt, it carries interest. Each workaround left in place makes the next update harder to build and test.

In banking, much of that debt sits in older programming languages. COBOL, a language designed for business data processing, still runs large amounts of transaction code at banks, insurers and government agencies. Much of that code executes on mainframe computers. These systems were built for an era of branch counters and teller terminals. They were not designed for millions of phones checking balances at all hours.

To bridge the gap, banks add middleware. This is software that translates a request from a modern app into a format an older system understands, then translates the answer back. Over the years, banks stack one layer on another as they add online banking, then mobile apps, then connections for outside fintech services. Each layer is another place where a timeout, a format mismatch or a capacity limit can stop a request.

The fragility shows up during change. An update to one component can break an assumption buried in another component that may not have been reviewed in years. Documentation for older code is often incomplete. Testing every path through a decades-old system is difficult. Some problems surface only after release, when real customers run into them.

Replacing the old systems carries its own risk. A core modernization project can involve moving every customer account and years of transaction history to new software without interrupting service. Banks often run old and new platforms side by side during a migration. That temporarily adds even more integration points. A migration that goes wrong can leave customers unable to log in or see accurate balances.

Staffing adds pressure. Fewer engineers learn COBOL and mainframe operations today than in earlier generations. Many of the specialists who built these systems have retired. When something breaks deep in a legacy stack, the people who understand it may be few. That can turn a short glitch into a longer outage.

#5436. Nvidia founder’s wife faces spotlight that MacKenzie Scott and Melinda French Gates know well

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:56 amNovember 14, 2026 at 11:14 am

As the fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair came to a head with his resignation as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, attention has turned in part to his wife, Lori Huang, who has stayed largely in the background during their 41-year marriage.

A New York Times profile, and other media coverage, placed Lori Huang alongside two familiar Seattle names — MacKenzie Scott, ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates — as tech billionaires’ spouses who have faced infidelity playing out in public.

Huang acknowledged to employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The admission followed Times reporting last month that a Chinese businesswoman he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as an intelligence asset. China has denied the espionage claims.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Kress spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Huang was worth about $145 billion as of Wednesday’s close, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, nearly all of it from his roughly 3.4% stake in Nvidia. That figure doesn’t reflect Thursday’s drop: Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at the open, pushing the company’s market value below $4 trillion, CNBC reported. Huang’s fortune peaked at as much as $195 billion in May, according to Bloomberg.

More than half of his 922 million shares belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are co-trustees, the Times reported, and she solely controls a separate trust holding about $5 billion in Nvidia stock.

Scott and French Gates each came out of their divorces with vast fortunes. Scott, whose split from Bezos was announced in 2019, left with about $38 billion. French Gates, who divorced Gates in 2021, received an estimated $25 billion in a settlement that was never publicly disclosed, The Independent reported.

Both have since steered billions into philanthropy. Scott has donated $26 billion through her organization, Yield Giving. French Gates left the Gates Foundation in 2024 with $12.5 billion for her own work.

George Rush, who co-wrote the Daily News gossip column Rush & Molloy, told the Times that the Huang situation differs from the Bezos and Gates splits in one key way: this relationship has the potential to move markets and carry global consequences.

The couple’s story has Pacific Northwest roots. Jensen Huang, born in Taiwan, was sent as a child to live with relatives in Tacoma, Wash., and later went to high school in Beaverton, Ore., according to Quartr. Lori Huang also graduated from an Oregon high school.

The two met in the early 1980s at Oregon State University, where Lori Huang, then Lori Mills, was one of only a handful of women studying engineering, the Times reported. They were paired as lab partners in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and Huang later told OSU that meeting her was “the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”

After graduating and marrying, the Huangs moved to Silicon Valley to work as chip designers. Lori Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, where she earned more than her husband did at LSI Logic, he told The New Yorker in 2023. Just before Nvidia’s founding in 1993, she gave up her career to raise their two children, Spencer and Madison, who both now work at Nvidia.

Huang has frequently credited her support. Speaking on a podcast in May, he recalled missing the kids’ karate tournaments while building the company and said she never complained. “That’s the gift that she gave me,” he said.

Lori Huang is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, according to the Times. The couple gave $50 million in 2022 to launch a research complex bearing their names at Oregon State. Last month, the foundation gave the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, led by Nobel laureate David Baker, nearly 7 million GPU hours of cloud computing.

#5435. FDIC and NCUA coverage explained: 10 things to know when your bank goes down

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A bank outage vs. bank failure explainer covering FDIC insurance, the $250,000 limit, credit unions and what happens to your deposits in each case

A banking app that will not load and a bank that regulators have shut down can look alike from a phone screen. They are different events with different risks. One is a problem of access. The other is a problem of solvency.

During a bank outage, apps, websites, ATMs or card networks stop working for a time. The money does not go anywhere. Balances are still recorded on the bank's books, and the deposits are there when service returns. The disruption can still cause trouble when a bill is due or a card is declined at the register. But an outage on its own does not put a deposit at risk.

A bank failure is a separate matter. It happens when a bank can no longer meet its obligations and regulators close it. In that case, whether a customer gets money back depends on deposit insurance.

In the U.S., that protection comes from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. The FDIC was created in 1933, during the Great Depression, under the Banking Act of 1933. The FDIC states that no depositor has lost a penny of insured funds since it began operating. Credit unions have their own insurer, the National Credit Union Administration, which backs member deposits through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund.

Deposit insurance has limits. Coverage stops at a set dollar amount, and it applies to some products but not others. How an account is titled can change how much of a balance is protected. Stocks, bonds and other investment products are not deposits, even when an insured bank sells them.

The bank outage vs. bank failure distinction matters in the moment. A frozen app usually calls for patience and good records. A failure calls for knowing exactly how coverage works.

The 10 slides that follow explain what an outage is and what a failure is. They cover how FDIC insurance works, the $250,000 limit and the ownership categories that can extend it, and what insurance leaves out. They also explain credit union coverage and what happens to accounts when a bank closes. They show how regulators handled the 2023 failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. The final slides cover how to tell a glitch from something more serious and how to check coverage before it matters.

A bank outage is a technical failure of access, not a loss of money. When a bank's app, website, ATMs or card network stops working for a time, the deposits behind those systems are still recorded on the bank's books. The balance owed to each customer does not change.

An outage affects the tools customers use to reach their accounts. A mobile app might refuse to load. Online banking might show an error page. An ATM might not dispense cash, or a debit card might not go through at a checkout. Any one of these channels can go down on its own, or several can fail at once.

None of those channels is the account itself. The app and the website display information drawn from the bank's records. The ATM and the card network send instructions to those records. When the connection breaks, the customer loses the view and the ability to give instructions. The underlying record of what the bank owes that customer stays in place.

That is the central difference between an outage and a bank failure. An outage is an operational problem. A failure is a financial one. A bank fails when it can no longer meet its obligations, and regulators step in to close it. An outage alone does not close a bank or change what it owes its depositors.

Deposit insurance reflects this split. Federal deposit insurance in the U.S. exists to protect customers when an insured bank fails. An outage does not trigger it, because the bank has not closed and no deposits have been lost. The money remains the bank's obligation throughout the disruption.

The practical cost of an outage is lost access. Customers may be unable to move money, pay a bill or withdraw cash until service returns. A payment that cannot go out during an outage is delayed, not lost from the account.

A bank failure is a solvency problem. Regulators shut a bank down once it can no longer cover what it owes, and that closure marks the failure.

An outage is a different kind of event. It is a technical breakdown that knocks apps, websites, ATMs or card networks offline for a time. Balances remain recorded on the bank's books while systems are down. A failure concerns the bank's finances, not its computers.

To a customer, the two can feel similar. Either one can leave a person unable to reach an account for a while. The causes differ, and so does the response.

An outage ends when the bank brings its systems back. A failure does not resolve that way. The decision to close a bank rests with regulators, not with the bank's technology staff.

The two problems can also occur independently of each other. A bank with every system running can still be insolvent. A bank whose app has been down for hours can remain financially sound. A working screen is no sign of solvency, and a frozen one is no sign of insolvency.

For depositors, the practical question in a failure is what protects their money. In the U.S., the answer is federal deposit insurance. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insures deposits at member banks. Credit unions have separate coverage through the National Credit Union Administration.

Deposit insurance is designed for failures, not outages. A bank that is temporarily offline has not failed, and its customers' deposits are still there. Insurance comes into play only after regulators have closed a bank that cannot pay what it owes.

A closure is also distinct from everyday payment trouble. A declined card, a delayed direct deposit or a transaction stuck in pending status is usually a processing issue. None of those, on its own, signals that a bank has failed.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC, protects customers of its member banks by insuring their deposits. If an insured bank fails, covered money is protected rather than lost along with the bank.

That protection is designed for one kind of event. Deposit insurance responds to a bank failure, which happens when a bank can no longer meet its obligations and regulators close it. It plays no part in an outage. While systems are down, the customer's balance stays recorded on the bank's books.

The agency dates to the Great Depression. It was created in 1933 under the Banking Act of 1933. The FDIC states that no depositor has lost a penny of insured funds since it began operating. That record is the agency's own claim, and it covers insured funds only.

Membership is the starting point. The FDIC insures deposits at member banks. A customer's first check is whether the bank holding the money is an FDIC member. Deposits at a bank outside the FDIC's membership get none of this coverage.

Within a member bank, protection has a ceiling. It applies per depositor, per insured bank and per ownership category. Each insured bank carries a separate limit. Money held at two insured banks is covered at each one.

The insurance also depends on the type of product. It applies to deposits such as checking and savings accounts. Investment products fall outside it, even when an insured bank sells them. Together, the ceiling and the product rules decide how much of a given balance the insurance reaches.

When a member bank fails, the FDIC delivers that protection in one of two ways. It often arranges for another bank to assume the deposits. If no buyer is found, it pays depositors directly.

Credit union members fall outside the FDIC. Their deposits are insured by the National Credit Union Administration through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund.

FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. The limit applies to each category separately. A depositor who holds money in more than one category at the same bank can therefore be insured for more than $250,000 there.

Each part of that rule does a different job. "Per depositor" means the limit attaches to the person, not to an individual account. "Per insured bank" means each FDIC member bank carries its own separate limit. "Per ownership category" means coverage is counted within each legal form of ownership, not across everything a person has on deposit.

The number of accounts matters less than the category they sit in. Consider a checking account, a savings account and a certificate of deposit, all held in one person's name at the same bank. All three fall into the single account category. Their balances are added together and measured against one $250,000 limit. Opening a fourth or fifth account of the same type at that bank does not create new coverage.

The ownership categories recognized by the FDIC include single accounts, joint accounts, certain retirement accounts and trust accounts. Each represents a different way of owning money. Each also carries its own limit for the same depositor at the same bank. Take a person with $250,000 in a single account and $250,000 in a qualifying retirement account at one bank. That person could be insured for $500,000 there, because the two balances fall under separate categories.

Spreading money across banks follows the same logic. Each insured bank is treated on its own. A depositor might hold $250,000 in a single account at one FDIC member bank. If that person holds another $250,000 in a single account at a different member bank, $500,000 would be insured in total.

The $250,000 figure is a ceiling on insurance, not on deposits. A bank can hold far more than that for one customer. Only the insured portion is capped.

Money above the limit within one category is uninsured. In an ordinary bank failure, a depositor has no guarantee of recovering that excess. Knowing which category each account falls into is the starting point for working out how much of a balance is protected.

FDIC insurance protects deposits, not investments or stored valuables. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities, cryptocurrency and the contents of a safe deposit box all fall outside its coverage. That stays true even when an FDIC-insured bank is the one selling or holding them.

Coverage applies to four deposit products: checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts and certificates of deposit. With each of these, a customer places money with the bank and the bank records what it owes back. That recorded obligation is what deposit insurance stands behind if the bank fails.

Investment products work differently. A stock is a share of ownership in a company. A bond is a loan to a company or a government. A mutual fund pools investors' money to buy securities. None of these is a deposit, and their value can rise or fall with the market. FDIC insurance does not make up losses on any of them.

The names can blur the line. A money market deposit account is a deposit product and is covered. A money market mutual fund is a mutual fund, which puts it on the uninsured side. The two can appear next to each other in the same banking app.

Annuities follow the same rule. A bank branch can be the place of purchase, but that does not change what the product is. An annuity bought there is still not an insured deposit.

Cryptocurrency is excluded as well. A bank or a bank-linked app may let customers buy or hold digital assets. Those holdings are not deposit products, and they carry no FDIC coverage.

Safe deposit boxes invite confusion because of the word "deposit." The box is a storage service, not an account. Cash, jewelry, documents or anything else inside it is not counted as a deposit. FDIC insurance does not pay for lost contents.

A bank statement can be sorted into two groups. Balances in checking, savings, money market deposit accounts and CDs count toward deposit insurance in a failure, up to the coverage limits. Investment holdings and box contents do not, whatever logo appears at the top of the page.

Credit union deposits are protected by the National Credit Union Administration, not the FDIC. The NCUA insures members' money through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, with standard coverage of $250,000 per member, per insured credit union, per ownership category.

The NCUA is a federal agency that is separate from the FDIC. It does for credit unions what the FDIC does for banks. A member who keeps savings at a federally insured credit union relies on the NCUA's fund if that credit union fails.

The coverage formula has three parts. The limit applies per member, so it attaches to the person who holds the money. It also applies per insured credit union, so money at two different insured credit unions is counted separately. The third part is the ownership category.

That third part means one member can be insured for more than $250,000 at a single credit union. For that to happen, the money has to be held in different ownership categories. Two accounts in the same category at the same credit union share one $250,000 limit.

This structure matches the FDIC's rules for banks. A member who compares a bank account with a credit union account faces the same standard dollar limit and the same three-part test. What differs is the agency and the fund that stand behind the money.

Share insurance comes into play only when a credit union fails, meaning it can no longer meet its obligations. A credit union whose app or ATMs stop working for a time has an access problem instead. Members' balances stay recorded on the credit union's books during that kind of disruption. Share insurance plays no part in that situation.

Members who want to check their own position can use the NCUA's share insurance estimator. It estimates coverage under the same rules: per member, per credit union and per category.

When the FDIC closes a failed bank, customers typically regain access to their insured deposits within a few business days. The agency settles those accounts in one of two ways. It either moves them to another bank or pays depositors directly.

Closures usually take place on a Friday. On that schedule, the weekend falls between the closure and the next business day. For a customer, the wait before insured money is reachable again is usually counted in days, not weeks or months.

One outcome is an assumption. The FDIC often arranges for another bank to take on the failed bank's deposits. Customers in that case do not need to open a new account or move money themselves. Their accounts move to the acquiring bank automatically. The balance remains a deposit. What changes is the institution that holds it.

The second outcome applies when no buyer is found. The FDIC then pays depositors directly for their insured balances. In this case, the money comes from the FDIC itself rather than through an account at a new bank. With no acquiring bank, there is no new account waiting for the customer. Deciding where to deposit that payout next falls to the customer.

Either way, the process deals with insured deposits. How much of a balance counts as insured depends on the coverage limit and on how each account is titled.

Records help during the changeover. A customer who keeps recent statements and a note of current balances has a reference point. Those records can be checked against the figures the acquiring bank or the FDIC reports after the transfer or payout. An acquiring bank, like any bank, generally has a duty to correct errors on accounts. A record made before the closure gives the customer something specific to point to if a balance looks wrong.

Every depositor at Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank was made whole in 2023, including those holding more than the $250,000 insurance limit. That outcome came from a systemic risk exception regulators invoked for those two banks. It was not a change to the standard rules.

Silicon Valley Bank failed on March 10, 2023. Signature Bank failed two days later, on March 12, 2023. Regulators applied the same exception to both closures.

The exception mattered because of how ordinary coverage works. Standard FDIC insurance stops at $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Any balance above that line is uninsured. In a typical failure, a customer holding more than the limit has no guarantee of getting the excess back in full.

In these two cases, the line did not decide the outcome. Depositors with balances above $250,000 were made whole alongside those with smaller accounts.

The decision covered Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. It did not raise the coverage limit for anyone else. It also does not commit regulators to take the same step the next time a bank closes. A customer who keeps more than $250,000 in one ownership category at one bank still relies on the standard limit, not on the 2023 precedent.

That distinction matters for planning. The default protection for a large balance comes from the standard rules, which count coverage separately for each insured bank and each ownership category. Spreading money across categories, or across more than one insured bank, can keep more of it within insured limits. A balance above those limits carries risk that the 2023 response did not remove.

The two failures also show where the line between an outage and a failure falls. Neither bank had a technical glitch that would clear once apps and websites came back online. Both were bank failures, the kind of event in which regulators close a bank that can no longer meet its obligations. Restored service would not have changed what happened to depositors' money. For customers of those banks, deposit insurance and the systemic risk exception decided the outcome, not the bank's systems.

A payment glitch, a bank outage and a bank failure can look alike at the checkout counter, but they are three different problems. A glitch is usually a processing issue with a single transaction. An outage cuts off access for a time. A failure means regulators have closed the bank.

The narrowest of the three is the processing issue. A declined card, a direct deposit that has not arrived or a charge stuck as pending usually reflects how a payment is moving through the system. On its own, it does not mean the bank's systems are down. It also does not mean the bank is in financial trouble.

An outage is broader. The bank's app or website stops loading, ATMs stop dispensing cash or card networks stop approving purchases for a period. These are technical breakdowns of access. The deposits themselves stay recorded on the bank's books while the systems are offline.

A failure belongs in a separate category. It is a financial problem, not a technical one. A bank fails when it can no longer meet its obligations, and regulators close it. For deposits, the protection that matters at that point is federal deposit insurance. The FDIC covers member banks, and the NCUA covers credit unions. A glitch or an outage does not bring deposit insurance into play, because no bank has closed.

The practical test is what has stopped working. If one payment misbehaves while everything else runs normally, a processing matter is the likely cause. If every channel to the bank goes dark at once, an outage is more likely. A failure does not show up as an error message. It shows up as a closure by regulators.

Good records help in all three situations. Keep track of your balance and save recent statements. During an outage, pending transactions can appear differently from posted ones. The balance on screen may therefore not match the figure you expect.

If a number still looks wrong after service returns, raise it with the bank. Banks generally have a duty to correct errors on customer accounts. Saved statements make it easier to show what the balance should have been.

Two FDIC tools answer the core coverage questions. BankFind shows whether a bank is FDIC-insured, and the Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator, known as EDIE, estimates how much of a depositor's money falls within the insurance limit.

BankFind comes first. FDIC insurance applies only to deposits at member banks. A BankFind search confirms whether the institution holding an account belongs to that system. Without that membership, FDIC deposit insurance does not protect the money held there.

EDIE handles the arithmetic that follows. The estimator asks how each account is titled. It then sorts accounts into ownership categories, such as single accounts, joint accounts, certain retirement accounts and trust accounts. Each category is measured against the limit separately. That is how one depositor can hold insured balances above the standard limit at a single bank.

The per-bank part of the rule works in two directions. Deposits at two different insured banks count against two separate limits. Several accounts in the same ownership category at one bank are added together and measured against a single limit. A depositor who opens a second savings account in the same name at the same bank does not gain extra coverage.

Only deposit products belong in an estimate. Checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts and certificates of deposit are the balances to enter. Brokerage or crypto holdings do not belong in the calculation, even when they were bought through the same insured bank.

Credit union members need a different tool. Their deposits are insured by the National Credit Union Administration, not the FDIC. EDIE does not apply to those accounts. The NCUA offers its own share insurance estimator for that purpose. It works from the same structure of coverage per member, per insured credit union, per ownership category.

Recent statements make these estimates easier to run. They list the exact account titles and current balances an estimator asks for. Account titles matter because the wording on an account determines which ownership category it falls into.

Accounts held outside the U.S. fall under other systems. Other countries run deposit guarantee schemes, but their limits differ by country. The scheme in the country where an account is held sets the terms for that money. FDIC tools do not measure that coverage.

The results of these checks do not depend on whether an app or ATM is working. Coverage rests on a bank's membership and on how accounts are titled. Running a check in advance means the answer is already known before any disruption.

#5434. Pending, posted or failed? How to read the status of your payment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Pending vs posted vs failed payments explained, covering ACH timing, wire cutoffs, card holds and app labels that show whether a bank transfer went through

A bank transfer can leave one account and take hours or days to appear in another. The money has not vanished. It is usually sitting in an intermediate stage. The label your bank or app attaches to it tells you which stage that is.

Every electronic payment passes through a sequence. It is requested, recorded, processed and settled into an account. Banks compress that sequence into a few words on a transaction screen, and those words carry specific meanings. A pending item has been recorded but not finished. A posted item is final and part of the account's official record. A failed or declined payment never moved any money. A returned payment is a separate case: it can look complete before it is sent back.

The difference has practical consequences. It affects whether you can spend money that appears in your account and whether a rent payment has reached the landlord. It can also show whether a charge that looks wrong may still change before it posts. The status shapes the next step, too. A pending transfer usually needs more time. A failed one needs fixing before a retry.

Timing depends on the payment rail behind the transfer. In the U.S., ACH transfers are processed in batches through the Automated Clearing House network. That network is operated by the Federal Reserve and The Clearing House. Standard ACH transfers are processed on business days, which exclude weekends and federal holidays. Wire transfers are sent individually and are generally treated as final once sent. Card purchases go through an authorization step before the merchant submits the charge for settlement. That is why the amount on a pending card transaction can differ from the final one. Peer-to-peer apps such as Zelle, Venmo and Cash App use their own status labels and their own rules on reversals.

This guide to pending vs posted vs failed payments breaks the topic into 10 parts. The first three slides explain what each status means. The next five cover how card, ACH, wire and app payments behave, including temporary holds that can tie up part of a balance. The final two explain why transfers fail or get returned and how to confirm whether a payment went through. They also cover what information to have ready when contacting the bank about a stuck transfer.

A pending payment is a transaction your bank has recorded but not yet finished processing. The money may already be set aside from your available balance, but the item is not final.

That unfinished state is why a pending entry looks different from the rest of the transaction history. Many banking apps and websites list pending items in their own section, apart from completed activity. Others mark each entry with a "pending" label. Either way, the bank is signaling that the payment has started but has not reached the end of the process.

The clearest effect of a pending item shows up in the account's two balances. The available balance is the amount the bank currently lets you spend or withdraw. The current balance, also called the ledger balance, reflects only transactions that have fully completed. While a payment is pending, the bank may reduce the available balance right away. The ledger balance can stay where it was until the item finishes.

This gap between the two numbers is the main reason people think a transfer has disappeared. Money leaves the available balance, yet nothing matching it appears in the ledger balance or on the statement. The funds are usually in a holding position while the payment works its way through.

A pending status applies in both directions. An outgoing payment can be pending on the sender's account, and an incoming deposit can be pending on the receiver's account. In each case, the bank has acknowledged the item without treating it as complete.

Because a pending entry is provisional, its details are not locked in. The amount shown can differ from the amount that eventually settles. The entry can also drop off without ever completing — for example, if a merchant or sender cancels the payment before it is finalized. Until the status changes, the pending amount works as a placeholder rather than a final record of what moved.

A posted transaction is one the bank has finished processing. It has been added to the account's ledger balance, sometimes called the current balance. Once an item posts, its amount no longer shifts, and it will not drop off the account on its own.

Posting marks the point at which a payment stops being provisional. For a card purchase, the merchant's charge has settled. For a deposit, the incoming money has been credited to the account record. For an outgoing transfer, the debit has been entered on the bank's books.

Posted items usually carry a posting date. That date can differ from the day the purchase or transfer was made. A purchase made on one day may post a day or more later. The gap reflects how long the payment took to finish processing. It does not mean the purchase itself was delayed.

The statement is the formal record of an account. Posted items are what a monthly statement lists. They are also what reconciliation, budgeting software and tax records rely on. Pending items generally do not appear there.

The word final has a narrow meaning in this context. It means the bank has completed its processing and the entry is part of the account history. It does not mean the account holder has run out of options. A posted credit card charge can still be disputed as a billing error under the Fair Credit Billing Act. Errors in electronic transfers to or from a bank account fall under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and its implementing rule, Regulation E. Each law sets its own dispute process. The original entry typically stays on the record, and a correction shows up as its own new line.

A posted deposit is not always fully spendable right away. Banks can hold some deposits, particularly checks, under the Federal Reserve's Regulation CC. That hold governs when the money can be used. It does not change whether the deposit has been recorded.

On the sending side, a posted debit is the clearest sign the bank completed its part of a transfer. It does not by itself show that the receiving bank has credited the recipient. That step happens on the other institution's books.

A failed or declined payment never completes. No money leaves your account, and none reaches the recipient. A returned payment is different. It can look finished before the money comes back.

The labels "failed" and "declined" describe a payment that stopped before any funds changed hands. A card declined at a checkout counter is a common example. The purchase is refused on the spot, and the balance stays where it was. A bank transfer or app payment can end the same way. Instead of a refusal at a register, it shows up as failed or declined in the transaction history.

With nothing moved, a failed payment usually leaves little trace on the account. There may be no entry at all, or a line showing the attempt with a status label rather than a deduction. The bill, rent or invoice the payment was meant to cover remains unpaid until a new payment goes through.

A returned payment leaves a longer trail. The original entry appears first, and it may even post. A second, offsetting entry appears later, when the money is sent back. Someone who checked the account only once could believe the transfer succeeded. A later look at the account shows the reversal.

A return usually carries a reason code. The code is a short label that identifies why the payment came back. In the U.S. ACH system, return reason codes start with the letter R followed by two digits. The code typically sits in the transaction details or in a message from the bank, not on the main account summary.

Timing is another way to tell the outcomes apart. A decline or failure usually surfaces at the moment of the attempt or shortly after. A return arrives after the payment has already started moving. That gap means it can appear after the sender has stopped watching.

The difference matters on the receiving end, too. A failed payment never shows up for the recipient. A returned payment can appear in the recipient's account and then be taken back out.

A card payment goes through authorization first and settlement second. The bank approves the purchase at checkout, and the merchant submits the charge for final payment later. The amount approved at the first step is not always the amount that posts at the second.

Authorization is the quick check at the register or online checkout page. The payment terminal sends a request through the card network, such as Visa $V or Mastercard $MA, to the bank that issued the card. That bank confirms the card is valid and that the account has enough money or available credit. It then approves or declines the request.

An approval reserves the amount, but it does not complete the payment. No money has reached the merchant at this point. The transaction exists only as a commitment that the funds are there.

Settlement is the second step. The merchant gathers its approved transactions and submits them for payment, often as a group rather than one by one. The issuing bank then sends the money to the merchant's bank through the card network. Once that happens, the item on the cardholder's account changes from pending to posted.

The gap between those two steps is where amounts can shift. A sit-down restaurant is the clearest example. The server runs the card for the bill before the diner writes in a tip. The authorization covers only the pre-tip total. When the restaurant submits the charge, the tip is included. The posted amount then comes in higher than the pending one.

Online orders can push the two steps further apart. A retailer may authorize the full order at checkout and settle the charge only when the goods ship. If an item sells out, the settled amount can be smaller. If items ship separately, the charge can arrive as more than one posted line.

Purchases made in a foreign currency can change as well. The conversion into dollars is applied when the charge is processed for settlement. If the exchange rate moves between authorization and settlement, the posted figure can differ slightly from the pending one.

A merchant that never submits an approved charge never collects on it. In that case the authorization does not become a payment. It drops off the account after a period set by the card issuer. This often happens when an order is canceled before it ships.

A pending charge that does not match the receipt is not, on its own, a billing error. The posted amount is the one to check. If the posted charge differs from the final receipt, the card issuer's dispute process is the route for challenging it.

A standard ACH transfer does not move instantly. It travels in batches over the Automated Clearing House network and advances only on business days, which leave out weekends and federal holidays.

The ACH network is the U.S. system behind many routine bank-to-bank payments. Paychecks sent by direct deposit commonly run on it. So do automatic bill payments and transfers between your own accounts at two different banks. Two operators process the traffic. The Federal Reserve runs one. The Clearing House, a company owned by large commercial banks, runs the other.

Batch processing explains much of the wait. Your bank does not send each payment on its own the moment you tap the button. It gathers payments together and submits them as a group. The network sorts them and passes them along to the receiving banks. Those banks then apply them to customer accounts. Each handoff happens on a set schedule rather than continuously.

ACH payments flow in both directions. An ACH credit pushes money from the sender to the recipient, as an employer does on payday. An ACH debit pulls money from an account with the account holder's authorization, as a utility or lender does with autopay. Both types follow the same business-day calendar.

That calendar decides when a transfer actually moves. A transfer started on a Saturday does not begin moving until the next business day. When a federal holiday falls on a Monday, that weekend transfer waits until Tuesday. Banks also set their own daily cutoff times for ACH requests. A request submitted after the cutoff is handled as part of the next business day's work.

This is why a payment can sit in pending status through a long weekend without anything going wrong. The bank has accepted the transfer, but the network has not processed it yet.

Same Day ACH is a faster option within the same network. It lets eligible payments settle on the business day they are submitted instead of a later one. It still follows business-day rules. A Same Day ACH request made on a Sunday does not settle that Sunday. Whether you can choose it, and on what terms, depends on the bank or service handling the transfer.

For a payment that has to arrive by a specific date, business days matter more than calendar days. A loan installment or tuition bill due the day after a holiday weekend has fewer processing days available than the same payment due midweek. Starting the transfer earlier leaves room for the batches to clear before the deadline.

A wire transfer submitted before your bank's daily cutoff time usually goes out that business day. Once it is sent, it is generally treated as final.

Each bank sets its own wire cutoff time. No single nationwide deadline applies to every institution. The cutoff can also differ between domestic and international wires at the same bank. It can differ between a request made at a branch and one made online, too.

A wire requested after the cutoff typically waits until the next business day to go out. Weekends and federal holidays push a late request forward in the same way. A wire started on a Friday evening may not move until the following week.

For U.S. domestic wires, the main system is Fedwire, run by the Federal Reserve. Fedwire handles each payment individually and settles it in real time. That one-at-a-time handling is why a domestic wire can reach the recipient's bank on the same day it is sent.

International wires usually pass through more steps. Banks commonly exchange the payment instructions over the SWIFT messaging network. The money may also move through one or more correspondent banks before it reaches the recipient. Each extra stop can add time, and each bank along the way follows its own processing schedule.

Finality is the trade-off for that speed. A sending bank can ask the receiving bank to send a wire back. Whether the money returns usually depends on the receiving bank and the recipient cooperating, or on the funds still sitting in the account. There is no simple cancel button once a wire has moved.

That finality makes wires a frequent target for fraud. A common scheme involves criminals impersonating a title company, a vendor or a relative and sending new account instructions by email or text. Calling the recipient at a phone number already on file, rather than one in the message, is a direct way to check those instructions before sending.

U.S. consumers sending money abroad have one narrow protection. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rules for remittance transfers generally let a sender cancel within 30 minutes of paying. That window applies only if the recipient has not already picked up or received the funds.

Before a wire goes out, check the recipient's full name, account number and the bank's routing number or SWIFT code. Asking the bank for its cutoff time on the specific type of wire being sent avoids an unexpected one-day delay.

A temporary card hold is money a merchant reserves on your card before it knows the final charge. The hold lowers the funds you can spend right away. It is a placeholder rather than the payment itself, and it is replaced or released once the real charge goes through.

Fuel pumps show how this works. When you swipe or tap at the pump, the station does not yet know how much fuel you will buy. It first asks the card issuer to approve a preset amount, which is called a pre-authorization. That amount reflects the station's own setting, not your actual purchase.

After you finish filling the tank, the station submits the true total for settlement. The final posted charge reflects the fuel you pumped. The pre-authorization should then fall away rather than add to that charge.

During that gap, the account can look confusing. The hold may show as a pending item for one amount, while the real charge appears for a different amount. To someone scanning the transaction list, that can look like a double charge. In most cases it is one purchase shown in two stages.

The effect depends on the type of card. On a debit card, a hold reduces the cash available in the linked checking account. On a credit card, it reduces available credit instead. With a debit card, the held amount is the account holder's own cash. That money cannot cover other bills while the hold remains.

That can cause knock-on problems. A large hold on a debit card can leave too little available balance for another payment. A payment that would otherwise go through may then be declined.

Fuel stations are not the only merchants that work this way. Hotels commonly place a hold at check-in, and car rental companies commonly do the same at pickup. In both cases the business is reserving funds against a bill that is not yet final.

Paying a cashier inside the station for a set amount of fuel avoids the open-ended pre-authorization. The charge is known up front. If a hold stays on the account after the final charge has posted, the merchant or the card issuer can confirm whether it has been released.

Zelle, Venmo and Cash App each use their own status labels. A label describes where a payment sits inside that service, not necessarily where the money sits in a bank account. The same status word can mean different things in different apps and on a bank statement.

The difference starts with how each service is built. Zelle is operated by Early Warning Services, a company owned by a group of U.S. banks. It appears inside many banks' own mobile apps. A Zelle payment moves money from one bank account to another, with no separate balance held in between.

Venmo, owned by PayPal $PYPL, and Cash App, run by Block $SQ, work differently. Money sent through either app usually lands first in the recipient's balance inside the app. It stays there until the recipient spends it or moves it out.

That structure creates two separate events for Venmo and Cash App users. The first is the payment between two people. The second is the transfer from the app balance out to a bank account. A payment can show as finished in the app while the move to the bank is still in progress on its own timeline. Both apps offer a standard transfer to a bank and a faster instant option that carries a fee.

Zelle payments between users who are already enrolled are generally described as arriving within minutes. That description is not a guarantee. A payment sent to someone who has not yet enrolled works differently. The money cannot reach the recipient until that person signs up with the email address or mobile number the sender used.

Reversal rules also vary from one service to the next. A payment that one app lets a sender cancel may be impossible to cancel in another. The conditions for cancelling differ as well. Some services treat a payment as final once the recipient has it. Under that rule, money sent to the wrong person may not be recoverable through the app itself.

A bank statement shows only money leaving or entering the bank account itself. A payment from one Venmo or Cash App balance to another, funded without touching a linked bank account, does not appear on that statement.

Six common causes explain why a bank transfer fails or gets returned. The sender lacks funds, a number is wrong, an account is closed or frozen, a fraud or compliance hold intervenes, the details don't match, or a limit is exceeded.

Insufficient funds means the sending account did not hold enough money to cover the payment when the bank processed it. A balance that looked adequate when the transfer was set up can fall short by the time it runs. Pending card purchases, scheduled bill payments and other debits can draw the account down in between.

A wrong account or routing number points the payment at an account that does not exist or cannot accept it. The routing number identifies the bank. The account number identifies the specific account at that bank. One transposed digit in either can stop the transfer.

A closed account cannot receive money. A transfer sent to one is rejected or sent back. This can happen when someone switches banks and an old account number stays saved in a payroll system, a bill-pay list or an app. A frozen account may still be open but restricted. That restriction can block incoming or outgoing payments until it lifts.

A fraud or compliance hold stops a payment while the bank or app reviews it. Activity that looks unusual for the account, such as a large transfer to a new recipient, can prompt that review. A held payment may go through once the review clears, or it may be canceled.

A mismatch in the recipient's name or other details can also cause a rejection or return. Some banks and apps compare the name the sender entered with the name on the receiving account. A nickname or a personal name entered for a business account can be enough to trip that check.

Exceeded limits are the last common cause. Banks and apps cap how much a customer can send, often per transaction and per day. A payment over that cap can be declined outright. The caps vary by institution and by service. The sender's account terms list them.

The quickest way to confirm a transfer is to open the transaction in your banking app or online account and read its status. If it still looks stuck, contact the sending bank with the date, amount and reference number.

The transaction detail screen usually holds more than the one-line entry in your account history. Tapping or clicking the item can show the status label, the date the payment was initiated, the account it went to and a reference code. That screen is the first place to look before assuming something has gone wrong.

Compare the two balance figures your bank displays. If only the available balance reflects the payment, the transfer is still pending. If both the available and current, or ledger, balances reflect it, the payment has most likely posted. This comparison shows where the money sits on your side. It does not show whether the money has arrived.

A confirmation number or trace number identifies one specific payment. Banks and payment apps typically generate these identifiers when a transfer is submitted. Save it, screenshot it or write it down. The receiving bank can use the same number to locate the payment on its end.

The recipient's account is the other half of the picture. Ask the person or business you paid to check their own transaction list, including any pending items. A payment can be complete on the sending side while it still waits to be credited on the receiving side.

Read alerts and emails about the payment closely. Banks and apps often send a notice when a payment is submitted, completed, declined or returned. A message about a decline or return may include the reason, which narrows down what needs fixing. Check spam folders as well. Confirm that any message came from your bank before acting on it.

If none of those steps settles the question, contact the sending bank or app directly. Have three details ready: the date of the transfer, the exact amount and the reference or trace number. Those details let a representative pull up the specific payment instead of searching through your history. Use the phone number printed on your card or listed on the bank's official website, not one from an unsolicited message.
