#5433. Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 10:45 amNovember 14, 2026 at 11:15 am

Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond company’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

Of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia. “We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.

Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes quickly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.

#5432. ‘Absurd’: Delta CEO says it takes longer to fly from ATL to LGA today than in the 1950s

Delta CEO Ed Bastian says one of his airline’s oldest routes is slower now than when it launched in the 1950s, and it’s “absurd.”

“Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd,” Bastian told Fortune’s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on Monday.

His complaint lands days after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights last week put the country’s congested air traffic control system back in the spotlight. Bastian said fixing it would bring ticket prices down by letting airlines add flights, but modernization can’t happen without investment, which doesn’t seem likely when the data-center buildout is diverting trillions in capital.

“We can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies, which affects all of us at a much higher level than any individual data center,” Bastian said.

Airplanes have become more advanced since the one equipped for the world’s first scheduled commercial flight from St. Petersburg to Tampa over a century ago. By Bastian’s account, the system they fly through hasn’t kept up.

Delta is also grappling with airfare pricing after the Iran war’s pressure on jet fuel prices squeezed the airline industry, and it has passed much of that cost onto consumers. Bastian said Delta’s tickets are 15% to 20% higher year-over-year because of jet fuel, adding that this wouldn’t have been possible to do if there wasn’t sufficient demand.

“We would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn’t have a consumer that was willing to pay it, and so that tells you the core demand is really healthy, even if pricing is where it’s at,” Bastian said.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ October release, U.S. airfares climbed 22.4% year over year as airlines raised prices to offset the higher cost of jet fuel. That helped the five major airlines generate $8.8 billion more in Q3 2026 than in Q3 2025, but passenger traffic grew less than 1%. Bastian said that instead of competing on fares with other airlines, Delta is trying to draw more passengers by distinguishing itself from its competition through service.

“If you don’t have people that are there to serve our customers in a premium manner, the rest of the stuff doesn’t really matter, and that’s the one thing that our competitors cannot replicate,” he said.

He said 15 years of cultivating that premium customer service culture came through during the FAA flight shutdown. While he said he typically hears compliments about the service on most weekends, this one was special because of the disruption coming from outside of Delta’s control.

“Unlike most weekends, when there’s always something going wrong or excuses somewhere, the overwhelming sentiment I received from customers was, ‘You have amazing people’ because they saw the stress, the conditions [were] none of our doing,” he said.

That’s also why Bastian said AI won’t replace Delta employees. Instead, the company will redeploy affected employees to the extent possible because “there’s always something to do.” He said this is because when there’s a crisis like the FAA one, customers prefer human support over machines.

“Obviously this past weekend, they wanted individuals to tell them what was going on, and there’s a lack of trust the more you put technology in place of humans, so humans are always going to be at the center of Delta,” he said.

#5431. XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

#5430. Did my transfer go through? 10 cases when a bank app crashes mid-payment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What happens if your bank app crashes during a transfer depends on timing, payment type and bank records — 10 scenarios explain how to check and what to do next

A bank app does not move money. It sends a request, and the bank's own servers decide whether to act on it. That distinction explains most of what happens when an app freezes, closes or crashes in the middle of a transfer. The screen on the phone is only a window. The record that counts sits in the bank's ledger.

Timing determines the outcome. If the app crashes before the request leaves the phone, nothing reaches the bank and no money moves. If the request arrives before the crash, the bank can complete the transfer even though the app has closed. The uncertain case sits between those two. The request may have arrived, but the confirmation screen never loaded. The app cannot say which outcome occurred until it reconnects and reloads the account.

That uncertainty is why people search for what happens if your bank app crashes during a transfer, often while looking at a balance that has not changed yet. The common questions are practical. Did the transfer go through? Will sending it again create a duplicate payment? Why does a pending transaction appear in the history when the balance looks the same?

The order of actions matters. Checking the transaction history first, ideally on the bank's website or a second device, gives a clearer answer than the app that just failed. Resending right away can produce a second payment if the first one succeeded. Restarting the phone or reinstalling the app may fix a recurring crash. It does not change what the bank has already recorded.

The details also depend on the payment itself. A transfer between two accounts at the same bank is handled inside that bank. In the U.S., a payment to another bank travels over a payment network such as ACH or the wire transfer system. A card payment made through a mobile wallet or a merchant app can leave an authorization hold even when the purchase never finished.

Rules and timelines differ by bank, by payment type and by country. In the U.S., the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Regulation E set out how banks handle errors on electronic transfers. The 10 scenarios below explain how each situation works, how to confirm what happened and when to contact the bank directly.

If your bank app crashes before you tap the final button to send a transfer, no money moves. The request never left your phone. The bank never received it, and your account balance stays where it was.

A mobile banking app is a front end. It collects the details of a transfer on your device — the account to pay from, the recipient, the amount and sometimes a memo or date. None of that information reaches the bank until the app packages it into a request and sends it over the network.

The bank's systems can act only on what arrives at their servers. A half-finished form on a phone screen is not a payment instruction. Neither is a review screen that shows the amount and recipient but has not yet been confirmed.

That covers several common moments. The app might close while you are typing the amount, picking a recipient from a saved list or reading the summary page. In each case, the transfer exists only on your device.

Some apps add a verification step before a transfer is submitted, such as a one-time passcode, a fingerprint scan or face recognition. Where that step comes before submission, a crash before you finish it means the transfer was never authorized or sent.

What you see after reopening the app usually reflects this. You may be asked to log in again. The transfer form may be blank, and the home screen may show the same balance as before. Your transaction history will have no new entry for the payment you started.

In practical terms, there is nothing for the bank to reverse and nothing pending to wait on. You can start the transfer again from the beginning. Re-enter the details and confirm each one before sending.

This certainty depends on knowing the crash happened before that final tap. If you pressed send and the app froze or closed afterward, the situation is different. The request may have reached the bank, and that case calls for more caution before trying again.

A transfer can still go through if your bank app crashes after the bank's servers receive the request. The phone only sends the instruction. The bank's own systems carry it out, whether or not the app stays open.

A mobile banking app works as a front end. When you tap to send money, the app packages the amount, the source account and the recipient into a request. That request travels over the internet to the bank's servers.

From that point, the work happens on the bank's side. Its systems check that you are signed in, that the account has enough available funds and that the recipient details are valid. If those checks pass, the bank records the debit against your account.

None of those steps depend on the phone. A crash, a frozen screen or a battery that dies a second later does not reach back and undo them. Closing an app sends no cancellation message to the bank.

That is why a user can reopen the app expecting nothing to have happened and find the payment already listed. The app lost its chance to display the result. The bank had already completed its part.

The same logic covers scheduled and recurring transfers. Once a future-dated payment or a repeating transfer is confirmed, the instruction is stored on the bank's systems rather than on the phone. A later crash does not erase it.

That has a practical consequence. A rent payment set to repeat each month keeps running even if the app crashes or is deleted from the phone. Stopping it requires cancelling it through the bank, typically in the app's scheduled payments section, on the bank's website or by contacting the bank directly.

What the crash does affect is the phone's view of events. The app may need to refresh its account data before it reflects what the bank has already done. How quickly the recipient sees the money depends on the payment type, not on the app.

A missing confirmation screen means the app never displayed a result. It does not mean the bank rejected the payment. The transfer may have gone through, may have failed or may still be processing. The app cannot tell which until it reconnects.

Every mobile transfer is a two-way exchange. The phone sends a request to the bank's servers. The servers then send back a reply saying whether the transfer was accepted. The confirmation screen is the app's display of that reply and nothing more.

A crash can break this exchange partway through. The request may reach the bank and be processed while the reply never makes it back to the phone. In that case the money can move even though the screen shows nothing.

A dropped connection creates the same gap. A weak cellular signal, a switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data or a phone entering an elevator can cut the link mid-request. The phone then has no way of knowing whether its message arrived before the connection failed.

From the app's side, a lost reply and a lost request can look identical. Both end in silence. Some apps show an error message or a timeout notice in this situation. That notice describes what the app experienced, not what the bank did with the transfer.

A spinning wheel or frozen screen works the same way. It shows that the app stalled while waiting. It says nothing about whether the bank's servers have already finished their work.

The uncertainty clears only once the app reconnects and loads fresh account data from the bank. At that point the account history shows whether the bank recorded the request. Until then, the app may be showing information it stored before the interruption.

The absence of a success message therefore carries little information on its own. It tells the user that something interrupted the process. It does not reveal where in the process the interruption happened.

The accurate way to treat an interrupted transfer is as unknown rather than failed. That distinction matters most for anyone tempted to tap send again before the account has refreshed.

The bank's ledger, not the app's confirmation screen, is the record of whether a transfer went through. After a crash, the clearest way to read that record is to sign in through a second channel. That could be the bank's website on a computer or the bank's app on a different device.

A confirmation screen is a message the bank sends back to the phone after it accepts a request. It is a notice about the record, not the record itself. The ledger is what the bank uses to calculate the account balance. Statements and any later dispute are also based on it.

A second channel helps because it avoids the device that failed. A crashed app can reopen with an older copy of the account data still on screen. A fresh session in a web browser, or the app on another phone or tablet, loads the account directly from the bank's systems.

The entry to look for is an outgoing transaction that matches the amount and the recipient. It should also line up with the time of the attempt. Some banks show a reference or confirmation number in the transaction details. That number is useful if the bank later needs to trace the payment.

The transaction list and the balance are best read together. The two do not always update at the same moment. Some banks also keep a separate page for transfer or payment activity, apart from the main account history. A transfer missing from the main list may appear there.

Other channels can confirm the balance as well. An ATM balance inquiry and a bank's telephone banking line are two options. Both may show less detail than the website, and neither replaces a full transaction list.

Clearing the app's cached data is a common fix for an app that keeps crashing. It does not change what the bank has recorded. The cache holds copies of account information stored on the phone. Deleting it removes those copies, not entries on the bank's side. The next sign-in reloads the account from the bank's systems.

Account alerts offer one more check for customers who have turned them on. Some banks send a text message or email when money leaves the account. An alert that arrived around the time of the crash points to a request the bank processed. A missing alert says less, because alert settings and delivery differ from bank to bank.

Sending a transfer again right after a crash can move the money twice if the first request already reached the bank. The safer order is to confirm whether the original went through, and resend only if it did not.

The risk comes from how the bank sees the second attempt. To the bank's systems, a fresh submission from a reopened app looks like a new instruction. It carries the same amount and the same recipient, but it arrives as a separate request. Unless something on the bank's side flags it as a repeat, it can be processed as a second, independent payment.

The app itself can steer a user toward that mistake. After a restart, the transfer form may open blank, as if nothing had happened. The account screen may still show an older balance until it loads fresh data. Neither view confirms that the first transfer failed. A blank form only means the app lost its place.

Error messages can mislead in a similar way. A timeout or "something went wrong" notice tells the user that the app did not receive an answer. It does not say the bank rejected the payment.

Undoing a duplicate takes more steps than preventing one. Once money lands in another person's account, getting it back can depend on the recipient agreeing to return it. It can also depend on the bank's own recall process. Many instant payment services treat a completed payment as final. A doubled bill payment may sit with the biller as a credit rather than return to the sender's account. In the meantime, the sender's available balance is lower than expected. That can leave less room for other bills or card charges.

The sequence that avoids a double payment is short. First, wait for the app to reconnect, or check the account through another channel. Look for the transfer in the activity list. If it appears, the payment is already in motion and no resend is needed. If it does not appear, and the bank's records show nothing received, resubmitting is reasonable.

When the picture stays unclear, one more check comes before a second payment. Asking the recipient whether the money arrived settles the question without risking a double charge.

Duplicate-detection checks let a bank's systems recognize when the same payment request arrives twice and process it only once. Many banks use some form of this safeguard. How it works, and whether a particular bank uses it, varies. That makes it a backstop rather than a guarantee.

The underlying idea in software design is called idempotency. An idempotent operation produces the same result whether it runs once or several times. In payments, that means a retried request should not move money a second time.

One way to achieve this is to attach a unique identifier to each transfer request, often called an idempotency key. In a common design, the app generates the identifier when the user confirms the transfer. The bank's servers store it alongside the outcome of that request.

If the connection drops and the app retries on its own, the same identifier travels with the retry. The server recognizes an identifier it has already handled. Instead of creating a new payment, it returns the result of the first attempt.

The web's own technical standards reflect the same idea. The HTTP standard classifies some request methods, such as PUT and DELETE, as idempotent. POST, the method commonly used to submit new data, is not. That gap is one reason payment systems add their own identifiers.

Some systems also look for patterns rather than identifiers. A payment that matches a recent one in amount, recipient and account may be flagged for review. Some apps respond by asking the user to confirm that the second payment is intended.

These checks have limits. They work best when the app retries a request it already sent. A user who closes the app, reopens it and builds the transfer again from scratch may produce a brand-new request with a new identifier.

To the bank, that can look like a deliberate second payment. Identical payments are sometimes legitimate, such as two equal installments to the same landlord or contractor. A system that blocked every repeat would stop real transactions too.

That tension is why a duplicate check cannot replace confirming the first transfer's status before sending money again.

A pending transaction means the bank has recorded a transfer request but has not finished settling it. A posted transaction is the final, completed entry on the account. After an app crash, a pending listing shows that the request reached the bank, even if no confirmation ever appeared.

The two labels describe different stages of the same payment. Pending marks a payment the bank has accepted that is still in progress. Posted marks one the bank has completed and written into the account record. A transfer typically appears as pending first and moves to posted later.

That sequence can make an account look inconsistent. Many banks display two balances, often labeled available and current. The available balance usually subtracts pending debits as soon as they appear. The current balance may reflect only posted activity. Someone checking after a crash can see the transfer listed while one balance still shows the old amount.

Each balance measures something different. The labels next to each figure, in the app or on the bank's website, explain which activity each one includes. The wording of those labels varies from one institution to another.

Pending entries can also change before they post. The description may be shortened or reworded once the transfer settles. The entry can vanish from the pending list and reappear under posted activity with a different date. If the bank rejects or cancels the transfer, the pending item can drop off without ever posting. In that case the money returns to the available balance.

A pending status does not guarantee that a transfer can still be stopped. Whether an in-progress payment can be cancelled depends on the bank and the payment type. Some transfers offer a cancel option before they settle. Others cannot be recalled once submitted.

The gap between pending and posted has no single length. It depends on the bank, the payment method and when the request arrived. Bank processing days can also affect when an item finally posts.

For anyone unsure whether an interrupted transfer went through, a pending entry answers the main question. The bank received the request. The remaining step is to watch that same entry move to posted. That change confirms the payment is complete.

Where the money is going shapes what a crash leaves behind. A transfer between two accounts at the same bank stays on that bank's own books. A payment to another bank must travel through an outside network, such as ACH or a wire system.

An internal transfer, sometimes called a book transfer, is the simplest case. The bank holds both accounts. It debits one and credits the other within its own systems. No outside party has to accept the payment. If the request arrived before the app closed, both accounts usually reflect it once the bank's records update.

Payments to an outside bank add more steps. In the U.S., many routine transfers move over the Automated Clearing House network, known as ACH. ACH processes payments in batches instead of one at a time. The Federal Reserve and The Clearing House both operate ACH systems. Nacha writes the rules that govern the network.

That batch design matters after a crash. A bank can accept a transfer request and hold it until the next batch goes out. During that window, the payment may show as scheduled or in process, not complete. Some banks let customers cancel an outgoing ACH transfer before it leaves. Whether that option exists, and how long it lasts, depends on the bank.

Wire transfers work differently. In the U.S., wires commonly move through the Federal Reserve's Fedwire Funds Service. Fedwire settles each payment individually. Once a wire is sent, it is generally treated as final. Recalling one usually requires the receiving bank's cooperation.

That finality raises the stakes of an interrupted wire. A second wire sent by mistake can be much harder to reverse than a repeated internal transfer. Many banks also add extra verification before releasing a wire, such as a one-time code. A crash during that step can leave the request unfinished instead of sent.

The payment type also points to where the evidence sits. An internal transfer between two accounts the customer owns appears on both of them. Checking the receiving account as well as the sending one gives a clearer answer. An ACH or wire payment to someone else appears only on the sending account. That account's history is the record to check.

A card payment can leave a trace on your account even if a merchant app or mobile wallet crashed before showing a receipt. The card issuer may already have approved an authorization, which places a hold on funds without a completed purchase.

Card payments follow a different path from a bank-to-bank transfer. When you pay by card, the merchant asks the card issuer to approve the amount. That approval is the authorization. The money itself moves later, when the merchant submits the transaction for settlement.

Those two steps can come apart when an app fails. The merchant's system may have sent the authorization request and received an approval while your screen froze or closed. From the issuer's side, the request arrived and was approved. From your side, nothing seemed to happen.

The result usually shows up as a pending charge in your card or banking app. An authorization hold reduces your available balance or available credit, even though no purchase was finalized. On a debit card, that means less spendable money in your checking account until the hold clears.

A hold is not the same as a charge. If the merchant never completes the sale, the authorization is never captured, and the hold eventually drops off. The card issuer sets how long that takes, and the period varies from one issuer to another. A merchant can also release a hold sooner by cancelling the authorization.

Mobile wallets such as Apple $AAPL Pay and Google $GOOGL Pay add a layer but do not change the basic flow. The wallet passes a digital token in place of the card number. The issuer still approves or declines the payment in the usual way.

A frozen checkout screen can prompt a shopper to tap the phone again or press the pay button a second time. If the first attempt was approved, a second attempt can produce a second authorization. The card's pending activity shows whether an approval already exists.

If a hold appears with no matching order, the merchant is the first place to check. The merchant can confirm whether an order exists and can ask for the authorization to be voided. The card issuer can see the authorization record and explain its status.

If the account history still leaves a transfer's status unclear, contact the bank directly. The bank's servers log the requests they receive. Its staff can check whether an interrupted payment arrived, even when the app showed nothing.

That log is the bank's own record of the attempt. It sits on the bank's systems, not on the phone. A frozen screen, a closed app or a dropped signal on the customer's side does not erase it.

A few details make the search faster. A screenshot of the error message or the last screen the app displayed gives the bank a starting point. The approximate time of the crash narrows the window staff need to review. The amount and the recipient's name and account details let them match the request to a specific record.

Use a contact route the customer already trusts. That means the phone number printed on the back of a debit card, the number on a statement or the secure messaging tool on the bank's website. Write down when the call took place, who handled it and any reference number. That note creates a record for later follow-up.

In the U.S., federal rules give consumers a formal path when an electronic payment goes wrong. The Electronic Fund Transfer Act covers electronic transfers into and out of consumer accounts. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Regulation E implements that law. It sets an error-resolution process that banks must follow. The reporting windows and liability limits depend on the type of problem. A bank's account agreement and the bureau's consumer guidance describe the terms that apply.

The protections are not uniform. Debit card transactions and most electronic transfers from consumer accounts fall under Regulation E. Wire transfers sent through systems such as Fedwire sit outside the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and follow separate rules. Billing errors on credit cards are handled under a different federal law, the Fair Credit Billing Act. Customers outside the U.S. fall under their own country's rules.

A crash on its own does not expose a customer's login details or signal that an account has been breached. An unfamiliar transaction that appears afterward still needs attention. Reporting it to the bank lets staff review it separately from the interrupted transfer. They can then decide whether it needs further investigation.

#5429. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5428. Top Chamber of Commerce official says the midterms weren’t just about prices: They were about 20 years of 2% growth

Less than two weeks after voters handed Democrats both chambers of Congress in an election defined by frustration over the cost of living and perceived corruption, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s top policy official warned a room of executives that Washington might already be misreading the message.

Neil Bradley, the Chamber’s executive vice president, chief policy officer and head of strategic advocacy, said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit that the affordability anger is real. He also argued it sits on top of something voters have been signaling for two decades that “no one has been paying attention to”: 20 years of roughly 2% real GDP growth, after 60 years of more than 3%.

That gap is the difference between a kid who grows up richer than their parents and one who doesn’t. Harvard economist Raj Chetty and his co-authors found in a 2017 paper that the share of Americans earning more than their parents fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s.

“The concept of the American dream isn’t 3% growth, but it’s highly correlated to it,” Bradley said.

Bradley’s real target was what Congress does next. “There’s a real temptation to hit the easy button,” he said, like capping credit card interest rates, price controls on pharmaceuticals, or limits on stock buybacks and dividends. These are “proposals that both ends of the political horseshoes are coming together on” and they might ease voters’ angst “for a brief period of time,” he said, “but they won’t solve our long-term challenges.”

The horseshoe part is accurate. President Trump called for a one-year, 10% cap on credit card rates in January, and Sens. Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley have a bill to do it. The Senate’s version of this year’s defense bill carries new restrictions on buybacks and dividends by defense contractors.

The list also lines up with the Chamber’s membership. Card issuers, drugmakers and any public company with a buyback program would pay for each of those buttons. Bradley’s alternative is growth: expand supply, expand trade, and expand the labor force “through legal immigration reform.”

Bradley’s numbers check out against the government’s. Real GDP grew at a compound rate of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 2005 and about 2% a year from 2005 to 2025, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data compiled by the St. Louis Fed. At 3%, an economy doubles in about 23 years, roughly the time from birth to a first job. At 2%, it takes about 35.

His election count holds, too. In the 11 national elections since 2006, voters took control of the House, the Senate or the White House away from the party holding it every time except 2012.

Chetty’s research complicates Bradley’s argument when it comes to the remedy. The paper found that “increasing GDP growth rates alone cannot restore absolute mobility” to the levels of the 1940s cohort. Shifting the distribution of growth back to the more equal pattern that cohort saw “would reverse more than 70% of the decline.” Bradley acknowledged this point, too: “Of course, a doubling in pie doesn’t guarantee that anyone’s individual slice will be bigger.”

Bradley’s case for optimism was what he called “a little-known record”: 5.68 million new business starts last year. “No one’s an entrepreneur if they’re pessimistic about the future,” he said.

Census tracks those as business applications, meaning requests to the IRS for an employer ID number, not businesses that opened. Summed from the bureau’s monthly data, applications came to about 5.67 million in 2025 before seasonal adjustment, the most for any full year since the series began in 2004.

The applications that Census flags as likely to become businesses with payroll tell a different story. Those totaled about 1.69 million in 2025 on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 1.86 million in 2023 and lower for a second straight year. More Americans are filing to start something, and fewer of the filings look like future employers.

About nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, according to The AP Voter Poll.

The new Congress is sworn in in January. The Congressional Budget Office’s January outlook has real GDP growing 1.8% a year in 2027 and 2028.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5427. Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 1:16 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 1:16 pm

Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

#5426. Bank outage rights: 10 federal protections for debit, card and deposit problems

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Bank outage rights under federal law cover debit errors, failed transfers, card disputes and deposit holds — here are 10 protections and steps for recovering your money

No federal law pays you simply because your bank's app froze, its ATMs went dark or its payment systems stalled for a day. Congress never wrote an outage-specific refund right. What consumers have instead is a set of broader protections built for electronic transfers, credit card billing, deposit timing and bank failures. Those rules can still recover money, but only when the right one applies and the customer acts within its deadlines.

Getting money back after a bank outage depends first on which payment rail broke. A duplicate debit card charge, a stalled ACH payment and a missing transfer between accounts fall under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and its implementing rule, Regulation E. A duplicate charge on a credit card follows a different path, set by the Fair Credit Billing Act and Regulation Z. A deposit held longer than federal deadlines allow falls under the Expedited Funds Availability Act and Regulation CC.

Timing also matters. Several of these protections run on fixed clocks measured in days or business days. Some start when a statement arrives, and others start when a customer learns something went wrong. A customer who reports a problem quickly keeps more options open than one who waits for the bank to notice.

Deposit insurance serves a different purpose. Coverage from the FDIC and the National Credit Union Administration applies when an institution fails. It does not apply to a temporary systems failure at a bank that stays open.

No general federal law requires refunds of overdraft charges or late fees triggered by a delayed payment. Whether those are reversed depends on what the bank agrees to do when a customer asks.

When a bank does not resolve a problem, federal regulators run complaint channels. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau takes many consumer complaints, and every bank also answers to a prudential regulator.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of bank outage rights and practical steps. They are not every consumer protection that could touch an outage. Each explains what applies, which deadlines matter and where the limits lie. Outcomes in any individual case depend on the facts and on the terms of the account agreement.

No federal statute gives bank customers an automatic payout when a bank's systems go down. Money lost or delayed during an outage has to be recovered through broader consumer protection laws. Each of those laws covers a specific type of transaction, not the outage itself.

The practical result is a narrower legal question. A frozen mobile app, a failed login or a delayed balance update is not, on its own, a legal injury that triggers compensation. What counts is what happened to a particular transaction and which law governs that kind of transaction.

Four bodies of federal law do most of the work. The Electronic Fund Transfer Act, implemented through Regulation E, covers debit card purchases, ATM withdrawals, ACH payments and many online transfers. The Fair Credit Billing Act, implemented through Regulation Z, covers billing errors on credit cards. The Expedited Funds Availability Act, implemented through Regulation CC, sets deadlines for making deposited money available. Federal deposit insurance, run by the FDIC for banks and the NCUA for credit unions, protects balances if an institution fails.

Each of these laws has its own procedures, deadlines and limits. A single outage can affect several of them at once. A stalled bill payment, a delayed deposit and a doubled card charge may each fall under a different rule, with separate notice requirements. Matching each problem to the right law is the first step toward recovering money.

The account agreement also matters. Federal law sets minimum protections, but the contract between a customer and the bank governs details such as fees and the terms for completing transfers. Some federal remedies are tied directly to those account terms.

Results vary from case to case. Whether money comes back can turn on the type of payment, when the problem was reported and what the bank knew or could control. A bank may also refund money voluntarily. That is a choice the bank makes, not a payment that any federal outage law requires.

Debit card, ATM and ACH errors linked to a bank outage can be disputed under Regulation E. The key step is to notify the bank or credit union within 60 days of the statement that shows the error. The notice can be made by phone or in writing.

Regulation E rests on the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, codified at 15 U.S.C. 1693 and following. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau implements the law through the regulation, which sits at 12 CFR part 1005. The statute creates the consumer protections. The regulation sets out the procedures institutions must follow when a customer reports a problem.

The rule reaches most of the electronic payments a bank outage can disrupt. Debit card purchases and ATM transactions fall under it. So do ACH payments, the electronic transfers used for direct deposits and many bill payments. Many online transfers are covered as well. Prepaid accounts have been covered since 2019.

Credit cards sit outside this framework. A disputed credit card charge follows a separate set of rules with its own notice requirements.

Outage glitches can show up in several recognizable ways. A single purchase can post twice, leaving a duplicate debit. A payment can process for the wrong amount. A transfer can leave one account and never be credited to the other. Each is the kind of error the Regulation E dispute process is built to handle.

The 60-day clock runs from the statement on which the error first appeared, not from the outage itself. A double charge from a brief disruption may not show up on a statement until weeks later. That statement is what sets the deadline. Reviewing each statement soon after it arrives leaves the most time to act.

Notice does not have to be on paper. A call to the bank's customer service line is enough to start the process. The institution may then ask for written confirmation of the oral notice within 10 business days. A customer who gets that request should send the follow-up before that deadline passes.

A clear notice makes the error easier for the bank to trace. It should identify the account and describe what went wrong. It should also give the amount involved, such as the size of the second charge or the missing deposit.

Filing a dispute does not guarantee a refund. The result depends on what the bank's records show and on the terms of the account agreement.

After a customer reports an electronic transfer error, Regulation E generally gives the bank 10 business days to investigate. A bank that needs longer can take up to 45 days, but only if it provisionally credits the disputed amount to the account within those first 10 business days.

Provisional credit addresses a practical problem after an outage. A duplicate debit, or a transfer that never landed, can leave an account short while the bank investigates. The credit puts the disputed amount back in the account before the investigation ends. It does not decide who is right.

The clock runs in business days, not calendar days. It starts when the bank receives notice of the error. Weekends and federal holidays generally do not count. A dispute reported late on a Friday therefore gives the bank more calendar time than the number alone suggests.

Provisional credit is not always permanent. If the bank concludes that no error occurred, it can reverse the credit. Before it does, the bank must tell the customer the date and amount of the debit.

Some transactions carry a longer investigation window of up to 90 days. It applies to point-of-sale debit card transactions, transfers initiated outside the U.S. and transfers involving an account in its first 30 days. A customer disputing a store checkout charge, or using a recently opened account, may face a slower timeline.

When the investigation ends, the bank must report the results to the customer within three business days. That report states whether the bank found an error. If the bank finds an error, it must correct it. A customer who disagrees with a finding of no error can request copies of the documents the bank relied on. The final outcome still depends on the facts of the transaction and the terms of the account agreement.

A written record makes these deadlines easier to track. A customer who notes the date of the report, the name of the representative and any reference number has a fixed starting point for every clock. Checking the account around the 10th business day shows whether a provisional credit has posted in cases where the bank has extended its review.

Federal rules cap a consumer's liability for unauthorized debit transfers at $50 or $500, depending on how fast the bank is told. The $50 cap applies when the consumer reports within two business days of learning a card or other access device was lost or stolen.

The caps come from Regulation E, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's rule under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act. They cover electronic transfers that the account holder did not authorize. That includes debit card purchases, ATM withdrawals and ACH payments taken from a consumer account.

These tiers matter after a bank outage because fraud attempts can follow a disruption. A customer locked out of online banking cannot watch the account in real time. Unfamiliar activity can go unnoticed until service comes back. Once access returns, the transaction history is the first place to check for transfers the customer never made.

The two-business-day clock does not start on the day the theft took place. It runs from the moment the consumer learns that the card, PIN or other access device is lost or stolen. The deadline is counted in business days rather than calendar days.

A report inside that window keeps the consumer's share of the loss at no more than $50. A later report can raise the exposure to as much as $500. The higher tier is not automatic. It covers transfers after the two-business-day window only when the bank establishes that a timely report would have stopped them.

The periodic statement sets a separate deadline. If an unauthorized transfer appears on a statement and the consumer does not report it within 60 days of the statement being sent, exposure can exceed both tiers. The consumer can then be liable for unauthorized transfers made after that 60-day period that timely notice would have prevented.

These deadlines can stretch. Regulation E requires a bank to extend the time limits to a reasonable period in extenuating circumstances. Extended travel and hospitalization are examples in the rule's official interpretation.

The caps apply to debit and other electronic transfers. Credit cards fall under a different federal law with its own rules. For any fraud claim, the final result depends on the facts and on the bank's investigation.

Section 910 of the Electronic Fund Transfer Act can make a bank liable for damages after a failed electronic transfer. That covers a transfer not made on time or in the correct amount under the account terms. It is a possible route to recovery, not a guaranteed payout.

The provision is codified at 15 U.S.C. 1693h. It ties the bank's duty to the terms and conditions of the account. That means the account agreement is the starting point for any claim. If the agreement promised that a transfer would go out by a certain time, and it did not, the gap between that promise and the result is what matters.

The law covers damages proximately caused by the failure. In plain terms, the loss has to flow directly from the bank's failure to move the money correctly. A claim therefore needs a specific, traceable loss, not just a general inconvenience.

The statute also sets out exceptions that limit this liability. One applies when the account lacked sufficient funds through no fault of the institution. Another covers circumstances beyond the bank's control, provided it took reasonable precautions.

A further exception covers a system malfunction the consumer knew about when starting the transfer. If a banking app displayed a warning that its systems were down, and the customer submitted a payment anyway, that exception may apply.

Whether a given disruption counts as beyond the bank's control depends on what caused it and what safeguards the bank had in place. No single answer covers every outage. Each case turns on its own facts.

Records can matter when those exceptions are in dispute. Useful evidence includes the time a transfer was submitted, any confirmation number and the date the money actually moved. Copies of any error or outage messages shown during the attempt also help. They show what the customer knew, or did not know, when the transfer began.

A credit card charge that posts twice during a bank or payment outage counts as a billing error under the Fair Credit Billing Act. To dispute it, a cardholder must send written notice to the card issuer within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.

The Fair Credit Billing Act is a federal law, and Regulation Z puts its rules into effect for credit cards and other revolving credit accounts. It does not cover checking accounts. A duplicate swipe on a debit card falls under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act instead, with its own deadlines and procedures. Cardholders who carry both kinds of cards should confirm which one was charged before choosing a dispute route.

The written requirement matters. A phone call to customer service may get a charge reversed informally, but the law's protections attach to written notice. That notice should go to the billing-error address the issuer lists on the statement. This address can differ from the one used for payments.

The notice should identify the account, the charge in question, its amount and the reason it is an error. For an outage-related duplicate, that usually means pointing to two identical charges from the same merchant for the same amount.

The 60-day clock runs from the statement, not from the day of the outage. A duplicate charge that posts near the end of a billing cycle may not show up until the following statement. In that case, the window opens with that later statement.

Once the notice arrives, the creditor must acknowledge the dispute within 30 days. It must then resolve the dispute within two billing cycles. The outer limit is 90 days, even if two billing cycles would run longer. While the dispute is open, the cardholder does not have to pay the disputed amount. The issuer also cannot report that amount as delinquent.

The act also limits what a cardholder owes when a credit card is used without permission. Liability for unauthorized use is capped at $50. That limit applies to credit cards only and is separate from the tiered caps that govern debit cards.

Copies of the notice, the statement and any reply from the issuer give the cardholder a record if the dispute stalls.

Regulation CC sets federal deadlines for when a bank must make deposited money available to spend. A systems outage does not automatically cancel those deadlines.

The rule carries out the Expedited Funds Availability Act. It appears in the Code of Federal Regulations at 12 CFR part 229. It sets the schedule a bank must follow before releasing money a customer has already deposited.

Certain electronic payments and cash deposited in person with a bank employee must be available on the next business day. For a customer waiting on an electronic deposit, that schedule is the baseline for judging whether an outage pushed the money past its due date.

Check deposits follow a separate track. Most must become available within a short, fixed number of business days. The rule's dollar thresholds are adjusted periodically. Anyone checking a specific deposit can confirm the current amounts in the text of the regulation.

An outage that delays a posted deposit does not, by itself, excuse a bank from these timelines. The rule does contain exceptions. One covers emergency conditions beyond the bank's control, and the regulation lists an interruption of computer or communication equipment among them. The bank must still act with the diligence the circumstances require.

Other exceptions cover new accounts, large deposits, redeposited checks and accounts that are repeatedly overdrawn. Whether any exception applies turns on the facts of the case and the terms of the account agreement.

When a bank relies on an exception, it generally must tell the customer why the funds are being held and when they will be available. That notice is worth keeping, because it states the bank's own reason for the delay.

A customer can document the timing directly. Note the date and time of the deposit and the date it posted. Compare that with the date the funds became available to spend. A gap beyond the required schedule is a concrete point to raise with the bank.

A deposit hold is a different problem from an electronic transfer error. A debit, ATM or ACH transaction that went wrong falls under a separate error-resolution process in Regulation E. Regulation CC deals with timing: when deposited money must be made available. Keeping the two apart helps a customer describe the problem accurately to the bank or a regulator.

Federal deposit insurance protects up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. That protection applies when an insured institution fails, and a temporary systems outage at a bank that stays open is not an insured event.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC, provides this coverage at insured banks. Federally insured credit unions carry the same $250,000 amount through the National Credit Union Administration, or NCUA. At either type of institution, the coverage is tied to the failure of the institution itself.

The limit is built in three layers. It applies to each depositor separately. It applies at each insured institution separately. It also applies within each ownership category separately. Common ownership categories include single accounts, joint accounts and certain retirement accounts.

A depositor whose accounts fall into more than one ownership category at the same bank can have more than $250,000 insured there in total. Balances at two different insured banks are each covered on their own, up to the limit at each one.

Coverage also has limits on what it protects. It applies to deposits such as checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts and certificates of deposit. It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities or crypto assets, even when a bank sells them.

A failure and an outage are different events. In a failure, regulators close the institution. In an outage, an institution that remains open cannot process payments, display balances or complete transfers for a period of time. Because the bank keeps operating, no payout from the FDIC or the NCUA follows from its systems going down.

This has a practical consequence for anyone trying to recover money. A deposit that does not appear, a delayed transfer or a wrong debit during an outage has to be pursued with the bank itself. That means using the error-resolution and dispute rules that cover the type of payment involved. The terms of the account agreement also apply. The result depends on the facts of each case.

The $250,000 limit matters only if an institution actually fails. A depositor who wants to know how much of a balance falls within it can review how each account is titled and which institution holds it.

Overdraft and late fees triggered by a bank outage are generally refunded at the bank's discretion, not because federal law requires it. A customer who wants those charges removed should ask the bank directly and treat the reversal as a request rather than an entitlement.

No federal statute orders a bank to refund a fee simply because its own systems were down when the fee was triggered. A deposit that posts late, or a payment that fails to go through during an outage, can leave a balance short and set off a charge. The law does not automatically undo that charge.

Regulation E, the rule that implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, also contains overdraft provisions. They require a bank to get a customer's opt-in before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases. A customer who never opted in cannot be charged an overdraft fee on those two transaction types. The opt-in requirement concerns consent to overdraft coverage, though. It does not create a separate right to have outage-related fees returned.

Banks often reverse such fees as a goodwill gesture when a customer asks. A clear request names the fee, the date it posted and the transaction that triggered it. Tying that transaction to the time of the outage gives the bank a specific item to review.

The account agreement lists the bank's fee schedule and the terms behind each charge. Reading the relevant section before calling shows which fee applies and how the bank describes it. Whether a fee comes off depends on the facts of the case and on that agreement.

A fee reversal is separate from the error-resolution process for an electronic transfer. If the outage itself caused a duplicate debit or a wrong amount, that error can be disputed under Regulation E's own procedures. Any fee that followed from it remains a distinct question for the bank to decide.

A customer who has not resolved an outage-related problem with a bank can file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau through its online portal at consumerfinance.gov/complaint. The bureau forwards each complaint to the company, which is expected to respond within 15 days.

The company is also expected to give a final response within 60 days. The complaint should name the specific transaction, its amount and date, and the outcome sought. That might be the reversal of a duplicate debit or a credit for a transfer that never arrived.

A complaint can also go to the federal agency that supervises the institution. The right agency depends on what kind of institution holds the account.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency oversees national banks. The FDIC and the Federal Reserve oversee other banks, depending on each bank's charter and its membership in the Federal Reserve System. The National Credit Union Administration oversees federal credit unions.

A bank's legal name often signals its charter. The letters "N.A." after a bank's name stand for "national association," which marks a national bank. A federal credit union carries "Federal Credit Union" in its name. For a state-chartered bank, the deciding question is whether it belongs to the Federal Reserve System. That membership determines whether the Federal Reserve or the FDIC is its federal supervisor.

Documentation supports any complaint, whether it goes to the CFPB, a regulator or the bank itself. Screenshots can capture error messages, failed transfer screens or outage notices, along with the date and time they appeared. Dated statements show when a transaction posted and for how much.

Reference numbers link each call, chat or dispute to a record the institution can pull up. Notes on every call should record the date, the representative's name and anything the representative said the bank would do.

A complaint creates a written record and prompts a company response, but it does not guarantee money back.

#5425. ‘Work on what people think is important.’ U.S. Steel’s CEO has advice for Democrats after the midterms: Focus on affordability, not court fights

U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt wants to see Democrats use their congressional sweep to focus on what voters have been asking for: improving the cost of living and affordability, not spending the next two years fighting Trump in court.

Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum, Burritt said Democrats have an opportunity to respond to the economic concerns that have plagued the American electorate and drove voters to the polls, warning that a focus on political battles would undermine the party’s chances in the next election.

He added that Democrats could find themselves in a difficult political position in the 2028 elections if they fail to address voters’ priorities. The midterm results shouldn’t be interpreted as an endorsement of the Democratic Party, but instead a warning for both parties that voters are dissatisfied, he said in a panel discussion with Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt and Fortune Executive Editor Lee Clifford.

“They were sending a message to everybody: work on what people think is important. Let’s make things affordable,” Burritt said.

The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, a sweeping reversal of the political fortunes for Republicans and a rebuke to President Donald Trump.

Democratic candidates repeatedly made affordability the centerpiece of their campaigns, arguing for cheaper groceries, healthcare, housing and everyday necessities.

Housing and food accounted for 46.9% of average expenditures in 2025 as housing expenditures climbed 5.8% and food spending increased 4.6%, according to the Census Bureau’s Consumer Expenditure Survey released in October.

A CBS News analysis of the election found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a major or crucial factor in their congressional vote.

But Trump was also a factor as well, with many voters treating the election as a referendum on him. According to the Associated Press’s Voter Poll, 39% to 60% of voters across age demographics used their vote to “show opposition” to Trump—compared to only 7% to 22% voting to show support.

The poll also showed that 33% of the electorate viewed “the state of democracy” as its most important issue.

The Democratic Party has signaled plans to investigate a range of issues, including Trump’s business interests, his administration’s immigration policies, the Justice Department’s actions, and the administration’s handling of the war in Iran. Congressional committees will gain the ability to issue subpoenas, compel testimony and demand documents once the new Congress convenes in January.

But for Burritt, the danger is that Democrats will mistake their electoral victory for a mandate to pursue a political agenda rather than address the economic concerns that helped deliver their majority.

Stitt offered a similar warning, saying Republicans had taken “a beating” in the midterms but that Democrats shouldn’t interpret the win as an endorsement of every policy on their platform.

“Don’t go out and have this pendulum swing, don’t go start attacking the other side,” Stitt said. “I think the American people get turned off by that.”

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.
