#5424. 10 backup ways to pay when your bank goes down, compared

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 backup ways to pay when your bank is down, from cash to a brokerage account, are compared by how much each relies on the failed bank

A bank outage is not a single failure. Sometimes the mobile app won't open while cards still work. Sometimes the website loads but card authorizations get declined at the register. In other cases the bank's ATMs stop dispensing cash, or several of these problems arrive together. Which piece breaks differs from one incident to the next. A customer at a checkout may not be able to tell which one it is.

That uncertainty shapes the practical question. A backup payment method only helps if it does not run through the bank that is having trouble. A second debit card from the same bank is not a backup. Neither is a payment service that pulls money from the affected checking account. Both depend on the same systems that just failed.

This list compares 10 backup ways to pay when your bank is down. It sorts them by a single test: how much does each option depend on the affected bank? It starts with cash, which needs no bank connection at the point of sale, and moves through cards and accounts held at unrelated institutions. It also covers mobile wallets, prepaid cards, payment-app balances, money orders, gift cards and brokerage cash management accounts. Each comes with its own limits on where it works and how quickly it can be used.

The options also differ in speed. Cash and a card from another issuer can pay for groceries or fuel right away. A postal money order can settle rent or a utility bill but does not work at a store checkout. A new credit union account can serve as a full second financial base, but it takes time to open.

That points to a pattern that runs through the list. Nearly every alternative payment method here has to be set up before an outage begins. Cash has to be withdrawn in advance. A prepaid card has to be loaded. A second account has to be opened and funded. A mobile wallet needs cards from more than one issuer already stored in it. Once the outage starts, the choices narrow.

The 10 options below are a selection, not a complete list or a ranking. Each slide explains what the option is, what it depends on and where it falls short. Where federal rules set limits on consumer liability, those protections are included too.

Cash is the backup that depends least on any bank, because paying with it needs no connection to an account at the register. It only works as a backup if the bills are already in your wallet or at home before an outage begins.

A cash withdrawal is itself a bank transaction. When you use a card at an ATM, the bank that issued the card has to approve the request. If that bank's systems are down, the withdrawal can fail even at a machine owned by a different bank. ATMs run by the affected bank may also be offline entirely.

Getting cash back at a supermarket checkout runs into the same problem. Cash back is processed as part of a debit card purchase. That means the issuing bank has to authorize it. During an outage, this route closes along with the card.

Cash also has limits once you have it. Under federal law, U.S. coins and currency are legal tender for debts. That status does not require a private business to accept cash when it sells goods or services. A store, restaurant or parking operator can adopt a card-only policy unless a state or local law says otherwise. Some jurisdictions have passed their own cash-acceptance laws. Whether a business must take bills depends on where it operates.

Denominations make a practical difference. Small bills are easier to spend at places that keep little change in the drawer. They also let you pay close to the exact amount for groceries, fuel or a ride. A stack of large bills can be harder to use at a small shop or a vending machine.

Storage is the main trade-off. Cash kept at home or carried on you has none of the fraud protections that apply to cards. Federal rules that cap liability for unauthorized card charges do not cover lost or stolen bills. Once cash is gone, it is usually gone for good. The amount kept on hand is a balance between covering essentials and limiting what could be lost.

A debit card issued by a different bank draws on a separate account, so it keeps working when your main bank's systems are down. The backup only works if that second bank is unrelated to the first and the account behind the card already holds money.

The reason lies in how a debit purchase gets approved. When a card is tapped or swiped, the request travels over a card network such as Visa $V or Mastercard $MA to the bank that issued the card. That bank checks the balance and approves or declines the charge. If the issuing bank cannot respond, the purchase fails. A card from a different bank sends its approval requests to a different set of systems.

Before relying on the card, confirm that the backup bank is a separate institution. Some banks operate more than one brand. Two names on two cards can still lead back to one company.

Funding is the other condition. Moving money from the main account into the backup usually requires the main bank's app, website or transfer systems. Those are the same tools an outage can take away. The balance has to be in place before trouble starts.

The card also opens a second route to cash. It can withdraw money from the backup bank's own ATMs, which do not depend on the main bank. Machines outside the backup bank's network may charge fees.

Debit cards carry a specific set of fraud protections under Regulation E, the federal rule that governs electronic fund transfers. Consumer liability for unauthorized debit transactions is capped at $50 if the loss is reported within two business days of learning about it. After that, liability can rise to $500. If the loss is not reported within 60 days of the statement that shows it, liability can be unlimited.

Those deadlines apply to a backup card just as they do to an everyday one. A card kept in reserve is used less often, so a loss or theft can go unnoticed for longer. Reviewing the backup account's statements on a regular schedule makes it more likely that a problem surfaces before the 60-day window closes.

A debit card also spends the account holder's own money directly. An unauthorized charge removes funds from the backup account itself, not from a line of credit. That money can be tied up while the bank investigates a dispute.

A credit card from a company with no tie to your bank keeps working when that bank goes down. Charges draw on the issuer's credit line, not on the money sitting in your affected account.

The issuer is the detail that matters. Visa $V, Mastercard $MA, American Express $AXP and Discover $DFS are payment networks. They route transactions between merchants and the institutions behind each card. Visa and Mastercard do not issue cards to consumers themselves. Banks and credit unions do. Those issuers approve or decline each purchase. A Visa card from your own bank depends on that bank's systems. A Visa card from an unrelated bank does not.

The same test applies to American Express and Discover cards. What counts is which institution stands behind the card, and whether that institution is the one having trouble.

A credit card also separates the outage from your cash. During a disruption, you may not be able to see your balance or confirm that a deposit has landed. Spending on credit sidesteps that uncertainty. The purchase becomes a debt owed to the card issuer, payable later.

Fraud protection is another point of contrast with debit. The Truth in Lending Act limits a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card charges to $50. The money at stake in a disputed charge belongs to the issuer, not to you. A fraudulent charge does not drain the funds you need for rent or bills while it is investigated.

Repayment is where the outage can catch up with you. A card bill set to autopay from the checking account that just went offline may not go through on schedule. That matters if the due date falls during the disruption. Knowing the due date and having another way to pay the bill helps avoid a late payment.

A card only works as a backup if it is ready to use. It needs to be activated and unexpired. It also needs enough available credit for essentials such as groceries or fuel. Many cards allow a cash advance at an ATM. Advances usually come with their own fees and interest terms, separate from those on purchases.

A mobile wallet is a way to present a card, not a separate source of money. Apple $AAPL Pay, Google $GOOGL Wallet and Samsung Wallet work as a backup only when they hold cards from more than one issuer.

Each wallet stores a tokenized version of a card. The phone holds a substitute number tied to that device instead of the actual card number. The merchant receives that token rather than the real account details. The payment itself still travels to the card's issuer for approval, the same way a purchase with the plastic card would.

That routing decides what happens during an outage. If the bank behind the card being used cannot approve transactions, a tap with that card is declined at the register. The phone, the wallet app and the payment terminal can all be working normally. The purchase still fails.

The fix is to load cards from different, unrelated issuers into the same wallet. A debit card from a main bank can sit alongside a credit card from another issuer and a debit card from a credit union. When one card is declined, the shopper can pick a different one and tap again. Each of these wallets lets the user change the default card or choose a specific card before paying.

Setup has to happen before any trouble starts. Adding a card to a wallet usually requires the issuer to verify it. That check often runs through a code sent by text or email, or through the bank's own app. An issuer that is offline may not be able to complete that step.

The wallet a person can use depends on the hardware they carry. For in-store payments, Apple Pay runs on iPhone and Apple Watch. Google Wallet runs on Android phones and Wear OS watches. Samsung Wallet runs on Samsung Galaxy devices.

Merchant acceptance is the other limit. In-store wallet payments rely on contactless terminals. Not every business has one or has switched the feature on. A small shop, a market stall or an older terminal may take only chip cards, swiped cards or cash. Many apps and websites also accept these wallets at online checkout, which extends their use beyond physical stores.

A wallet also depends on the device itself. A phone with a dead battery or a lost watch puts every loaded card out of reach at once. Carrying at least one physical card from a second issuer covers that gap.

A reloadable prepaid card holds money loaded onto it in advance, kept apart from your checking account. If the card comes from a company unrelated to your main bank, it can keep paying when that bank's systems go down.

The card runs on a payment network such as Visa $V or Mastercard $MA. Merchants generally accept it the way they accept a regular debit card. The difference is where the money sits. Each purchase draws on the card's own stored balance rather than on a checking account. A wave of declined authorizations at your main bank has no bearing on that balance.

Timing is the catch. A common way to top up a prepaid card is a transfer from a checking account. That route closes as soon as the bank goes offline. A prepaid card works as a backup only if the balance is already on it before trouble starts.

Some cards can also be reloaded with cash at retail locations. That method adds money without any bank connection at all. Reload options vary by product, and the card's terms list which ones it supports.

Independence has limits. Most prepaid cards are issued by a bank, often in partnership with a separate company that runs the program. If the bank behind the prepaid card is the institution having the outage, the card fails with it. The cardholder agreement names the issuing bank, which answers that question.

Terms differ widely from one product to the next. Since April 2019, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's prepaid rule has required most prepaid accounts to show a short fee disclosure before purchase. That form lists charges such as monthly, reload and ATM fees. Its standard layout lets shoppers compare competing products side by side.

The same rule extended error-resolution and lost-card protections to prepaid accounts. Some of those rights apply only once the card is registered with the provider. An unregistered card can also be harder to replace if it is lost or stolen.

Federal deposit insurance is less straightforward. Coverage can extend to a prepaid balance only when certain conditions are met, including how the funds are held and recorded at an insured bank. A cardholder cannot assume it applies. The cardholder agreement states whether the balance is eligible.

Money already held in a PayPal $PYPL, Venmo or Cash App balance can be spent without passing through your bank. Zelle is different. It moves money from one bank account to another, so it stops working when your bank does.

What matters is where the money sits. A balance inside the app is recorded by the app's operator, not by your checking account. A payment the app pulls from a linked bank account is a separate case. If that linked account is at the bank having the outage, the payment fails even though the app itself is running.

The balance has to be in place before trouble starts. An app can't be topped up from a bank that is offline. A balance can build up when friends, relatives or clients send you money. Funds can also be moved in ahead of time from a working account.

These apps are most useful for person-to-person payments. They can split a dinner bill, repay a roommate or send money to a family member. Both people generally need to use the same service. A Venmo balance pays other Venmo users, and a Cash App balance pays other Cash App users.

Store purchases are more limited. PayPal is a checkout option at many online retailers, and Venmo can be used with some online merchants. Each app also offers its own debit card that spends from the app balance. These are the PayPal Debit Mastercard $MA, the Venmo debit card on the Mastercard network and Cash App's Visa $V debit card, called the Cash Card. They can be used at physical stores that accept those card networks.

A linked card from an unrelated issuer adds a second route. If the app can fund payments from a credit or debit card at an unaffected institution, a purchase can still go through when the balance runs short.

Withdrawals are the weak point. Moving an app balance out to a bank account depends on that bank being reachable. During an outage, money in the app can be spent inside the app's network. It can't easily be moved to the bank that is down.

Zelle is built into the apps and websites of participating banks and credit unions. It holds no balance of its own. Every Zelle payment leaves one bank account and arrives in another. When your bank's app goes down, the Zelle option inside it goes down too. It works as a feature of your bank, not as a replacement for it.

A USPS money order is a prepaid paper payment that can cover rent or a bill when bank transfers and online bill pay are unavailable. Each domestic postal money order is capped at $1,000.

The buyer pays the full amount at the post office counter before the money order is issued. That up-front payment is what makes it reliable. A personal check can bounce if the account behind it is short. A money order cannot, because the funds were collected before it was printed.

During an outage, the way a buyer pays for the money order matters. Post offices accept cash, debit cards and traveler's checks for money orders. They do not accept credit cards. A debit card from the bank that is down may be declined at the postal counter, just as it would be at a store. Cash or a debit card from an unrelated bank avoids that problem.

The $1,000 cap shapes how larger payments work. Rent above that amount requires two or more money orders. Each one carries its own purchase fee. USPS adjusts that fee periodically, and the current price is posted at the counter and on the USPS website.

A money order is built for payments that are mailed or handed over in person. Typical uses include rent, a utility bill, an insurance premium or a payment to a contractor. Buying one requires a trip to a post office during its business hours, which limits it to planned payments rather than spur-of-the-moment ones.

Filling one out correctly protects the buyer. The payee's name should go on the front right away. A blank money order can be completed and cashed by whoever holds it. The detachable receipt stub carries the serial number. With that stub, the buyer can check whether the money order has been cashed. The stub is also needed to request a replacement if the money order is lost or stolen. That replacement process carries its own fee.

Postal money orders do not expire. The recipient can deposit one at their own bank or cash it at a post office with identification. The payment still goes through even if the buyer's bank stays offline. The funds were collected at the post office, not drawn from the buyer's account.

The main tradeoffs are timing and convenience. A money order sent by mail travels no faster than a mailed check. It suits bills with some time left before the due date.

Gift cards already in a drawer can cover groceries, fuel or a meal while your bank is down, because they spend a balance that sits outside your checking account. Closed-loop cards work only at one retailer or a group of retailers, while open-loop Visa $V or Mastercard $MA cards work at many more places.

A closed-loop card is tied to the business that sold it. A card from a supermarket chain, a gas station brand or a restaurant group pays only at that company's locations or website. That limits where it helps. It also means the card's value depends on the retailer's own system, not on the bank that is having trouble.

An open-loop card carries the Visa or Mastercard logo and runs on that network. It can be used at most merchants that take those cards, in stores and often online. The tradeoff is cost. These cards usually carry a purchase fee on top of the loaded amount. Closed-loop cards are usually sold at face value.

The gift cards that help most in an outage are the ones you already own. Buying a new card during an outage requires a working way to pay for it, such as cash or a card from another institution. A closed-loop card from the store where you already buy groceries or fuel fits easily. It matches spending you would do anyway.

Check balances before relying on them. Most cards list a website or phone number on the back for balance checks. Knowing the exact figure matters at the register. If a purchase costs more than the card holds, ask the cashier to charge the card for its remaining balance and pay the difference another way. Some retailers can split a payment this way and some cannot.

Fuel pumps add a complication. Many pumps place a temporary hold before fueling begins, and a gift card with a small balance may be declined. Paying inside for a set amount avoids that problem.

Some open-loop cards must be registered online with a name and ZIP code before they work for online purchases. Doing that in advance prevents a declined order later.

Gift cards generally carry fewer protections than bank-issued debit and credit cards. A lost or stolen card with no registration can be as hard to recover as lost cash. The Federal Trade Commission warns that anyone demanding payment by gift card is running a scam. A bank outage does not change that.

A checking account at a credit union or bank with no connection to your main one is the most complete backup on this list. It holds its own money and usually comes with its own debit card, app and online access.

Most other backups cover one piece of the problem. Cash handles in-person purchases. A spare credit card handles card payments. A separate deposit account can handle nearly all of it at once. It can pay bills, receive transfers, supply cash through ATMs and pay at a register.

The account has to be truly separate. A second account at the same bank runs on that bank's systems. If those systems go down, both accounts go down together. The backup has to sit at a different institution.

Some online banks operate as brand names of a larger bank. The FDIC treats deposits held under different brand names of one bank as deposits at a single institution. Checking which institution actually holds the account helps avoid a backup that turns out to be the same bank under another name.

Credit unions are one option for this role. They are member-owned cooperatives. Joining usually means meeting an eligibility rule, such as living in a certain area, working for a certain employer or belonging to a particular group.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insures bank deposits. The National Credit Union Administration insures deposits at federally insured credit unions through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. Both cover $250,000 per depositor, per insured institution, per ownership category. Ownership categories include single accounts, joint accounts and certain retirement accounts. Money at a second insured institution counts toward that institution's limit, not the first one's.

Timing is the main drawback. Opening an account involves identity verification. A new debit card can take days to arrive by mail. None of that can happen once an outage has started. The account needs to be open, funded and active well before it is needed. Its card should already be activated and its online login already set up.

A backup account also needs money in it. An empty account with a working card cannot pay for anything. Some institutions charge maintenance fees or require minimum balances. Those terms vary from one institution to the next.

An account left untouched for long periods can be classified as dormant. State unclaimed property laws can eventually require a dormant balance to be turned over to the state. Occasional use keeps the account active and confirms the card and login still work.

Some brokerages offer cash management accounts that come with a debit card and check-writing and sit outside your main bank. They work as a backup only if the firm's banking partners are not the bank that has gone down.

These accounts behave much like checking accounts. Money sits in the account, and the debit card pays at a register or withdraws cash at an ATM. Checks can cover rent or a bill. The difference is who actually holds the money. A brokerage is not a bank, so it does not take deposits on its own.

The usual structure is a sweep. Uninvested cash in the account is moved into deposit accounts at one or more partner banks. Card payments and check clearing also tend to run through a bank that works with the brokerage. That arrangement decides whether the account is a real backup during an outage.

If your everyday bank is one of the brokerage's partner banks, the two accounts are less separate than they look. An outage at that bank could reach the brokerage account as well. Firms that run sweep programs generally disclose which banks take part. That list answers the main question for any backup: does it depend on the bank that failed?

The same list matters for deposit insurance. Swept cash can be eligible for FDIC coverage at the partner banks. That coverage is counted per depositor at each bank. Money you already keep at one of those banks in the same ownership category is added to whatever the sweep places there. Program terms, the number of partner banks and any limits differ by firm.

Cash in these accounts is not the same as invested money. Shares or funds held in the account have to be sold before the proceeds can be spent. Most U.S. stock trades settle one business day after the trade date. Until a sale goes through, market prices keep moving. The value available to spend is not fixed in advance.

Like any other backup account, a brokerage cash account has to be opened and funded before an outage. Opening one involves identity verification. Funding it usually means a transfer from an existing bank account. That transfer may not go through once the main bank is unreachable.

#5423. OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

#5422. How to finance nature

Free daily briefing on global business news.

From debt-for-nature swaps to wildlife bonds, new financial deals are bringing private investors into conservation

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Most people don’t think of going to a climate summit to close a financial deal. But this year’s U.N. climate summit is shaping up differently.

A week before COP31 was due to open in Antalya, Turkey, Bank of America $BAC and a sustainable investing group founded by King Charles III launched a nature fund seeded with $40 million. It backs companies that protect ecosystems, from supply-chain tracking to DNA-based wildlife monitoring.

More deals making time was set up for the summit. The COP organizers are putting on a Finance Day that will cover how to make nature projects something investors can actually buy and a Nordic development fund has planned a session where climate funds would pitch investors directly.

There are several financial instruments for financing nature. The oldest and best known is the debt-for-nature swap. A country with heavy debt gets some of it bought at a discount, then renegotiated on better terms in exchange for spending part of the savings on conservation. Bolivia struck the first in 1987, which was worth $650,000.

The deals have grown since. Ecuador’s 2023 swap for the Galapagos Islands bought roughly $1.6 billion of its bonds for $656 million and freed about $450 million for conservation. Many of the biggest swaps relied on a safeguard. Guarantees from the U.S. government promised to repay investors if political turmoil interrupted payments, which made the new debt safe enough to buy.

The market went quiet for a while, with only about $6 billion in swaps with private capital being done from 2021 to 2024. Renewed interest returned in February, when Britain’s biggest asset manager, Legal & General, committed up to $1 billion to anchor a new generation of deals.

Bonds are another route, and come in a variety of setups. The World Bank’s “rhino bond” was one. In 2022 it raised $150 million from investors who gave up their interest payments, about $9 million in all, so the money could go to protecting black rhinos in two South African parks. Investors were due their principal back in March 2027, plus a bonus of up to $13.8 million if the rhino population grew.

Others looked more like ordinary business. Funds like the one with King Charles III put money into companies and expected a commercial return. Payments for ecosystem services, usually run by governments, rewarded the conservation of a forest or wetland, and environmental credits, which works like carbon offsets, sold verified conservation as a tradable certificate.

It's still early to judge how well many of these instruments work. Some of the biggest deals are only a few years old, and their conservation commitments will take much longer to measure.

But there's pressure to scale them: the market is being built against an enormous funding gap. Private finance classified as nature-related has grown from $9.4 billion in 2020 to $102 billion in 2024, but even that jump left a vast amount of conservation unfunded, with BloombergNEF estimating the debt swap market could be as large as $1 trillion.

The deals themselves have drawn criticism. Debt Justice, a British campaign group, found that four swaps cut national debt by an average of 3%, while ordinary restructurings cut it about seven times more.

A French advocacy group calculated that Belize put $84 million of a $553 million deal toward nature. In Gabon the figure was $67.5 million, with the rest going to repay debt and pay fees.

Then there is Washington. Political risk guarantees from the U.S. government underpinned swaps in Ecuador, Belize, Gabon and El Salvador, and that went away after Donald Trump returned to office.

That leaves private investors to carry more of the load. But getting them to invest means finding conservation projects that can deliver a return, and there aren't enough of those yet. McKinsey cited fragmented data and ecosystem outcomes that are hard to price as two reasons why.

Even if private investment grows, the hardest conservation work may remain beyond its reach. Markets can channel money toward nature where they can extract a return. They are less equipped to pay for protection whose benefits are diffuse, long-term or impossible to monetize.

#5421. Honeywell Technologies CEO says 50 years of automation have gotten too complex for the humans running it

The automation that runs hospitals, data centers, and refineries got its start in the 1970s. Honeywell Technologies chairman and CEO Vimal Kapur says it has since grown too complex for the people still watching over it.

Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kapur said those facilities run themselves for the most part, “maybe 95%,” with a person left in the loop to handle the exceptions. “Over the last 50 years since this got created, the systems have become highly complex because we kept adding more and more software and physical infrastructure to it,” he said. “So human cannot keep up with that at this point of time.”

He pointed to recent news as an example. “What happened in the last two weeks is an example of complexity,” Kapur said, where “humans are not able to keep up with it,” producing an “undesired incident.” He didn’t say which one, but the options are almost too numerous to count.

On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency was focused on a copper-to-fiber upgrade by contractor L3Harris in El Dorado, Ark., that flooded routers with connection attempts and disrupted some radar feeds, while adding, “we don’t actually have the root cause.” On Nov. 12, Microsoft 365 began an outage that lasted more than a day. As of press time, many Americans were unable to access their bank accounts.

Kapur’s answer is what the industry calls “physical AI,” of which he said humanoid robots are a “very small portion.” His version goes into “every large asset which exists: hospital, data center, life sciences facilities, refineries.” It adds “a layer of learning system, the human knowledge” on top of the existing automation “so that you are able to make human more productive.”

The obstacle is data: “We assume that data is available abundantly on [the] internet,” Kapur said. “But when you look at a physical system, the data is in some system which is in this building or in this hospital. Those data [are] not in public domain.” Turning it into something useful takes people “who have deep domain knowledge,” he said. He called data access “the first friction” in an April talk at Goldman Sachs.

Honeywell sells automation to building, industrial, and process customers, and now sells the AI layer that goes on top. When it spun off its aerospace business on June 29, completing its three-way split, the company said it was positioned to lead “the industrial sector’s transition from automation to autonomy.” In October it launched Forge Cognition, an AI platform built with Nvidia and Dell that can run buildings in an autonomous mode, which haven’t been fully switched on, its CTO told Fortune at the time. On stage, Kapur put it more modestly: “Physical AI is not about job replacement; it’s about making humans more productive.” At Goldman in April, he said, “we’ll likely build systems which are more augmented and less autonomous.”

Dave Bozeman, CEO of freight broker C.H. Robinson, who shared the stage with Kapur, described the same problem from the paperwork side. “Variability is now structural,” he said, and supply chains “continue to be super complex.” His company’s answer is what it calls “Lean AI”: AI agents built to do “bespoke, very specific tasks,” with “orchestrating type of agents” on top. The first target is order-to-cash, which he called “a very manual process. Millions of transactions.”

Bozeman also pitched it as help for workers, who he said don’t want to do “those mundane tasks every day” and would rather “go up that value stack.” He cited “over 60% productivity gains since the end of 2022.” The company’s Oct. 28 earnings release measures that as shipments per person, per day in its North American Surface Transportation unit, up more than 65% over the same stretch. The other half of that ratio is people. C.H. Robinson had about 17,400 employees at the end of 2022 and about 11,900 at the end of 2025, according to its filings, a drop of nearly a third that FreightWaves tied to automation and AI.

“That doesn’t mean that it won’t be hard from a change perspective,” Bozeman said.

The problem Kapur describes was laid out more than 40 years ago. In 1983, Lisanne Bainbridge, a psychologist at University College London, published “Ironies of Automation” in the journal Automatica. She argued that designers automate what they can and leave the operator “to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate.” Those leftover tasks include taking over when conditions turn abnormal. Her central irony was that “the more advanced a control system is, so the more crucial may be the contribution of the human operator.”

She also warned about what watching does to people. Operators’ “physical skills deteriorate when they are not used,” she wrote, and of the person reduced to monitoring a system: “The human monitor has been given an impossible task.” Her paper argued that automation “may expand rather than eliminate problems with the human operator.” That’s the test for an AI layer added to the stack.

Kapur said the shortage of skilled workers is what makes this urgent. “The skill shortage is the biggest problem we all face,” he said. “Anywhere there’s a touch labor where the humans need to work with hand, those workforce is becoming less and less available.” In the Goldman talk, he blamed retirement in part.

A 2024 study puts numbers on it for manufacturing. Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute found U.S. manufacturers could need as many as 3.8 million additional workers between 2024 and 2033, and that 1.9 million of those jobs could go unfilled if workforce problems aren’t addressed. Sixty-five percent of manufacturers surveyed called attracting and keeping talent their primary business challenge.

Kapur gave his own company a much shorter clock than 50 years. Honeywell Technologies has more than 50,000 employees, and he said he personally took training on Copilot. “Next 18 to 24 months, we all have to reskill ourselves,” he said.

#5419. ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue…

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.

#5418. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

“She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and launches go off as planned.”

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and said it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

#5416. ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers

As U.S.-Canadian relations go frosty, one American food brand is having to be more intentional about appealing to its northern neighbors.

Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane said the made-in-the-U.S.A. moniker doesn’t carry the same positive connotation as it did in decades past. As a result, he said, the Chicago- and Pittsburgh-based food giant—behind Jell-O, Lunchables, and Heinz ketchup—is having to tweak its messaging.

“Brand America is not as strong as it once was, and that’s been the case for some time,” Cahillane told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “We’re having to overcome brand America. Whereas, in the ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, into the ‘80s, brand America was a badge of honor, it’s a little bit more complicated today.”

Ongoing trade tensions, including a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods, have chilled Canadian attitudes towards American productions, as have repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump about making Canada the “51st state,” claiming it relies too heavily on the U.S. economically. While Canadians have continued to pour money into U.S. investments, many have also made a concerted effort to boycott American goods in favor of Canadian counterparts.

In some areas, these boycotts are taking a toll on the U.S. economy. A report from the Canadian government published last month found that despite Canadian visitations to the U.S. beginning to increase, visitations from Canadians are 29% lower as of September 2026 than they were two years ago. According to the U.S. Travel Association, those decreases in visits cost the U.S. economy $4.5 billion last year.

Kraft Heinz has worked to adapt to Canadians’ changing attitudes toward American goods by giving its consumers reassurance their products are being made in the Great White North, according to Cahillane. In March, subsidiary Kraft Heinz Canada announced a $250 million investment to bolster operations at its Montreal production facility.

“We had to remind the Canadian consumer that all of the Heinz ketchup that they’re consuming in Canada is made in Canada,” Cahillane said. “We have a couple of big plants up there, and so when we talk to people about the local nature of our products, it may be brand America, but it’s produced in your backyard by your friends and neighbors, grown locally,” he added.

As Kraft Heinz navigates a turnaround after a 10-year slump, the company is beginning to find more solid footing outside the U.S. Despite reporting falling revenue last quarter, it was particularly offset by growing sales in Canada. Its Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen debuted in Canada in July, and, according to Cahillane, it sold out three months of inventory in a week.

Kraft Heinz is also finding ways to navigate tariffs after initially being hit hard by the implementation of the import taxes. The food giant reported in May 2025 it would need to shift suppliers and potentially reformulate products as a result of the levies.

“We’re already local. We have to be hyperlocal,” Cahillane told Fortune. “We have to build in redundancy. We have to build in the ability to do things faster than we ever have before, and that becomes hyperlocal for us.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5415. Amazon Reportedly Has an Ambitious Secret Plan to Ensure That You Never Shop Anywhere Else

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A proposed initiative would give shoppers fewer reasons to leave Amazon.

Amazon’s secret plan goes beyond selling you everything. It also wants to be the place where you decide what to buy in the first place.

According to a recent Reuters report citing an internal document, Amazon is working on a secret initiative called World Product Graph to catalog products across the Internet, including items that it doesn’t currently sell. The project involves gathering data on essentially every item for sale on the web to keep shoppers from taking their research elsewhere.

World Product Graph could ensure that Amazon is the first place shoppers visit to figure out what they want to purchase. A detailed database could help customers compare product models, understand features and explore alternatives without jumping between search engines, manufacturers’ websites and competing stores.

That would give Amazon a stronger hold over the product research space, challenging Google while giving shoppers another reason to choose it over Walmart and other retailers.

“Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites,” the document read, according to Reuters. “These answers exist, ​but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums.”

The project could also help Amazon navigate a shift in how people shop. Currently, some shoppers are using AI agents to research products and potentially make purchases. AI agents need reliable product information to make recommendations, which is something the World Product Graph could provide.

If the proposal becomes reality, it could offer Amazon an advantage that goes beyond competitive pricing. The site could offer information that makes other shopping sites feel less useful by comparison.

In a statement to Reuters, Amazon said it is “constantly working on new ideas and technologies.”

“Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans,” the company said in the statement.

The leaked document presents the proposal as a future press announcement, with October 1, 2027, as a target launch date. Reuters was not able to confirm a timeline or if Amazon would move forward with the plans.

Amazon currently has a stronger hold on shoppers who know what they want rather than those who are still deciding. A 2025 Morgan Stanley research report cited by Reuters found that 57% of online shoppers began product research on Google, compared with just 16% on Amazon.

Once shoppers have a specific product in mind, the rankings reverse. Amazon becomes the leading starting point, accounting for 41% of searches, compared with 23% for Google and 18% for Walmart.

Google currently leads in discovery, while Amazon has the advantage when customers arrive with a clearer purchase in mind.

#5414. Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

#5413. Michigan’s next governor hasn’t talked to Trump yet—but wants to work with him on a 50% auto tariff set for her first day

Michigan Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson hasn’t spoken to President Donald Trump since winning the state’s governor’s race as part of the blue tsunami that swept across the nation earlier this month.

“Not yet, but I intend to,” Benson said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit in an interview with Fortune editorial director Kristin Stoller. “We’ve all got to work together to better our economy, to better Michigan.”

Top of mind, though, is a tariff that could land on her first day in office. After negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks, and parts to 50% beginning Jan. 1, 2027. That’s the same day Benson takes over from term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

Benson said she hopes for opportunities to collaborate, “first and foremost, in reducing the impact of these tariffs.” She recalled touring auto parts distributor Detroit Axle in October, where she said the owner told her: “I’m sending millions of dollars into paying these tariffs, and it’s money that I had saved to expand my business, to create more jobs.”

Last year, Detroit Axle said it might have to shut down a warehouse and lay off more than 100 workers, although it later backtracked. But owner Mike Musheinesh told the Associated Press, “It’s a market of who is able to survive; it’s not a matter of who can thrive.”

Benson said a governor can uniquely go to Canada and broker a Michigan-specific agreement to protect jobs and lower costs, something she promised to pursue on the campaign trail. She also said she intends to negotiate “aggressively” with the federal government for carve-outs that lessen the tariffs’ impact. While campaigning, she argued levies on Canadian imports had set the average Michigan household back $5,600—more than any other state.

Tariffs are just one piece of Benson’s broader plan to fix affordability.

“Our campaign was about affordability through the lens of costs down, wages up, knowing that there’s two sides of that coin,” Benson told Fortune. Michigan’s per capita incomes “have also been stagnant for far too long,” she said, adding that most jobs in the state’s economy pay $60,000 or less. In 2025, Michigan ranked in the lower half of median wages in the U.S., according to the Michigan Center for Data and Analytics.

Benson said part of the governor’s job is bringing in new, higher-paying jobs and training workers to fill those roles so paychecks will “go up and not stay stagnant.” On the cost side, she pitched herself as “the CEO of state government,” saying she plans to streamline how the state delivers health care, housing development, and childcare to save money.

“You’re actually running an institution, and you have metrics and a strategic plan and delivering results,” she said regarding referring to herself as the CEO of Michigan. As Michigan’s secretary of state, she overhauled the state’s DMV offices, which she said eliminated wait times and made the agency “a poster child for efficiency.”

Michigan voters also sent progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate over Republican Mike Rogers. Benson said the commonality between the two wins was “costs down and wages up,” along with ending corruption.

“It’s a team effort,” she said of lowering costs. “It’s partnerships, but there’s a lot you can do as the CEO of the state to drive down costs and bring more well-paying jobs in.”

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5412. He Became a Chick-fil-A Franchise Operator at Age 26. Now He Runs Two of Its Highest-Grossing Restaurants.

It took $10,000 to launch his first business in Baltimore — then he relocated to Brooklyn.

In 2010, Brandon J. Hurst had just graduated from college. He had three options on the table. First, he could stay at Alabama State University, where he had received his Bachelor’s degree, to get a Master’s degree in accounting. Second, he could apply to law school and then go work on Wall Street. Or third, he could take a $12-an-hour job in Chicago working at Chick-fil-A with no guaranteed career path in sight.

“This is what I did,” Hurst says in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “Two weeks after graduation, I packed everything I owned and drove 14 hours straight to start a brand new life in Chicago to work inside of a Chick-fil-A restaurant.”

The opportunity offered him a chance to learn the business directly from an operator. He moved there to become a director of operations at the branch — an opportunity he couldn’t pass up.

“I knew whatever I would be doing, I had to be in some type of entrepreneurial capacity,” he says.

Chick-fil-A offers an unusually affordable way to enter the restaurant business: Its initial franchise fee is $10,000 and has stayed that way for the past 50 years, per The New York Post. Applicants must use their own money, not borrowed or gifted funds, to pay the franchise fee.

However, that payment does not buy ownership of a restaurant.

Instead, Chick-fil-A selects operators to run locations that the company finances. The company handles major startup expenses, including construction and equipment, and retains ownership of the restaurant’s assets. Operators manage the business rather than acquire an asset they can eventually sell.

That differs from traditional franchising, where franchisees typically fund the startup investment and own a business operating under another company’s brand. ADP puts most franchise startup costs between $100,000 and $300,000, with restaurants and hotels among the most expensive options.

Chick-fil-A’s franchise business is also highly competitive. The Post reported that about 100,000 people apply annually to be operators, and of those, 200 are selected, or about 0.2%.

Selected operators must work full-time in the business and divest other non-passive business interests. Chick-fil-A explicitly says the program is not a passive investment. Operators do not receive a traditional corporate salary. Instead, their income comes from a profit-sharing model.

They earn a percentage of the store’s net profits and typically take home anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 a year. High-performing operators earn more than $500,000 annually.

So operators need comparatively little upfront capital, but they do not build equity in the restaurant. They cannot sell it or pass it down to their children when they retire.

In 2012, Hurst was selected for Chick-fil-A’s leadership development program. For the next three years, he helped operators launch restaurants around the country.

The work gave him repeated opportunities to practice opening a business without immediately taking responsibility for his own. He supported 14 operators, 12 of whom were external candidates who had never owned or worked at a Chick-fil-A restaurant.

“You ever heard the saying, ‘If you want to master something, teach it’?” Hurst says. “That’s exactly what I had the opportunity to do.”

The experience let him repeatedly practice opening restaurants before taking responsibility for one himself.

In April 2015, at age 26, Hurst opened his first Chick-fil-A restaurant in downtown Baltimore. He wanted to help Chick-fil-A figure out how to operate in dense urban neighborhoods, where restaurants couldn’t rely on the large drive-thrus familiar to suburban customers.

Hurst was in Baltimore for five years before passing the torch to other local operators and relocating to Brooklyn, New York. He opened his first Brooklyn restaurant across from Barclays Center in 2019, followed by a second in Clinton Hill in November 2024.

Today, he describes his restaurants as among Chick-fil-A’s highest-grossing locations. According to Restaurant Business, Chick-fil-A’s stand-alone restaurants averaged nearly $9.2 million in sales in 2025. Its busiest location brings in more than $20 million annually, while its top-performing mall restaurant recorded $14.4 million in sales in 2025.

Presented with these statistics, Hurst said his restaurants were “well north of those numbers,” without providing an exact figure.

He credits the neighborhoods, customers attending Barclays Center events and, above all, his employees, for his success.

Chick-fil-A stood out to Hurst because he wouldn’t have to create a concept or a brand-new menu.

“Although I have a strong entrepreneurial spirit, I don’t have a whole lot of patience for building something from the ground up,” he says. “I can cook, but I’m more of an operational strategy and leadership development person.”

Chick-fil-A already provided a brand and systems that allowed Hurst to “hit the ground running” and focus on his strengths.

The financial barrier to entry was also important. Hurst was able to open his first Chick-fil-A restaurant at age 26 because of the relatively low $10,000 upfront cost when compared to other franchises.

Hurst says future franchise operators should determine their capacity to shoulder risk, then ask what they are willing to sacrifice. “You may have the financial means, but are you ready to invest the time and resources it will take?” he asks.

Hurst says his growth depends on retaining employees.

To that end, he purchased a multi-family building in Brooklyn where team members can live at below-market rents. He also provides access to free mental health care, including up to 10 sessions with a therapist, and telehealth services for employees and their households. Eligible college students can receive reimbursement for textbooks.

The numbers show that his investments are working. He says his leaders have an average tenure of about four years. For regular team members, retention rates greater than 12 to 16 months are a win.

Hurst says that hiring is about finding people who want to serve others. One question he asks is: “Tell me about a time you wanted to give up and why you didn’t.”

The answer helps him understand how someone handles adversity in a busy, high-pressure restaurant. Another question he asks is: “How do you define care for yourself?” The answer helps him understand what meaningful support might look like for that person.

But supporting employees also means allowing them to take responsibility. Hurst says one of his ongoing challenges is building an organization that doesn’t depend too heavily on him.

“If every major decision, relationship or problem” has to come through the founder, he says, “then I really haven’t built the capacity to scale.”

Hurst hired an executive assistant about five years ago, who helped him organize his calendar and create space for other work, including his forthcoming book, Outthink Yourself, which comes out in January.

“I wrote the book for anyone who is navigating growth, whether you’re in your first job leading a team or building a business,” Hurst says. “This book was a four-year process in the making.”

Hurst organizes his approach to growth around three stages: See, become and build.

The first is understanding the opportunity, problem or risk in front of you. The second is identifying the skills and capabilities you need to pursue it. The third is building systems that make progress sustainable.

He traces that framework through his own career. Assessing the Chicago job required him to get comfortable with uncertainty. Training other operators helped him become a stronger leader. Running two restaurants required him to build teams that could sustain the business.

His next ambitions include expanding his Chick-fil-A portfolio and working with entrepreneurs through speaking engagements and training workshops. He has also begun developing a second book focused more directly on putting his ideas into practice.

“More locations, more books,” Hurst says. “I do have very high aspirations for myself.”
