#5411. Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

#5410. Newly reelected Sen. John Hickenlooper sketches Democrats’ AI line: race China, but regulate frontier models like nuclear weapons and airplanes

Sen. John Hickenlooper wants American AI to win in the international AI arms race. He just isn’t sure it needs to be able to rebuild itself without limits.

“Maybe we don’t need recursive learning, unlimited,” the Colorado Democrat told Fortune’s Diane Brady on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, where he teleconferenced in. He described machines “reinventing themselves sometimes outside the fence line of their domain that they’re supposed to stay in.”

“That should cause real concern,” Hickenlooper said.

Hickenlooper, a member of the Senate Commerce Committee, won his second and last term two weeks ago, leading Republican state Sen. Mark Baisley 61% to 35% on election night. While his seat was expected to go his way, eight seats won Democrats control of the Senate in last Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which data centers and the AI buildout was one of the most referenced issues that influenced voters’ decisions.

His comments come as the buildout continues and as AI companies use their models to speed up their research. In September, more than 20 researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, published a paper warning that automating AI research could set off an “intelligence explosion.” Alan Chan, one of its lead coauthors, said that valid safety mechanisms aren’t in place.

Hickenlooper said he isn’t against the labs moving fast. “They are pushing as fast as they can. I understand that, and that’s good,” he said, referencing the international rivalry. “We want to make sure that our frontier AI is the best in the world because it has the potential to dominate the globe.”

He said there are still ways to make sure the U.S. does that safely: for example, there are rules already on the books for other technologies. “We regulate nuclear weapons. We have regulations before an airplane can go into service,” he said. “We need to look at what are some of the fundamental safeguards and guardrails that we should put in place.”

Brady asked about Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The Senate Banking Committee has asked Huang and Lutnick to testify next month. While Hickenlooper said his questions about the case were “not that pressing,” Hickenlooper, who is not part of the committee, said he wants to know the basics first.

“What is our relationship to China, and how secure do we feel in sharing our technology with them at any level?” he said. “Because I don’t feel comfortable with that.”

Hickenlooper backs the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to help curb data centers. The permitting bill would speed approvals for energy projects and require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades built to serve them. The Senate voted 73-25 last week to begin debate on it, and President Donald Trump endorsed it.

Hickenlooper said data centers should first guarantee there will be no loud noises or hazards and nuisances in communities. Under the bipartisan bill, the cost of new power lines and substations “will be completely borne by the data center.”

He called the bill a compromise. Trump “doesn’t like wind. He doesn’t like solar,” Hickenlooper said, but the bill would put both on equal footing with natural gas. While the bill has limitations, he said, what it looks like now is one that is “much improved” from where it started.

Hickenlooper read the midterm results as a test rather than a win for his party to bank. “It’s not a mandate,” he said. “I think it’s more of a to-do list, almost an audition.” Democrats, he said, have to show they can lower costs and add jobs.

“When you’re trying to get a deal done, you’ve got to figure out who you’re negotiating with,” he said. “You got to see what’s in it for them and find a way that you can both benefit from the final agreement.”

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5409. Your Business Is Losing Money on AI You Don’t Control — Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Every silent AI update breaks your workflow, and you pay your provider an 85% margin to fix what it broke.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

As a big believer in a domesticated superintelligence, I can’t pass up the Cheeky Pint podcast where OpenAI CEO suggested it’s a terrible idea to keep processing your personal data on your personal computers because his company’s data centers could process your data more efficiently. He walked the remark back after immediate backlash.It’s hard to recognize, yet your business likely lives in that world of centralization already. When using inference via API, you often rent access to a black box that shifts its behavior, pricing and reasoning effort without your knowledge or consent.

Ask yourself: how many times has your team asked for more budget due to inconsistent behavior from GPT or Claude? In Harvard Data Science Review, Stanford and UC Berkeley researchers Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou tested identical prompts on GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 across snapshots three months apart. GPT-4’s prime-number accuracy fell from 84.0% in March 2023 to 51.1% in June, while its chain-of-thought boost collapsed from 24.4% to -0.1%.

Everyday workflows suffered similar drops. On a happy-number task, GPT-4’s accuracy fell from 83.6% to 35.2%, while directly executable code plummeted from 52.0% to 10.0% because extra formatting broke pipelines. Instruction-following on answer extraction collapsed from 99.5% to 0.5% under the same model name and API.

A 2024 Carnegie Mellon and HKUST study by Wanqin Ma, Chenyang Yang and Christian Kästner found that 58.8% of prompt and model combinations lost accuracy after an API update, and 70.2% of those drops exceeded 5 percentage points. Across updates, 10.9% of individual predictions regressed and 63.8% of those failures occurred at maximum confidence, breaking working predictions 87.9% of the time even when overall accuracy rose.

Researchers Emanuele La Malfa and colleagues at Oxford and the Alan Turing Institute warned in a 2025 AAAI paper — first published in Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research — that language-model providers deprecate models on short schedules, collect prompts under commercial licenses and alter serving layers while keeping your pinned model ID unchanged. The end customer takes the hit and is forced to reinvest in adapting to another model that’s not smarter but cheaper to run.

Anthropic is currently defending against a consolidated consumer class action in California federal court (In re Claude Service Degradation Litigation, No. 3:26-cv-07699-RFL) alleging that the company wrongfully degraded its paid Claude Pro ($20/mo), Max 5x ($100/mo), and Max 20x ($200/mo) tiers between March 4 and May 6, 2026. In April 2026, the problem became so obvious that Anthropic had to publish an anti-crisis investigation into Claude Code complaints where it pointed to three changes they intentionally degraded without touching the model. They lowered default reasoning effort from high to medium, introduced a bug that discarded earlier reasoning after idle sessions, and added a brevity instruction that hurt coding output.

In September 2025, Anthropic acknowledged three infrastructure bugs that corrupted responses and misrouted traffic. One routing error grew from 0.8% of requests to 16% of Sonnet 4 traffic and hit roughly 30% of active Claude Code users. Customers paid full price for degraded service, and transparency arrived only after complaints.

The financial incentives behind this opacity are enormous. OpenAI closed a funding round at an $852 billion valuation and discussed a round above $1.2 trillion, while Anthropic prepared for a public listing above $2 trillion alongside roughly $895 billion in non-cancellable compute commitments. High switching costs and forced migrations serve those valuations because every broken workflow requires more API calls to test, more compute for quality assurance and more tokens to rewrite system prompts so your business is not sued by your customers one day for a change in your product you don’t even control.

In 1970, Nobel laureate George Akerlof showed in The Quarterly Journal of Economics how quality uncertainty creates a “market for lemons.” A 2026 CHI study by Alexander Erlei and colleagues at Göttingen, Cagliari, TU Delft and Columbia proved that this trap hits AI buyers. Without disclosure in a high-lemon market, 92.2% of delegations went to low-quality AI systems, whereas partial accuracy disclosure in a low-lemon market cut lemon delegations to 5.5% and raised earnings by 36.4 coins.

Regulators will not fix this soon. While Serena Booth argued at ICML 2025 that consumer protection laws apply to AI, a 2026 FAccT study by Abeba Birhane, William Agnew and colleagues found 249 instances across 100 news articles where AI firms used 27 capture mechanisms to fight oversight. Meanwhile, a 2026 report by Miles Brundage and 47 co-authors noted that frontier AI gets less independent scrutiny than consumer goods, with baseline AAL-1 audits costing $300,000 to $600,000 and AAL-2 reviews exceeding $1 million.

Data centers are great for training large models because they concentrate highly interconnected hardware at scale. Once a model is trained, however, is there any specific reason you share trade secrets and intellectual property with a data center?Tier one superintelligence models run on a domestic intelligence unit that costs less than three months of tokens. For most business workflows — drafting, classification, summarization, contract review and code assistance — an open-weight model on local memory keeps prompts inside your building.In case you love to share your data for the greater good of pre-IPO corporations, here are a few tips from me, based on nearly two decades of experience in this field:

Good news: you can copy/paste this article into a vibecoding tool, so it will implement most of the life-saving solutions within 20 minutes.

You will spend some time on research and likely need more than one AI agent to make it work, yet not addressing this issue today might cost you your entire business tomorrow. The ball is in your court. For now.

#5408. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5407. Why Growing Brands Have an Edge Over Established Competitors in the AI Search Race

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s why — and how — high-growth brands can leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

My agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. Aside from having differentiated products, our most successful clients have had one thing in common: the ability to move swiftly and with agility to navigate shifts in micro and macro markets.

The same pattern is holding true with clients gaining market share through AEO (answer engine optimization). Brands are finding an edge by moving quickly to tackle the growth opportunity of a highly dynamic search landscape — one in which user behavior is changing by the day.

Here’s why — and how — they’re able to leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

Legacy content matters less than you’d think. Large language models (LLMs) carry a measurable recency bias. A decade’s worth of archived content doesn’t provide established companies with the head start many executives assume it does.

Speed wins in a market that changes monthly. AEO is one of the most dynamic disciplines in marketing today; what works this quarter may be obsolete next quarter. Large organizations rarely move with the agility this demands. Meanwhile, more and more less mature companies are hiring for fluency in LLMs and the content that feeds them.

Legacy assets can become liabilities. Structuring new content for AEO is far easier than retrofitting thousands of existing pages. Newer brands can build clean site architecture and easily retrievable content, all free of accumulated technical debt, from day one. They can also borrow credibility through comparison content, which performs exceptionally well in AEO and traditional SEO. Positioning yourself directly against an established competitor also puts your brand in the same conversation.

Paired with disciplined execution, those structural advantages can translate quickly into results and growth.

Dense paragraphs serve neither readers nor LLMs. “TL;DR” summaries, key takeaways, numbered lists and FAQs with concise answers are easy for both humans and machines to digest. When your content answers a likely prompt clearly and succinctly, it becomes a likely candidate for citation.

The most common obstacle I see among business leaders is time. Producing content for owned channels (your blog, LinkedIn, YouTube) and earned media (bylines and features on third-party platforms) is essential for building AEO momentum, but leaders rarely have time to take over those responsibilities on their own.

Work with your marketing leader to identify team members who can contribute insights on relevant topics, and commit to a sustainable cadence. Twice a week across your properties is a reasonable benchmark.

When I say “consistent,” I mean both in cadence and message; every piece must reinforce your positioning. If you sell the leading SaaS bookkeeping platform for local retailers, don’t publish content aimed at big-box chains. Inconsistency scrambles the signal LLMs use to understand who you are.

Through networking events, discovery calls and pitch meetings, I hear common questions, especially around emerging channels like AEO. Our client services leaders see the same thing: As trends develop, identical questions emerge across verticals and growth stages.

When your customers and prospects keep asking the same question, that’s a signal for you (or your team) to address that question publicly. Create a system for capturing these questions and feeding them directly into your content calendar. It’s the most reliable way to stay relevant and remain part of the conversation.

LLMs need an unambiguous picture of who you are and what you do. Audit your company address and contact details across your website and social profiles, update your Google Business Profile, and confirm that every online directory listing is accurate and current. This is basic hygiene, but it’s frequently overlooked.

Attributing revenue to AI search with precision remains difficult, largely because much of today’s buyer journey happens without a click to your website. We rely on a three-part framework that delivers reliable directional data:

Visibility and share of voice: Use an AI visibility tracking tool (we use Profound) to monitor how often your brand appears relative to competitors on high-priority industry prompts.

Citations and traffic: Use web analytics (we use Google Analytics) to measure traffic arriving from LLM citations.

Conversions and revenue: Track conversions in your analytics platform, including LLM referral traffic, which in my experience does account for a small share of total conversions. Supplement this with post-conversion surveys asking customers where they first discovered your brand. The data is directional rather than exact, but it provides a decent idea of impact.

None of these strategies is especially complex. What they require is resources, budget and prioritization from leadership. Especially for the B2B tech sector, where LLMs use is proliferating at all points of the purchase journey, leveraging inherent advantages in AEO is one of the most effective paths to the growth that piques investors’ interest.

My agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. #5406. How Airbnb cofounder and US Design Chief Joe Gebbia fixed a $100 million government problem for $1.5 million

For two decades, Washington tried to drag its federal retirement process out of the paper age. Contractors poured millions into the effort, but the system stayed bogged down in paperwork. Then Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia showed up with a handful of engineers and, by his account, did in six months what the government had struggled to do for 20 years.

Gebbia, now the country’s first chief design officer, said the effort dates back to 2002, when federal records were digitized under President George W. Bush. The government had tried and failed for two decades to move retirement online, he said.

“There’s about $100 million spent on contractors that produce nothing,” Gebbia told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. His team, he said, brought the retirement application process online for roughly $1.5 million.

The overhaul was an early win for Gebbia, who arrived in Washington in 2025 knowing little about federal retirement. The system ran on paper, with personnel files kept in a limestone mine in western Pennsylvania, and some retirees waited months for their full pension benefits. It also became his proof of concept for a much bigger job: fixing how Americans deal with their government online.

Gebbia never expected to work in government. He was serving on Tesla’s board and running Samara, his prefab backyard-home startup, when a text from Elon Musk in January 2025 invited him to hear about the problems federal agencies were struggling to solve. One issue in particular caught his attention: retirement.

To tackle it, he turned to a lesson from Airbnb’s early days.

When Airbnb had about 30 hosts in New York City, Y Combinator cofounder Paul Graham urged its founders to leave California and meet those hosts in person. Those conversations revealed problems the founders couldn’t see from behind their desks.

Gebbia took the same approach with federal employees, interviewing recent retirees and people preparing to leave government service about their worries, frustrations, and what they needed from a new system.

“You need to understand who you’re designing for,” Gebbia said. “You need to be close to the problem so that you can understand it from their point of view.”

He recruited a couple of former Airbnb engineers and designers, and in roughly six months the team had built an online retirement application. A memo then went out across the federal workforce requiring employees to use it, Gebbia said.

The Office of Personnel Management said in July that its Online Retirement Application handled more than 155,000 applications over the previous year and ended paper processing for more than 95% of federal retirement applications.

Going digital hasn’t eliminated the wait, however. Retirement claims took an average of 73 days to process in October, according to OPM’s monthly processing report. Digital claims moved faster, at 59 days, than paper ones, at 150.

The retirement project didn’t go unnoticed. Soon other cabinet members were calling. “Can you come fix this for our agency?” Gebbia recalled them asking.

Rather than tackle one website at a time, Gebbia pitched the White House on a broader role, which led to the creation of the National Design Studio and his appointment as chief design officer in August 2025.

The scale of that job is enormous. Gebbia said roughly 40 million people visit federal websites every day, and Americans spend an estimated 10 billion hours a year trying to get things done on them. Too often, he said, people simply give up.

“This is a design injustice,” Gebbia said. “We’re the United States of America. Our websites from our government can and should be as good as the next best website from the private sector.”

His team’s answer is America.gov, an AI-powered site launched Sept. 29 that draws on more than 29,000 government websites and lets Americans ask questions instead of hunting through pages of links. The launch had a rocky start: the chatbot contradicted some of President Trump’s public claims, then began declining “political questions,” the Associated Press reported.

Gebbia said the next phase will let users complete tasks, such as enrolling in a Medicare plan, without leaving the chat. The site is housed at the General Services Administration, a structure he sees as key to making the work outlast his tenure.

His benchmark is an Apple Store experience: not literally, he said, but as shorthand for good design and modern software.

“What if you didn’t have to go to 29,000 websites?” he said. “What if you just went to one?”

Gebbia also weighed in on the turmoil at Nvidia, where Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Tech leaders, including Elon Musk, have since backed a petition urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

Gebbia said his support for bringing Huang back comes with a caveat. “When I say reinstate, it means reinstate to then run a due diligence process effectively,” he said. That would be the right move for shareholders, the public, and AI, he argued, as long as the investigation is allowed to “play out as it should.”

“Look, Nvidia is like one of the greatest companies ever of all time,” Gebbia said. “And it got there because of founder mode, because it’s founder-led.”

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5405. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5404. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5403. The AI-Driven Agency Apocalypse Has Arrived. Here’s How to Survive It.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As AI disrupts every industry and generating new business becomes tougher, the agencies that retain their clients will be the agencies that survive.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you’ve been feeling like the future of your agency is bleak, you are not alone. Every agency owner I’ve spoken to in the past year has been experiencing the same reality. New business is shrinking as our model, which relies on providing external expertise to bring business value, is heavily under attack by AI. This is a situation we must accept as fact if we are to properly navigate it.

Even though this is the worst year on record for net-new business in the seven years of running my agency, we’ve managed to retain our existing clients and have not seen a significant drop in monthly revenues or had to let staff go. We have not grown, but we have not shrunk either. And in 2026, that’s a big win.

I believe the reason we have managed to sustain our base, and why I am ultimately not feeling as stressed as some of my peers, is that we have been doing two things right since well before the recent AI impacts affected our industry:

Let’s dive into both of those in more detail so you can audit and adjust your delivery model as needed to ensure you survive this AI-caused agency apocalypse.

Before we review the contractual changes you need to institute, it is imperative that your team is doing top-notch work. Without that, nothing you do will help you survive. You need to be the best in class in your niche to even have a chance. B-grade delivery (or worse) no longer has a fighting chance.

It’s time for an audit! Review how many clients you have on locked-in, long-term managed service or support agreements. If you are used to selling your services on a fixed-fee and fixed-term model, where you are charging the same amount per month even if you don’t lift a finger and those contracts last for many months or years, your days are numbered.

Your clients will jump ship the moment that contract ends. This means you are on the clock to make things right. Our first client is still our client to this day, over six years later, and I believe it’s because they’ve never been forced to sign a contract of that nature. None of our clients ever have.

What do we do instead? We sign indefinite monthly agreements that have a straightforward adjustment, pause or cancellation clause. If you want to see the exact terminology of that clause, you can find a sample statement of work in my free book, How Do I Find Clients?

But the spirit of that clause is quite simple: value creation. Alongside each client, we agree what value we will bring for them each month and set our monthly compensation based on that value creation. If, at any point, the client feels that there’s a need to adjust that equation, take a short pause or cancel, they have the right to do so.

This clause has ensured our clients have always felt comfortable proceeding with us and staying on those agreements well beyond any fixed term we could have locked them in for. So, if you have any contracts that are locking clients in long-term, perhaps it’s time to adjust those contracts and ensure that your clients feel you are really there to support them.

Locked-in terms are only one part of the equation. Your other, and perhaps biggest, enemy is locked-in pricing. I always tell my students: Every single time a client receives an invoice from you, they are doing a mathematical equation in their head that has two possible outcomes: “worth it” or “not worth it.”

To fight resentment, you need to make sure that every single time they do that equation, the result is unequivocally “worth it!” The way you do that is by putting yourself in the shoes of your clients before you send that invoice. If you believe that there’s any reason they might feel a reduction in the monthly invoice is warranted, you need to apply it preemptively and communicate it openly. That conversation, believe me, goes very well every time.

It sounds very simple because it is. When you send the invoice, communicate the situation clearly. Take this as an example: “You were away on vacation for a week, and then I was sick the last few days of the month, so I’ve reduced the invoice by $1,000. Hope you don’t mind.” And guess what? Of course they don’t mind! But they certainly appreciate it, and they remember it. This type of decision builds stronger relationships.

Before you dismiss this, think about how you would feel if you got the full invoice in that situation. Your thought process would sound more like: “Man, I was away for a week, and nothing got done, and then they were sick and missed the call at the end of the month, and they’re still charging me the full price. That’s absurd!” Of course, that builds resentment. Fight against it!

Some of you may feel challenged by the two ideas I’ve just shared, but I’m going to challenge you even more. The reality is, if you feel that these are difficult changes for your business or a risk to your success, what you’re actually feeling is a fear of losing control and a scarcity mindset. Both of these are feelings you need to fight and resist. Your survival is at stake.

If you’ve been feeling like the future of your agency is bleak, you are not alone. Every agency owner I’ve spoken to in the past year has been experiencing the same reality. New business is shrinking as our model, which relies on providing external expertise to bring business value, is heavily under attack by AI. This is a situation we must accept as fact if we are to properly navigate it.

Even though this is the worst year on record for net-new business in the seven years of running my agency, we’ve managed to retain our existing clients and have not seen a significant drop in monthly revenues or had to let staff go. We have not grown, but we have not shrunk either. And in 2026, that’s a big win.

I believe the reason we have managed to sustain our base, and why I am ultimately not feeling as stressed as some of my peers, is that we have been doing two things right since well before the recent AI impacts affected our industry:

#5402. Days after Microsoft and the FAA went dark, Chase and Wells Fargo customers can’t get to their money

If you had trouble logging into your bank’s website on Monday, you’re not alone. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of the day unable to log in or move money, with the bank saying the outage spread from it’s website and app to some branches and to outside apps that connect to Chase accounts. Wells Fargo, Capital One, and Zelle also had problems with their online banking platforms as customers reported trouble.

Reports started Monday morning and climbed quickly. Downdetector logged nearly 4,500 Chase reports shortly after 1:30 p.m., most of them about website logins. By 2:22 p.m., the count had passed 20,000.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told Fortune. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

Customers described a wider disruption than that statement suggests. Comments on Downdetector mentioned problems with ATMs and in-person systems as well as online banking and Zelle. Some customers opening the Chase app got a message reading, “Some services aren’t available.”

The problems also reached apps outside the bank. Plaid, which links bank accounts to payment, investing and budgeting apps, said its own network was working normally but that it was seeing connection problems with Chase accounts. Customers trying to link or refresh a Chase account through another app may have gotten errors as a result.

Downdetector listed Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Bank of America among the banks with spikes in outage reports, along with U.S. Bank, Truist and Zelle. By 2 p.m. Eastern, Bank of America saw about 2,000 with U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo seeing about 1,000 each. Wells Fargo did not confirm the outage.

It’s also affecting local branches. On the subreddit r/TalesFromYourBank, one person wrote: “I’m at work and haven’t been able to take a single client.” Three others corroborated to their bank phone systems being down.

Bank of America and U.S. Bank had not explained their customers’ problems as of Monday afternoon. Downdetector counts user complaints, not confirmed outages, and it was not clear whether the Chase and Wells Fargo failures shared a cause.

The outages follow several other technology failures in recent days. Microsoft restored service on Saturday after a global outage took down Outlook and Teams, and said a technical problem, not a cyberattack or AI, was the cause. No bank has tied Monday’s problems to the Microsoft outage.

Meanwhile, a Federal Aviation Administration comminications problem grounded flights across the country on Friday, with service not fully restored until Monday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cables at one location that caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later.

Chase has had large online outages before. In 2010, its online banking was down for more than a day, and CEO Jamie Dimon apologized publicly. The bank said then that it would refund late fees to customers who missed payments during the outage, as long as they called to ask.

#5400. He Rose From Call Center to CEO of a $61 Billion Company. Here’s How He Got Promoted Quickly.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This CEO’s path offers a lesson for anyone looking to climb the corporate ladder.

Have you ever wondered why some employees rise through the ranks quickly while others seem stuck?

Antonio Neri, the CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), had a meteoric rise at the company. He began his career at HPE as a call center employee in Amsterdam in the 1990s. He worked his way up, job after job, and became CEO of HPE in 2018. At the time of writing, HPE’s market capitalization is $61 billion, up from $31 billion at the end of 2025.

Now Neri is revealing how he got the top job. In a recent interview with Business Insider, Neri said that the key to unlocking opportunities at work begins with one principle: Carry out your promises. In other words, if you say you’re going to do something, make sure you do it. Follow through.

He added that you should be transparent about your career goals. Your manager should know where you see yourself in three to five years, and you should have an outline of the steps you need to take to get there.

“Hold the manager accountable, but most importantly, hold yourself accountable, too, because it’s a two-way street,” Neri said.

Another tip Neri offered was to ask managers and colleagues for developmental opportunities, or workplace programs, resources and experiences designed to help employees build new skills. These events could help advance your career.

Common types of development programs include online courses, coaching and one-on-one mentoring initiatives.

Neri said that getting ahead starts with finding assignments that help you grow and introduce you to more people across the company. Building relationships with colleagues and senior leaders can put you on their radar when new roles or opportunities become available.

However, visibility is only one aspect of the equation. Neri advised being deliberate about which opportunities you pursue when you are presented with multiple routes. Is the opportunity going to bring you closer to your five-year career goals?

“Don’t overdo it, but also don’t be quiet behind the scenes,” he said. “Speak when it’s necessary and then listen most of the time.”

Leaders at PwC and Chipotle say getting promoted takes more than doing your job well. They say employees can stand out by showing that they can be trusted with greater responsibility before receiving a bigger paycheck.

For example, Dallas Dolen, a PwC executive who oversees 7,500 employees, told Business Insider earlier this year that promotions start with responsiveness. Employees who answer urgent messages and help colleagues are more likely to get promoted.

“You have to be willing to, at midnight, jump on the plane,” Dolen said.

Meanwhile, Chipotle COO Jason Kidd looks for employees who support their teams, anticipate problems and offer solutions. He has weekly dinners with regional employees where he assesses how they think and if they are worthy of a promotion.

Kidd told Business Insider that Chipotle promoted 23,000 employees last year, and all of the company’s regional vice presidents were internal hires.

#5399. ‘A complete evaporation of confidence’–6 critical things Nvidia, and interim CEO Colette Kress, need to nail on the first Jensen-free earnings call

Nobody—not even Nvidia’s board—knows who will lead the new regime at Nvidia now that Jensen Huang is gone. For now, longtime CFO Colette Kress is in the driver’s seat as interim chief, and she’s been handed Atlas’s job of holding up the sky during Nvidia’s fiscal 2027 third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday.

Kress has to be the “voice of stability” while she also attempts to get the investment community reoriented to the fundamental issues at Nvidia that impact the business and valuation of the stock, said Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global.

First and foremost, analysts are still expecting a typically gargantuan quarter, with $109.3 billion in revenue, according to S&P’s Visible Alpha consensus—which is routine for Nvidia and will be mission critical for Kress. The quarterly figure is up about 92% from $57 billion last year, but the number has to be delivered in the right way. Nvidia’s gotten the world used to over performance and now the company needs to sizzle with confidence at one of the most vulnerable moments in its history.

“There’s a complete evaporation of confidence at the moment, and there’s so much uncertainty around a lot of qualitative issues,” said Otto. “The narrative needs to come back to fundamentals. How is the business doing? Is it achieving what it said it’s going to achieve?”

Nvidia’s stock is down 20% since the company’s last quarterly earnings on August 26, losing roughly half a trillion dollars in market cap, amid a broader selloff in AI and related tech stocks that have since rallied. Tuesday could be a moment for Nvidia to make its case (or at least, its first impression) as a post-Jensen business. Or it could be a bloodbath.

Here are six key things to pay attention on Nvidia’s earnings conference call.

Nvidia told investors in August to expect third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, which puts us in the range of about $105.8 billion to $110.2 billion. That outlook assumed no data center compute revenue from China.

Visible Alpha consensus sits at $109.3 billion with earnings of $2.47 per share. The data center segment—Nvidia’s crown jewel—is expected to deliver $101.8 billion of the topline total, with estimates ranging from $99.7 billion to $110.8 billion. Nvidia’s third quarter ended in late October, which means the results were not affected by Huang’s ouster. Still, any signs of weakness in the business during Huang’s final days at the helm would likely add even more uncertainty to the company’s prospects.

Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, wrote in commentary that the earnings report “will be a major referendum on the AI trade following its leadership shake-up, particularly its outlook for demand, margins and financial commitments.” Colossal results “won’t resolve the questions surrounding Jensen’s departure,” he wrote.

This is Otto’s top issue. “Do they maintain their guidance for next year?” she said. “If that’s not the case, then there’s going to be some volatility.” That’s putting it lightly.

In August, Kress said Nvidia’s preliminary expectation was for revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028 (roughly equivalent to calendar 2027), with supply remaining a bottleneck at least through the end of next year.

At the time, Huang said Nvidia had never guided financial figures a year in advance, but with demand running well above 70%, he felt confident about it. The true test will be whether that confidence outlives his ouster.

“It is the case that we’ve never forecasted or never guided to a year in advance,” said Huang at the time. “And even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%.”

That means $699.2 billion in fiscal 2028 revenue, if Huang’s confidence holds up, according to Visible Alpha’s revenue consensus. In the official announcement of Huang’s resignation last week, Nvidia’s newly installed board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company expects “operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” We’ll see.

For now, it’s Kress and the board has said it will consider internal and external candidates to replace Huang, whether that’s one person, or a sharing of power in multiple new roles. Otto called the leadership transition “essentially a regime change” and said investors want to hear what comes next.

“What changes might be made and how might this affect their existing strategy?” she said.

There are also constituencies, mainly other tech founders, who want to see Huang return to his CEO role. Portfolio managers don’t love holding stock that tanks, especially a stock that has been such a rocket ship: Nvidia shares have surged more than 1,300% since ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch.

“For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations,” Woods wrote. “Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it.”

Giuseppe Sette, cofounder and president of Reflexivity, wrote in commentary that a reinstatement “would most likely trigger a sharp, immediate relief rally,” but on a “less durable and more volatile path than the classic founder-return analogues, since this is a scandal-driven exit rather than a strategy-driven one.”

Nvidia has become an important financial backer of its customers, through direct investments and guarantees to backstop debt, with neocloud companies ranking among the biggest beneficiaries.

Total future commitments, spread over the next five fiscal years and thereafter, amount to $366 billion, with $120 billion falling in the remainder of fiscal 2027, which ends in late January. Supply and capacity makes up $279 billion of that total, up from $119 billion the quarter before.

John Belton of Gabelli Funds wrote that the initiatives are “polarizing for the stock giving ongoing concerns about ‘circular financing.’”

Recent media reports have suggested that Kress, and Huang himself prior to his exit, were rethinking Nvidia’s role as the AI industry’s “central bank” and were planning to tighten the purse strings.

Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, said the AI trade splits two ways. “Those collecting checks for building the future and those writing the checks hoping the future eventually pays them back—investors had better know which ones they own.”

Nvidia’s market success rests on the strength of its technology, so it’s crucial that it flawlessly execute the baton pass from its current Blackwell product line up to Vera Rubin, Nvidia’s newer, next generation platform.

“This is the year,” said S&P’s Otto. “We’ve seen Blackwell doing quite well, and what we would want to understand is how should we be thinking about Rubin for the rest of this year and next year.”

In August, Nvidia said Rubin was ramping into full production, with server racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle, and Nebius. In August, Kress said Rubin would account for about 20% of data center revenue in the third quarter, and that hyperscale growth would reaccelerate in the fourth quarter and into fiscal 2028 as Rubin supply spreads.

Otto said she’s got her ears pricked for “any kind of color” that shows whether expectations “are aligned correctly to the way that they’re describing the market.”

In August, Nvidia lowered the bar for gross profit margin expectations, blaming the industry-wide rise in memory prices. It guided to a third-quarter gross margin of 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, down from 75% in the second quarter.

Kress told investors at the time that margins would “bottom” in the fourth quarter at 71% to 72%, then settle at 72% to 73% as Nvidia’s own product price increases take effect. “We want to be direct about this rather than let it linger as an open question,” said Kress.

Wall Street analysts currently expect 73.1% gross margin in the third quarter and 70.2% for the fourth, and then rising to 72.2% next year, according to Visible Alpha estimates.

A negative change in margin expectations could land pretty heavily on a stock that has seen some whiplash.

All six of these issues mean analysts on Tuesday’s conference call need to ask Kress the hard questions. And analysts—whether due to fear of losing access or a myopic focus on their short term financial models—have a reputation for shying away from tough questions.

Asked whether sell-side analysts will press on the leadership ouster and espionage scandal in front of a global audience, S&P’s Otto didn’t want to predict. She also didn’t want to guess whether Kress would be joined by new Chair Harvey Jones on the call to have a second hand on deck to field questions.

“It could go in a million different directions,” Otto said. “It’s probably more effective to ask Kalshi.”

Her advice for anyone listening: “Buckle up. I think it’s going to be an interesting call.”

Nvidia is scheduled to report at 1:20 p.m. PT on Tuesday, with the call slated for 2 p.m. PT.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Pepsi’s dirty soda line started as a pop-up. Now it’s testing new syrups, a delivery kitchen and stores of its own.

If you find yourself walking around the Formula 1 track in Las Vegas this week, you’re likely to spot a mirror-chrome Airstream gleaming under the desert sun. Like an oasis, it’s serving Instagram-worthy drinks you won’t find anywhere else.

The drinks are called DRIPS by Pepsi, and it’s the company’s answer to the dirty soda craze: classic sodas loaded with syrups, cold foam and popping boba. The trailer is how PepsiCo tests and markets them.

Even though PepsiCo is a nearly a $100 billion company, the DRIPS team runs like a startup.

“We actually work as almost an intrapreneur within the company,” says Scott Finlow, chief marketing officer of PepsiCo Away From Home.

Here’s how it built a dirty soda brand from scratch, and what it’s learned along the way.

Pepsi has been courting young drinkers for decades. In 1963, it invited them to “Come alive! You’re in the Pepsi Generation.” That pitch later became “The Choice of a New Generation.” DRIPS is a continuation of that playbook.

This time, PepsiCo took its cue from Gen Z, who wanted drinks they could personalize with “a little bit of flair, a little bit of fun,” Finlow says. As Gen Z sees it, why should the root beer float be the only soda with personality?

That craving fueled the rise of dirty soda, popularized by Swig, a Utah drive-thru chain that coined the term. So PepsiCo built its own version. It developed a menu and a brand, then took DRIPS on the road in a converted Airstream. DRIPS has since popped up at festivals like Austin City Limits and landed on menus at Saucy, KFC’s chicken-tender chain, and Vail Resorts.

PepsiCo’s chefs are “the magicians behind these drinks,” Finlow says. They start with a popular flavor trend, pair it with a cultural moment and build the drink on a PepsiCo brand, adding texture like boba or layers of cold foam.

For example, bananas are big this season (who knew?). For F1, the team created a banana float made with Mug root beer. “Very rapidly, we can take a flavor trend and then a big moment in culture like F1,” Finlow says, “and we can then get in the kitchen with those chefs.”

The menu spans what the team calls “vibe states,” from indulgent to refreshing. Buzzy brands like poppi and Celsius are now in the mix. Energy in particular is becoming “an increasingly important base for crafted drinks as Gen Z shifts toward cold caffeinated drinks,” Finlow says.

Every recipe is also designed for the restaurants that serve DRIPS, down to the hand movements and the time it takes to make each drink. PepsiCo supplies operators with recipe kits, ingredients, marketing and help adding the drinks to their point-of-sale systems.

Now PepsiCo is packaging what it has learned for operators. Just today, it launched DRIPS by Pepsi Signature Mixes, its first standalone syrups, built on data from DRIPS pop-ups and customer feedback. Each of the five no-added-sugar syrups has several flavors in one pump, from Island Escape (mango, pineapple and coconut) to Mocha Mood (chocolate, caramel and warm spice). A new Lipton Green Tea concentrate mixes with still or sparkling water, so restaurants can make refreshers without new equipment

PepsiCo is also exploring standalone DRIPS stores in Austin and New York City. Finlow calls them “lab stores,” where the team can test prices, flavors and how fast staff can make each drink. Meanwhile, PepsiCo is piloting a DRIPS test kitchen in Manhattan that delivers six flavors.

Like any startup, the team is learning as they go and pivoting accordingly. Making sure the drinks work in busy restaurant kitchens is “the single biggest ongoing challenge,” Finlow says. There’s also pressure to grow fast, what he calls “a healthy tension” familiar to any founder going from early stage to scale.

So far, DRIPS is more of a pour. Last month at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, there was a line of mostly Gen Zers waiting to get their dulche de leche and gochujang on. The trailer did close to $10,000 a day in sales and served up to 130 drinks an hour at peak, Finlow says. The top seller was a Pepsi mixed with peach, lime and lychee jelly called Pole Position.

If you find yourself walking around the Formula 1 track in Las Vegas this week, you’re likely to spot a mirror-chrome Airstream gleaming under the desert sun. Like an oasis, it’s serving Instagram-worthy drinks you won’t find anywhere else.

The drinks are called DRIPS by Pepsi, and it’s the company’s answer to the dirty soda craze: classic sodas loaded with syrups, cold foam and popping boba. The trailer is how PepsiCo tests and markets them.

#5397. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

#5396. The 1 Skill AI Will Never Master — No Matter How Advanced It Gets

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As AI does more, we need to know its limits.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Everywhere we look, we’re confronted with new things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

Despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.

AI assistants like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini have enormous strengths when it comes to communicating more persuasively.

Their ability to capture, analyze and synthesize massive amounts of information is unparalleled. AI can quickly provide data on just about any subject. More than that, it can sort through the data, looking for trends and differences among viewpoints. AI’s ability to research exceeds the skills not just of interns, but of entry-level employees like Research Assistants and consultants, and even mid-level knowledge workers. Even teams of knowledge workers. That’s why many of these positions are being partially or entirely automated across many sectors, including at companies like McKinsey.

AI doesn’t stop at simply collecting information. It can make arguments for and against positions, too. It will structure those arguments logically and support them with facts. It can identify and respond to counterarguments to your position.

It will even make arguments against using AI itself. I asked ChatGPT if AI should be eliminated, and it quickly answered, “Probably not.” Then it responded with many paragraphs nuancing the answer. Gemini responded, “Eliminating artificial intelligence entirely would mean losing transformative advancements.”

AI can frame arguments for diverse audiences. I asked ChatGPT how it would frame advocating for zoning reform to progressives and conservatives (housing policy is one of my areas of expertise). It identified seven issues like equity and property rights and suggested thoughtful ways to navigate them with both groups.

AI can even craft stories. I asked it for compelling stories to advance housing reform, and it offered 10. The first was about “The young couple who can afford the mortgage — but can’t afford the house.” Good place to start.

So, what’s missing from AI’s approach to persuasion? There are three areas where AI will continue to fall short.

First, getting what we want begins by adopting what I call “the persuader’s mindset”: It’s about them, not you. Which means you have to put them first. Only when you truly understand your counterpart, put their needs front and center, and show them how you can meet them (while also meeting yours), will they be eager to work with you not once but repeatedly.

Adopting this mindset requires you to be fully in tune with your audience. AI can offer general understandings of an audience. It cannot, however, do a few critical things. It cannot relate to someone interpersonally since, well, it’s not a person. Groups are comprised of individuals with nuanced views. Humans can poke, probe, dig and explore in ways AI can’t — with emotional intelligence.

Second, AI’s approach to persuasion is, unsurprisingly, logic-first. This is, in many ways, a virtue: AI can quickly bring an abundance of data to bear on any issue.

The trouble with this logic-first approach is that it’s not in accordance with how our brains work. All the neuroscience and all the psychology show that humans are wired to feel first, then reason. This means that you need to start with feelings before turning to logic.

Indeed, AI recognizes this limitation. When I asked Gemini what areas it would struggle with in persuading, it replied: “Gemini faces distinct limitations in persuasion whenever success relies entirely on deeply human emotional intelligence, physical presence or lived experience.” ChatGPT emphasized that it cannot experience any emotions it’d be responding to.

AI’s logic-first approach will fall flat if it isn’t coupled with sufficient emotional intelligence. That’s where only humans can come in.

Third, AI can’t bring the human elements to interacting with others.

Humans listen not just to what others say, but how they say something. Were they excited or anxious? We watch for body language. She grimaced when I said that — uh oh! Maybe I shouldn’t have said it.

Humans can bring dynamism to how they share their ideas. They can be charismatic, warm and exciting. AI? Not so much.

Ultimately, the best way to leverage AI for all of your persuasive endeavors is to lean on its strengths — research, data, logic, arguments and the like — and then build a human-centered, emotionally intelligent edifice on top of it.

Everywhere we look, we’re confronted with new things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

Despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.
